Annex 2, Section 7.1 lets people enroll themselves by phone, including signing up “friends, family and colleagues.” That produces a “partially verified” National Identification Number (NIN) good for opening bank accounts and registering SIM cards before any fingerprints are taken. The committee called it an open door to “systemic identity fraud.”

* Paying twice for storage. The $19.82 million data center, flagged by LITCON, duplicates capacity Liberia already has.

A chapter on data

Protection that appeared in a January 2026 draft was deleted before the agreement was signed, the committee said. So were chapters on anti-corruption and state auditing.

Signing away the registry’s job

The third ground goes to what the NIR exists to do. Article 7.1 of the agreement gives OeSD the exclusive right to assign NINs. It also makes OeSD the only provider of ID cards and identity checks. Under Sections 3.1, 3.2(d) and 7.3 of the NIR Act of 2011, those powers belong to the NIR alone. The committee cited the Supreme Court’s Feb. 12, 2026 ruling in LAC v. LRA that a concession cannot override a statute.

Other clauses reached further:

A toll on daily life

Articles 7.3 and 12.1 would make paid OeSD verification mandatory for nearly every public and private service, from banking and SIM cards to permits and court business. The committee said that goes beyond the NIR Act, and that Executive Order 147 cannot legally expand it.

* Skipping the Legislature. Article 5.3 lets the two parties waive conditions precedent by mutual agreement. One of those conditions is legislative ratification. Lawmakers called the clause “ultra vires and unacceptable.”

* Liberia in a London courtroom. Article 31 sends disputes to UNCITRAL arbitration in London and waives Liberia’s sovereign immunity from enforcement. That would expose Liberian state assets abroad.

* Other agencies’ work. Appendix 4 lists work and residence permits among the concession’s requirements. Those belong to the Ministry of Labour and the Liberia Immigration Service.

* Few jobs for Liberians. The deal sets no measurable targets for Liberians in senior management or in the workforce over its 10-year life. It does not require any role for Liberian-owned IT firms.

* ⁠On money, the committee said it rebuilt the financial model from OeSD’s own Annex 5 tables. It found a lopsided structure that pushes costs and risks onto the Republic while guaranteeing the operator’s returns.

The document itself was a mess. The agreement was signed April 30, 2026, but Annexes 2 and 4 are dated May 4 and Annex 1 is dated May 5. The whole fee schedule and revenue split sit in those annexes. That leaves “no legal certainty that the economic terms were agreed upon at signing,” the committee said.

The text sent to lawmakers also contained duplicated pages, missing clauses from Article 3 and Article 12.2, broken cross-references and an unsigned template memorandum for Ecobank. It even got the NIR director’s name wrong, calling Andrew Peters “Peter Andrews.”

Back to the drawing board

The report was signed by members of both committees. They are led by Rep. Foday E. Fahnbulleh, chairman of Investment and Concessions, and Rep. P. Mike Jurry, chairman of Ways, Means, Finance and Budget. It now goes to the full House, which the committee urged to “reject and decline ratification” of the agreement “in its entirety.”

The committee also wants the House to give the Executive three directives:

1. Enforce the law. Restore the NIR’s statutory role as a service bureau, overseen by its Board of Registrars and the General Auditing Commission.

2. Bid it out. Follow the PPCC’s July 2025 order and the 2026 regulations. That means a valid Certificate of Concession, a value-for-money assessment, and weighing upgrades to the existing biometric system against competing bids.

3. Protect the data. Make any future vendor comply with the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2026, the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the mandates of the NEC, the Liberia Revenue Authority, the Liberia Immigration Service and the Ministry of Health.

FrontPageAfrica sent detailed questions to NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters about the committee’s findings. He had not responded by press time.

None of that helps Rick Scott, or the traveler from Foya. ID card issuance has been suspended since June 2025. New Narratives reported that the program also stalled over about $1.7 million the government owed Techno Brain. Fewer than 15 percent of the population holds an official ID card, according to Biometric Update.

The question lawmakers are now asking is not whether Liberia needs a modern ID system. It is who decided that one Austrian company, contracting through a 35,000-euro Vienna entity, should build it, and why nobody else was allowed to try.

World.title: Liberia: Attorney General Summoned Over IB Atlantic IV Release Order; Crew Still Held Past Deadline
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Justice Ministry’s failure to obey a court order to release the vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has turned into a direct confrontation with the judiciary.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Criminal Court “A” has summoned Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo to answer allegations of contempt.



Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon issued a writ of summons ordering Lamin-Blamo to appear before the court at the Temple of Justice on Friday, Nov. 20, at 9 a.m. She must show cause why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the court’s order to release the ship and its crew.

As of Thursday, when the writ was issued, the vessel and all seven crew members were still in state custody. The court’s deadline had passed at 4 p.m. Wednesday.

The summons puts the country’s chief legal officer before a judge to account for the government’s failure to obey a court order. It comes in a case that has dragged on for nearly three months without a full public explanation of what the vessel was doing or the legal grounds for holding it.

‘Show cause’



The writ, dated Nov. 19 and issued under the authority of the First Judicial Circuit, Montserrado County, is explicit. It orders the attorney general to explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the release order.

Assistant Clerk of Court Gideon A. Eshun issued the summons to Montserrado County Sheriff H. C. Sulonich or his deputy for service. The court told the sheriff to report back to the clerk’s office on how the summons was served.

The writ is not a finding of contempt. But it is a serious step. It requires the government’s top lawyer to answer personally for her ministry’s failure to comply.

It also raises a larger question: Can the government keep people and property in custody after a court has ordered their release, without going back to the court for permission?

Deadline passes, crew stays put

Judge Banwon had ordered the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its crew after their lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition challenging their detention. The ministry was given until 4 p.m. Wednesday to comply.

It did not. At about 5 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPageAfrica observed that the order had not been carried out. Lawyers for the seven crew members confirmed their clients were still being held.

By Thursday, nothing had changed. That left the court to take the extra step of summoning the attorney general.

Reached late Wednesday and asked why the release had not happened, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah gave no explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPageAfrica.

His answer left the central question unaddressed: On what legal basis is the government still holding the ship and its crew after the court’s deadline expired?

Ministry ‘struggling’ for an explanation

Sources at the Justice Ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, told FrontPageAfrica earlier that the ministry was struggling to come up with an explanation for the continued detention.

Part of the difficulty, the sources said, was the government’s own earlier public statements that it was investigating the vessel’s movements and how it came to be intercepted. No findings from that investigation have been made public. That left officials hard-pressed to justify holding the ship and crew in the face of a court order.

The sources said the ministry was considering releasing the vessel and crew early Thursday to comply with the order. That did not happen.

Lamin-Blamo is now expected to explain in court why the order was not obeyed on time, and to present whatever legal justification the government has for keeping the ship and crew in custody.

The ship that slipped away

The IB Atlantic IV is a 41-year-old, Comoros-flagged general cargo ship. It first drew attention this summer when it lingered off York Island in Tewor District, Grand Cape Mount County, alarming residents and fishermen.

Before that, the ship had already tried to get into Liberia. On July 13, a Liberian businessman, Kuiah, wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) on behalf of a company called Madris Group of Companies Inc. He asked for docking rights and a dive team at the Freeport of Monrovia, describing the vessel as disabled and “in distress.” FrontPageAfrica later reported that Kuiah, a former deputy at Roberts International Airport who was dismissed, was the company’s sole owner. LiMA turned the request down. The ship was still in Sierra Leonean waters at the time and had not docked anywhere, yet it was already seeking a Liberian berth.

Once the vessel drifted onto the Liberian side of the maritime border, the order came to search and seize it. It kept moving. On Aug. 4, then-Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were in pursuit. He told FrontPageAfrica that the Coast Guard’s boats were not equipped to chase a ship far out to sea. With Nigerian help, the military tracked it off Rivercess County but could not board it.

Investigators also looked into reports that a smaller vessel had approached the IB Atlantic IV and tried to throw something aboard. The government said a Liberian fishing vessel had gone out to meet the ship, and the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority opened an inquiry.

The ship was finally seized by Ivorian authorities on Aug. 9. On Aug. 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah confirmed the arrest and said Liberia was working with Côte d’Ivoire to bring it back. It returned under Liberian Coast Guard command on Aug. 27.

The chase unfolded amid a widening national drug-trafficking scandal, and speculation about contraband aboard ran high. But authorities have never publicly established that any narcotics were found on the vessel.

Its return was supposed to give the government a chance to investigate and give the public a full account. Instead, the ship and crew stayed in custody for nearly three months with no findings released. That drove the vessel’s management and crew to court.

Friday’s test

For the seven crew members, the case has meant months of uncertainty, held aboard a ship whose presence in Liberian waters is still unexplained.

The government is now being asked to answer for more than the vessel. It must also explain why it kept the ship and its crew in custody after a judge ordered them freed.

That answer is due Friday at 9 a.m., when Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court “A” at the Temple of Justice.

World.title: Who Tried to Sell Liberia’s Identity?
World.content:
The $54.7 million national ID deal ignored the procurement regulator, shut out every competitor and stripped away the safeguards protecting Liberians’ biometric data. Rejecting it is not enough. The President must find out who tried to slip it past him, and hold them to account

A NATION’S IDENTITY is not a commodity. It is the record that says who belongs, who can vote, who can open a bank account, who can cross a border and come home. The National Identification Registry was created to keep that record in Liberian hands, under Liberian law.

THAT IS WHY the House joint committee’s report on the $54.7 million concession with OeSD International should alarm every Liberian. The committee found more than 40 defects in the agreement. Several, it said, were violations of the law committed before the deal was even signed. No vote of the Legislature can cure them.



STRIP AWAY THE technical language and the story is simple. In May 2025, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission refused a request to hand the contract to OeSD without competition. Then, on May 30, the NIR signed a contract with OeSD anyway. In July 2025, the PPCC ordered open international bidding and a formal concession plan. That order, the committee says, “was never followed.”

RIVAL FIRMS, INCLUDING Liberian ones, came forward. They were ignored. No Certificate of Concession was obtained, though the regulations say a concession without one “shall be void.” No summary of terms was published. No county consultations were held. Liberian officials even made their due-diligence trip to Austria at OeSD’s expense, vetting a company that was paying their way.

WHAT EMERGED WAS a contract that would have handed a private company the exclusive power to assign every Liberian’s national ID number. It would have made paid verification mandatory for banking, SIM cards, permits and the courts. It would have sent disputes to London and waived the Republic’s immunity over its assets abroad. It would have charged nearly $20 million for a data center Liberia does not need, when LIBTELCO already has one. And it would have done all this without requiring that Liberians’ fingerprints and faces be stored in Liberia, or that the government hold the keys to them.

THE CONTRACT EVEN contained a clause letting the parties waive legislative ratification. Chapters on data protection, anti-corruption and state auditing that appeared in a January 2026 draft were gone by the time it was signed.



THIS WAS NOT carelessness. Mistakes do not repeat themselves at every step, each time in the same direction. A process that ignores the regulator twice, shuts out every competitor and quietly deletes the safeguards is a process designed to avoid scrutiny.

PRESIDENT JOSEPH NYUMA Boakai approved this agreement and sent it to the Legislature in July. Sources tell this newspaper he was badly misled by those who brought it to him. We are prepared to believe that. A President cannot read every annex. He must rely on the people around him to tell him the truth.

BUT IF THE President was misled, then someone misled him. And the people who did so are still in place.

THE HOUSE SHOULD adopt the committee’s report and reject the deal in full. That is only the first step. Killing a bad contract does nothing to fix the process that produced it, or to stop the same people from trying again under a new name.

WE THEREFORE CALL on the President to act on three fronts.

FIRST, ORDER AN independent review of how this concession was put together. It should establish who decided to bypass the PPCC, who signed the May 2025 contract, who approved the OeSD-funded trip to Austria and who removed the safeguards from the January draft. The General Auditing Commission and the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission are equipped to do this work, and the findings should be made public.

SECOND, HOLD ACCOUNTABLE those responsible. Officials who knowingly ignored a binding order of the procurement regulator, or who put a deal before the President without telling him it had been rejected, should be suspended while the review runs. Where the review finds wrongdoing, they should be dismissed and, if the law was broken, prosecuted. A government that came to power promising to rescue Liberia from impunity cannot let this pass with a quiet withdrawal.

THIRD, START OVER, the right way. That means open international bidding, as the PPCC ordered more than a year ago. It means a real value-for-money test that weighs upgrading the systems Liberia already owns. It means fair room for Liberian technology firms. And it means firm guarantees, written into the contract, that Liberians’ biometric data stays in Liberia under Liberian control.

THE REGISTRY’S LEADERSHIP owes the public answers too. This newspaper has put detailed questions to the NIR. We are still waiting.

MEANWHILE, ID CARD issuance has been suspended since June 2025. Liberians still need the card to bank, register a SIM card and get basic services. They have waited long enough for a working system. They should not also be asked to pay for one built to dodge the rules.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE has done its part. Now it is the President’s turn. He should find out who tried to slip this deal past him, and past the Liberian people, and make sure it never happens again

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Hails Diaspora Medical Mission, Welcomes 100-Surgery Annual Cardiac Care Plan
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has praised Hands International for its humanitarian medical intervention in Liberia, describing the organization’s contribution as a significant boost to the country’s healthcare delivery system.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The President made the remarks Wednesday, November 18, during an appreciation and farewell ceremony at the Executive Mansion, marking the conclusion of a seven-day free international medical and surgical mission conducted at the 14 Military Hospital.



The mission, which brought together more than 60 visiting medical professionals, provided free consultations, specialized treatments, and surgical interventions to thousands of Liberians.

According to the 14 Military Hospital, the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures without recording a single death, while providing services to over 1,800 patients and conducting more than 4,000 medical encounters.

President Boakai particularly commended members of the delegation, many of whom he described as “retired but not tired,” for returning to Liberia to use their professional expertise in service to humanity.

He also welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.



The President described the decision to return to Liberia and offer specialized medical services as more than an ordinary humanitarian intervention, saying it demonstrated genuine love and concern for fellow human beings.

“One thing you’re going to do when you leave here is that this community and the people you have met will now live in your mind,” President Boakai told the delegation.

He also renewed his appeal to Liberians in the diaspora to regard the country not simply as a place to visit occasionally but as their home, where they can invest their time, skills, and resources to support national development.

Cardiac Care Initiative

Meanwhile, Dr. Reynold S. Agard, President of Hands International and head of the visiting delegation, announced that the organization intends to work with local health authorities and cardiology specialists to establish a sustainable cardiac care program.

Dr. Agard said the decision followed concerning findings during the medical mission, which revealed cases of dangerously high blood pressure, untreated heart conditions, and other potentially life-threatening cardiovascular diseases.

He said the organization intends to strengthen Liberia’s local capacity to diagnose and treat heart conditions, particularly among children, drawing on lessons from its previous interventions in Nigeria.

The proposed target of 100 children’s heart surgeries annually could provide critical intervention for families facing limited access to specialized cardiac treatment.

However, the initiative would require sustained collaboration with local medical institutions, specialists, and health authorities to build the capacity needed to deliver the services.

Government Commends Intervention

Earlier, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel A. Stevquoah welcomed the delegation to the Executive Mansion and expressed the government’s appreciation for its contribution to Liberia’s healthcare sector.

“Liberia welcomes you and we thank you for your service to the Liberian people,” Stevquoah said.

President Boakai welcomed the organization’s plans to establish a sustainable cardiac care program in Liberia, with a target of performing 100 heart surgeries for children annually.

He described the mission’s contribution as impactful and deserving of national appreciation.

In special remarks, Defense Minister Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh also expressed gratitude to the delegation, noting that the mission responded to President Boakai’s call for Liberians in the diaspora to return home and contribute their expertise to national development.

“Liberia has strengthened its defense in health, and the military is a force for good,” Tweh said.

He expressed pride that the 14 Military Hospital was selected to host the medical mission, which provided what he described as critically needed healthcare services.

Diaspora Connection

Mrs. Christine Neyor, who helped facilitate the mission through her longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard, her primary care physician, described the intervention as one of the largest medical missions ever undertaken in Liberia.

She said she and her husband, Hon. Christopher Neyor, leveraged their longstanding relationship with Dr. Agard to bring the team to Liberia and provide free medical services to residents.

Also speaking, Erasmus T. Williams, Head of the Diaspora Affairs Office at the Executive Mansion, praised Hands International for its contribution and expressed hope that the organization would return to Liberia in the near future.

Mission’s Impact

Providing an overview of the mission’s activities, Captain Dr. Augustine Kollie of the 14 Military Hospital said the visiting team operated in Liberia from November 8 to 14, 2026.

He reported that the team performed more than 46 surgical procedures with zero mortality, served over 1,800 patients, and recorded more than 4,000 medical encounters.

Hands International is a nonprofit humanitarian organization that provides healthcare assistance to underserved communities and promotes sustainable community transformation through partnerships and international collaboration.

As a symbolic gesture of appreciation, President Boakai presented Liberian seal lapel pins to members of the visiting delegation. Dr. Agard was also presented with traditional Liberian attire in recognition of his leadership and the organization’s humanitarian contribution.

World.title: Boakai Seeks Specialized Family Courts Across Liberia to Protect Children, Resolve Domestic Disputes
World.content:
The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has submitted a proposed legislation seeking to establish specialized Family Courts across Liberia to strengthen the protection of children and improve the resolution of family-related disputes.

By Obediah Johnson

The bill, titled the Family Court Act of Liberia, was submitted to the Liberian Senate on Thursday, November 19.



The proposed legislation also seeks to amend relevant provisions of the Judiciary Law, the Civil Procedure Law, and the Domestic Relations Law, while providing for the establishment of a specialized Family Court in each county of the Republic.

In a letter accompanying the submission, President Boakai said the proposed Act comprehensively outlines the court’s jurisdiction, powers, structure, and other related matters.

He said the legislation is intended to improve judicial efficiency by creating a specialized forum to handle civil and quasi-criminal family matters.

According to the President, establishing the courts would help reduce case backlogs in Circuit and Magisterial Courts while ensuring the timely adjudication of disputes.



The proposed law also places emphasis on child protection and family welfare, with the President highlighting the need to prioritize the best interests of children as provided under the Children’s Law of 2011.

It would establish legal mechanisms for handling matters involving child custody, guardianship, adoption, child protection, and rehabilitation.

Beyond judicial efficiency, President Boakai said the proposed legislation would promote social stability by addressing family disputes that have historically undermined community cohesion.

He noted that the specialized courts would provide holistic interventions integrating legal, social, and psychological support to help resolve family conflicts and promote unity and stability.

“The Act ensures constitutional compliance, aligning with Article 65 of the Constitution, which vests the Judiciary with authority to interpret laws and resolve disputes, while granting the Legislature the power to establish specialized courts,” the President stated.

Boakai described the proposed Family Court as a significant step toward modernizing Liberia’s judicial system, emphasizing that disputes affecting children and families require a more sensitive, efficient, and fair approach.

He said the establishment of the courts would strengthen the rule of law and advance social justice throughout the country.

“I respectfully request the Legislature to give due consideration to this Act and enact it into law in the interest of the Liberian people,” President Boakai stated.

Meanwhile, the proposed legislation has been forwarded to the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petition for legislative scrutiny.

World.title: Tanzania’s smart ID puts Zambia’s ageing NRC under the spotlight
World.content:
By Aristide Bance

Tanzania has launched a multi-purpose national ID with travel ambitions. Zambians who have long called for a modern NRC are asking why they are still waiting.

LUSAKA / DAR ES SALAAM: Tanzania’s launch of an upgraded national identity card has revived a question that I as a Zambian has been asking for years: why is the country’s own National Registration Card, the green NRC, still so far behind?

Tanzania’s government introduced the upgraded card to integrate citizens’ personal records,simplify access to public and private services, and facilitate cross-border travel to selected countries. Prime Minister Dr Mwigulu Nchemba received the first card at the official unveiling in Kibaha on 18 November 2026.

What Tanzania has launched

More information on one card. The National Identification Authority (NIDA) says the new card has eight information sections, up from four on the previous version. Those sections are meant to hold birth certificate details, health insurance information, TIN, blood group and passport-related information for countries with ID-travel agreements with Tanzania. Because the

card doubles the available space, more institutions can link their services to the national identification system.

A more durable card. Earlier versions had personal details printed on the surface, where they could fade over time. The new card uses laser engraving to embed details within its layers,reducing the risk of fading.A digital wallet. Alongside the physical card, a NIDA Wallet is expected to give citizens digital access to their identity details on their phones. Health insurance is already linked to national ID numbers, and NIDA is in talks with tax authorities about connecting TINs so citizens can use their ID numbers for tax services.

More capacity behind the card. The launch also included a new card-production system and 10 vehicles for NIDA registration officers, and a second phase of the digital ID project is planned that would add iris and facial recognition. The minister said the government is strengthening its ICT systems to speed up the production and processing of identity records, and that personal data must be handled in line with the Personal Data Protection Act, 2022.



A careful transition

One notable feature of the rollout is that it does not leave existing cardholders behind. The upgraded cards will be issued to people registering from now on, and the new version does not invalidate existing national identity cards. Existing holders may be told how to switch when their cards wear out, in the same way as with passports.

There is also a caution on the figures. Reports indicate that the 23.7 million figure quoted at the launch refers to ID numbers rather than physical cards, so the number of people holding a physical card may be lower than the headline suggests.The travel promise, and its limits.The most eye-catching claim is that the card could replace the passport on some journeys.

NIDA’s director general said Tanzania has agreed with some countries, including Kenya and Uganda, that Tanzanians will travel using the NIDA card. He said NIDA is working with immigration authorities to operationalise the arrangement, which would let eligible citizens travel to participating countries without necessarily carrying passports.

The arrangement is not yet in effect. Until it is formally announced, travellers should keep carrying passports at border posts such as Namanga and Mutukula. Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda have long allowed their citizens to cross between them using national IDs, and Tanzania has so far stood outside that arrangement, so joining it would be a genuine step for East African

integration.

Zambia’s long wait

For Zambians, none of this is a new conversation. A 2017 Lusaka Times opinion piece by myself called the NRC an embarrassment that should be phased out, said it lacks proper security features, and pointed out that Zambians need a second card when voting, while other countries combine voter information with their smart ID cards. The piece argued that digitising the NRC

would make people think twice about stealing other people’s identities.I have been among the readers who has returned to the issue. In a comment under that article, I argued that the outdated NRC costs Zambians even more money. In 2019, after the government said it was digitalising NRC issuance, I commented that Zambians had been waiting for new NRCs for a very long time and said he doubted they would arrive.

Problems that remain

The practical limits of the current card are visible today:

Issuance is tied to Zambia. The NRC can only be applied for and obtained in Zambia, in

person, because the law provides for issuance only within the country. That is a hurdle

for Zambians living abroad who need to replace or obtain a card.

being issued by hand, and said the quality of the cards had made it hard for some people,especially farmers, to do business. Opposition leader Ackim Antony Njobvu warned that defective or inaccurate NRCs could stop citizens from registering to vote or casting their ballots.

Opposition leader Ackim Antony Njobvu warned that defective or inaccurate NRCs could stop citizens from registering to vote or casting their ballots. Separate documents. As the 2017 commentary noted, the NRC remains a stand-alone

card that does not carry the linked services Tanzania’s card is built around (Source:

zambianobserver.com).

Zambia’s own plan

There are signs that change is coming. The Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security says government will roll out a single identification card, and has already enrolled more than one million citizens on the Integrated National Registration Information System. The ministry’s spokesperson said the single ID would replace multiple forms of identification, including the NRC and passports. The project builds on Zambia’s civil registration modernisation under that digital platform, which is designed to capture and manage identity data more efficiently.

What Zambia can learn from Tanzania

Tanzania’s rollout offers several practical lessons for Lusaka:

1. Design around services, not only identification. Tanzania’s card is built to link health insurance, tax and other services, and NIDA describes the aim as moving from a basic identification service to integrated digital identity infrastructure.

2. Protect existing cardholders. Keeping old cards valid during the transition avoids the disruption and cost of a forced, one-off replacement.

3. Put data protection first. Tanzania has tied the rollout to its Personal Data Protection Act, a safeguard that matters more as cards hold more linked records.

4. Be honest about what is not ready. Tanzania’s travel feature is still being operationalised, and officials are not yet telling travellers to leave their passports at home.

Zambia’s single-ID project will face the same test between announcement and delivery.

What to watch

Whether Zambia publishes a firm timeline and design for the single ID, including what happens to existing NRCs.

How the card will handle voter identification, which Zambians have long wanted to see merged with national identification.

Whether NRC issuance rules, including the in-person requirement, will change for Zambians abroad.

Whether Tanzania’s ID-travel arrangements with Kenya and Uganda are formally announced, which would set a regional benchmark.

The comparison is not entirely fair to Zambia, which has begun enrolling citizens in a new registration system. But for readers like myself, who has waited since at least 2017 for the NRC to change, the lesson from Tanzania is that a modern ID is possible. The question now is whether Zambia delivers one soon.

World.title: Useful Idiots Demand an Apology from Ian Khama
World.content:
By Dr. Field C. Ruwe

CLARIFICATION

To avoid misunderstanding, it is important to clarify what “Useful Idiots” means. In general,calling someone an “idiot” is simply a generic insult. By contrast, the political expression “useful idiot” is commonly used in political commentary to describe a gullible person whom a narcissist, autocrat, or dictator recruits or manipulates into carrying out his dirty work

without fully understanding the consequences of his actions.

YOU MUST APOLOGIZE!

In social and interpersonal dynamics, “useful idiots” are allies, friends, acquaintances, or admirers of a public figure or manipulative person who rush to defend that person when criticized or attacked. Driven by emotional loyalty and group identity rather than objective truth, they struggle to consider criticism of their colleague or idol. To them, any criticism of

that person feels like a personal attack.

“You must apologize!” is a common tactic used by useful idiots to divert attention. In psychology, this approach is often associated with DARVO (Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender). By insistently demanding that the alleged “offender” apologize first, a useful idiot portrays the person he supports as the victim and pressures the critic to apologize

or comply. Most useful idiots lack the full context: they see only the critic, not the provocateur who instigated the impasse.

AFRICA’S NEWEST DICTATOR

Lately, useful idiots have emerged, calling on former Botswana President Ian Khama to apologize for describing Hichilema as “Africa’s Newest Dictator”—a label Khama explicitly tied to allegations of human rights abuses and democratic backsliding. Addressing Botswana’s House of Chiefs, Khama asked why the Botswana government had sent a representative to Hichilema’s inauguration. He accused Hichilema of restricting democratic space, suppressing political opponents, and violating human rights.

As I have stated previously, human rights violations began as soon as Hichilema took office.Despite pledging to uphold the rule of law and protect fundamental freedoms, he began targeting political opponents. The U.S. State Department reported that Zambia continued to face systemic human rights challenges during Hichilema’s first full year in office.In its 2025 and 2026 World Reports, Human Rights Watch described an increase in authoritarian tendencies, citing the use of the Public Order Act, criminal defamation laws,and the Cyber Security and Cyber Crimes Acts to harass and detain journalists, critics, and opposition figures. These developments prompted UN human rights chief Volker Türk to express concern.Hichilema did not comply. By the time of the general election, the political climate had deteriorated significantly. The election ended with a joint police and military crackdown on opposition presidential candidates and eleven supporters, resulting in loss of life. This is what prompted Khama to call Hichilema “Africa’s newest dictator.” When useful idiots urged him to retract his statement, he stood by his words.

FACTS DON’T LIE

People who speak factually often decline to apologize because they prioritize objective truth and regard an apology as an admission of guilt. They believe they can substantiate their claims with evidence; therefore, if a statement is objectively accurate, saying “I’m sorry” may compromise their integrity and lend credibility to an inaccurate account of events. That

is Khama’s position, and it is one I stand for.

When profiling, critiquing, or featuring a president, politician, public figure, or military figure, I rely on verifiable facts, prioritize primary and authoritative sources, and follow rigorous editorial and legal standards. In the case of Hichilema, I have cited verifiable facts to highlight warning signs about the state of democracy during his presidency.

Since taking office, Hichilema has repeatedly exhibited behavior and used tactics often associated with dictators seeking to consolidate power. After five years of disastrous rule,Hichilema has fostered a godlike or messianic persona, portraying himself as the only one capable of solving the nation’s problems and casting Zambian politics as an “us versus them”

struggle. For this reason, I have not hesitated to describe him as a dictator in the making.

STOP HICHILEMA AND HIS USEFUL IDIOTS

Dictators rarely seize or hold power entirely on their own: they rely heavily on a network of useful idiots. Currently, useful idiots are helping Hichilema test institutional boundaries to determine the limits of executive impunity. Observing widespread public apathy, useful idiots are actively minimizing and reframing Hichilema’s anti-democratic measures as routine

governance. In doing so, they are systematically shifting the window and normalizing democratic backsliding within Zambian political culture. They have to be stopped.On November 25, 2026, Zambians across all sectors of society must unite in peaceful civic action to prevent Hichilema and his useful idiots from eroding our democratic institutions and steering the nation toward dictatorship. I will join you all in spirit.

The author is a Doctor of Education and a multicultural researcher affiliated with Northeastern University, Boston, Massachusetts, USA. His recently published scholarly work appears in the “Pacific Journal” under the title “Phenomenon of Social Media in Sub-Saharan Africa: Leapfrogging From Traditional Communication to Digital Dialogic Communication.”

World.title: Kitwe Chingalika hold on to top spot
World.content:
Lumwana Radiants produced the standout performance of Matchweek 10 in the National Division, Northern Zone, thrashing Mathkat United 5-0 on Saturday, while leaders Kitwe United laboured to a narrow 1-0 win over Indeni FC to stay top.

Lumwana were ruthless from the start.

Shadrack Chinyumba Kambwili opened the scoring in the 20th minute before Mabanga Kelvin struck twice in quick succession in the 25th and 32nd minutes to put the game beyond doubt before half time.

Chanda Kapata added a fourth in the 75th minute and Joseph Chanda completed the rout in the 88th minute, as Lumwana climbed to third place on the log with 14 points from nine games.

Kitwe United, however, needed a moment of composure to keep their place at the summit.

Veteran defender and captain Moses Lolozi converted from the penalty spot in the 63rd minute to secure a hard-fought 1-0 win over Indeni FC.

Lolozi, the former Indeni and Mufulira Wanderers defender, has played active football for over 20 years.

The win kept Kitwe United top with 18 points from nine games, two points clear of second-placed Forest Rangers.

Forest Rangers were held to a 3-3 draw by Chambishi FC in the match of the day.

Idriss Kisha scored twice for Forest in the 9th and 80th minutes, with John Kosamu also on target in the 38th minute.

Chambishi, though, refused to give in. Joshua Chimwanga gave them the lead in the first minute, Mwila Kalumba made it 2-1 in the 26th minute, and Jonathan Tanganyika grabbed a late equaliser in the 76th minute.

The draw leaves Forest Rangers second with 16 points, while Chambishi are fourth with 14 points.

In the other fixture, FC Leopards beat Ndola United 1-0, thanks to an 18th minute penalty by Roderick Khembo Junior.

Leopards are fifth with 14 points, level with Lumwana and Chambishi but behind on goal difference.

At the bottom, the pressure is mounting on Jumulo FC and Mathkat United.

Jumulo sit ninth with nine points, while Mathkat remain rooted to the bottom with just three points from nine games, having conceded 20 goals.

World.title: Central Province farmers urged to plant early
World.content:
Central Province Meteorological Officer, Chongo Tembo, has urged farmers in the district to plant early and medium-maturing crop varieties in the wake of the highly appreciated El Nino.

Mr Tembo says Serenje is expected to receive normal to below-normal rainfall compared to other parts of the province, making crop selection and planting decisions critical for farmers.

Mr Tembo said early maturing varieties would help farmers cope with shorter or unreliable rainfall periods, while medium-maturing varieties would be suitable in areas where rainfall is expected to be more stable.

“Plant early maturing varieties where rains are expected to be low or short, and go with medium where rains are steadier and better,” he said.

Mr Tembo encouraged farmers to select crop varieties according to the expected rainfall patterns to reduce the risk of crop failure.

He also urged farmers to follow the seasonal forecast and subsequent weather updates issued by the Meteorological Department to guide their farming activities.

Meanwhile, Principal Agricultural Officer, Jane Moonga, encouraged farmers to diversify into alternative livelihood activities to sustain their households during the anticipated El Niño period, while contributing to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

And Serenje District Commissioner, Ellen Mibenge, called for rapid dissemination of weather information in local languages to ensure communities understood the forecast and adopt appropriate measures to safeguard household food security.

She said communicating the information in languages understood by the majority of residents would help communities prepare for the anticipated weather conditions and mitigate their effects.

World.title: Government urges cattle farmers to embrace CBPP testing
World.content:
Minister of Fisheries and Livestock , Olivia Chiboola, has urged cattle farmers in Namwala district to present all their cattle for testing under the Government’s 100 per cent cattle testing programme aimed at containing Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP).

Ms Chiboola says it was important for every cattle owner to ensure that all their animals were tested to help authorities identify infected cattle and prevent further spread of the disease.

The Minister was speaking at a community engagement meeting for cattle farmers held at Chief Mungaila’s palace grounds in Namwala district, where she led a team of livestock technical officers in sensitising farmers on the importance of comprehensive cattle testing.

She commended farmers for their cooperation with the Government from the initial stages of CBPP surveillance, which commenced in June, through to the implementation of the 100 per cent testing programme.

Ms Chiboola said the Government was determined to safeguard the district’s cattle population and ensure that Namwala continued contributing to national livestock production and the country’s ambition of increasing beef exports under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

She said maintaining a healthy national herd was critical to strengthening the livestock sector and achieving Zambia’s beef export targets.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, Director of Livestock, Charles Maseka, urged farmers not to present only a portion of their cattle for testing.

Dr Maseka said all cattle should be brought forward to enable veterinary officers to conduct comprehensive testing and establish the disease status of the district’s livestock population.

He said the Government remained committed to ensuring that cattle in Namwala were free from animal diseases through sustained surveillance, testing and vaccination programmes.

And Namwala District Commissioner, Ephraim Shandavu, expressed optimism that continued community engagements in Nalubamba, Mungaila Muchila and Mukobela chiefdoms would strengthen the fight against CBPP.

Mr Shandavu said the sensitisation meetings were important in encouraging farmers to cooperate with veterinary officers and comply with disease-control measures.

Meanwhile, cattle farmer Neto Milimo commended the Government, for introducing the 100 per cent cattle testing programme.

Mr Milimo said the initiative would help identify infected animals and enable veterinary authorities to isolate them from healthy cattle, thereby preventing further transmission of the disease.

He said farmers were encouraged by the Government’s commitment to protecting the livestock industry and safeguarding their source of livelihood.

World.title: Government empowers vulnerable households through FSP
World.content:
Government, through the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services has reaffirmed its commitment to empowering vulnerable but viable households with sustainable livelihood opportunities to improve household food security in the country through the Food Security Pack (FSP) programme.

Lusaka Province Senior Community Development Officer, Micah Simululwe, says the Alternative Livelihood Initiative under FSP is one of the interventions through which the government is supporting vulnerable households to diversify their sources of income beyond crop farming.

Speaking during the village chicken pass-on ceremony in Lusaka, Mr Simululwe explained that FSP has three major components namely rain-fed cropping, wetland cropping, and the Alternative Livelihood Initiative which provides non-crop agricultural inputs such as chickens, ducks, goats, sheep, fish fingerlings and beehives for beekeeping.

He said Lusaka district, through the Lusaka Central Sub-Centre, was allocated 100 beneficiaries drawn from Silwizya and Kabulonga Wards, who each received five village chickens comprising four hens and one rooster in December 2025.

“The programme has adopted a pass-on model to ensure sustainability and extend the benefits to more vulnerable but viable households where the beneficiaries were trained and expected to multiply the chickens received before passing on an equivalent number to another identified beneficiary,” Mr Simululwe explained.

He further added that the model was anchored on the principle of receiving, multiplying and passing on, which would enable more households to benefit from the initiative.

Mr Simululwe also disclosed that the Ministry has introduced the Food Security Pack Management Information System (FSPMIS) to improve the management, monitoring and implementation of the programme through a digital platform.

He said the system was intended to enhance efficiency and transparency, minimise double dipping and reduce audit queries by providing digital records of all programme operations.

Meanwhile, one of the beneficiaries, Jennifer Sibanda, thanked the Government for the intervention, saying it had positively transformed her livelihood and enabled her to become financially independent.

Ms Sibanda said she successfully multiplied the chickens she received and passed on the required number to another beneficiary.

“The initiative has given me an opportunity to generate income through the sale of chickens, and now I no longer depend on other people to provide for my needs”, she said.

And a new beneficiary, Jonathan Kaseba, pledged to multiply the chickens received and pass them on to another beneficiary next year to ensure that more vulnerable but viable households benefit from the programme.

World.title: Fashion and Fabric Hub commissioned in Chilanga
World.content:
Government has commissioned a fully equipped Fashion and Fabric Hub and a 16-kilowatt solar system at Mount Makulu Secondary School in Chilanga district, valued at over K900,000.

The Fashion and Fabric Hub was rehabilitated and fully furnished with the financial support of the Elsa Milar Foundation through its implementing partners, the African Education Programme.

Speaking during the commissioning, Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Education Services, Kelvin Mambwe, says the Hub is equipped with modern textile tools and modern industrial tailoring machines aimed at preparing learners with vocational practical skills for the real-world experience.

In a speech read on his behalf by Director for Secondary Education, Yvonne Mweemba, Dr Mambwe stated that the skills acquired will enable learners to sit for their O-Level examinations with confidence, progress to A-Level and tertiary education, and emerge as industrial entrepreneurs able to manufacture Zambian brands and substitute imports.

Dr Mambwe pointed out that the government is transforming the education system from passive listening to active doing through the Competence-Based Curriculum, which emphasises practical skills and critical thinking.

He explained that the curriculum moves learners from merely memorising theories to demonstrating mastery.

Dr Mambwe indicated that the installation of the 16-kilowatt solar system is aimed at ensuring that practical lessons are never disrupted due to power failure.

He added that the government has set an ambitious target to generate 10,000 megawatts of electricity by 2031, which requires aggressive diversification of the energy mix, with decentralised, off-grid renewable energy solutions being key to achieving the target.

“With this 16-kilowatt solar installation, a practical lesson will never be disturbed by power disruptions, and it will contribute to the decentralised energy mix, thus contributing to national development,” Dr Mambwe added.

Chilanga Acting District Commissioner, Maureen Chilende, thanked the Elsa Milar Foundation for the donation, saying it will equip learners with practical vocational skills in fashion and design and open up career pathways for their personal development.

Ms Chilende encouraged learners to utilise the Fashion and Fabric Hub, acquire vocational skills, master the craft and use it for self-development.

She also urged school management to safeguard the equipment jealousy for future generations.

Speaking at the same event, Mount Makulu Secondary School Head Teacher, Berdennett Mulemi, described the Fashion and Fabric Hub as a milestone achievement in the implementation of the Competence-Based Curriculum.

Ms Mulemi said the facility is tailored to the Grow Zambia Agenda and engineered to drive the 2023 Competence-Based Curriculum.

She observed that for Zambia to grow, the education sector must shift from theoretical academic models to practical, hands-on career pathways.

“I am happy to share that Mount Makulu is fully exploring practical career pathways for learners in subjects such as Natural Sciences, Home Economics and Creative Arts, which will help pupils realise their skills and abilities at an early stage,” she said.

Ms Mulemi added that consistency in education is key, and the solar system will ensure all classes run without interruption.

Meanwhile, Mount Makulu Secondary School pupil, Gilbert Mbalakanyi, thanked the Elsa Milar Foundation, describing the Fashion and Fabric Hub as a dream come true.

Mr Mbalakanyi said pupils previously learnt through notes and books, but the modern facility will now enable them to gain practical skills and become better designers and future textile professionals.

He noted that the Hub reflects the Competence-Based Curriculum, which will help learners become self-reliant and develop entrepreneurship skills.

“We appreciate the rehabilitated Fashion and Fabric Hub and the installation of the solar system, which will create a better learning environment for pupils and we assure you that we will take good care of the facility, use it wisely and report any damage or misuse,” he appreciated.

World.title: Isoka receives livestock pasture seed to improve animal nutrition
World.content:
Isoka district has received 350 kilograms of livestock pasture seed to improve animal nutrition and increase livestock productivity in support of the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Council Public Relations Officer, Peter Sichali, said the consignment comprised 130 kilograms of Mombaca and 220 kilograms of Brachiaria pasture seed.

Mr Sichali said the seed would be distributed to individual livestock farmers and groups that previously benefited from the Government’s Livestock Restocking Programme.

He said the initiative was aimed at improving livestock feeding, which would contribute to better animal growth, improved beef quality and increased milk production.

“Improving the quality and availability of pasture is important in ensuring that farmers maintain healthy and productive animals. This initiative will help strengthen livestock production at household level,” Mr Sichali said.

He said improved animal nutrition would also support the Government’s ambition of increasing beef production for export, while creating opportunities for farmers to improve their livelihoods.

Mr Sichali said the provision of pasture seed was part of efforts to strengthen the livestock value chain and enable farmers to contribute to the national target of generating US$1 billion in beef exports.

He urged livestock farmers to make effective use of the seed and adopt improved pasture management practices to enhance productivity.
