World.title: Jennifer Lopez claims not being a ‘typical’ White actress made it harder to land Hollywood movie roles
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Jennifer Lopez is receiving criticism after claiming that she has struggled to land acting roles in Hollywood because she is not White, describing how she has been forced to create her "own lane" as a Latina entertainer, in an interview published on Friday.

Lopez made the remarks in an interview with The New York Times, pushing back on the notion that she gets thousands of acting offers, claiming instead that Hollywood has often overlooked her because of her ethnicity.

"Even from the beginning of my career, I got offered things, but I was only offered a few things. I had to kind of create things for myself," the actress said. "And the reason, I think, is because I just wasn't the typical kind of, like, to be honest, a White actress. You know what I mean? And it's still kind of the same today."

'BLUE BLOODS' STAR JENNIFER ESPOSITO SAYS SHE WALKED AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD AFTER YEARS OF REJECTION AND ‘ABUSE’

Lopez’s more recent film credits include "Office Romance" (2026), "Shotgun Wedding" (2022), "Hustlers" (2019) and "Second Act" (2018).

She also secured several leading roles in the late 1990s and early 2000s, including "The Wedding Planner," "Out of Sight" and "Maid in Manhattan," and was cast as the late singer Selena Quintanilla-Perez in "Selena."

JENNIFER LOPEZ ADMITS SHE 'WOULD'VE HAD SEX' WITH ENTIRE STAR-STUDDED 90S MOVIE CAST

The Puerto Rican actress said Hollywood continues to look for "certain" things when casting performers, suggesting that the industry's preferences have historically made it more difficult for actors of color to secure roles.

Lopez acknowledged, however, that the screen industry has made progress in improving diversity and representation.

"There's a certain thing that they look for, and it's more diverse now for sure, and that's good," the actress said.

"But because of that, you have to kind of create your own lane in a lot of ways," she added. "If I want to do something, I don't wait for somebody to offer me…I try to do it, and then if something comes along, great."

IDRIS ELBA REJECTS 'WOKE' JAMES BOND CASTING PUSH, WARNS AUDIENCES 'WON'T GO FOR A BLACK MALE' IN THE ROLE

Fox News co-host Tomi Lahren pushed back on Lopez’s claims, writing on X: "LOL, sure Jan."

Internet personality Oli London noted Lopez’ robust net worth and catalog of big-screen appearances, writing on X: "JLO has appeared in 44 films and is worth $400 million."

Actress and "America's Next Top Model" personality Adrianne Curry-Rhode also chimed in, calling Lopez' comments "next level delusion."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"You are old now. You were a bad actress, but very hot...that's why you got casted," Curry-Rhode wrote in a post to X.

Movie critic Christian Toto told Fox News Digital, "Lopez has worked steadily over the past two decades, bouncing from major film projects to concerts and her solo music career. She's undeniably talented and has earned every gig that came her way. Still, for her to suggest she's been penalized by Hollywood for the color of her skin is absurd. How many out-of-work actors would kill to snag a fraction of the work Hollywood has sent her way?"

World.title: Solo diners are asking restaurants for half-size portions, sparking debate over menu flexibility
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As solo dining continues to surge in popularity, there is debate over whether it’s acceptable for guests dining alone at a restaurant to request a smaller portion size of a dish.

Reservations for one saw a 22% increase year over year in the third quarter of 2025, according to a report from restaurant technology company Toast.

One appealing part of dining out with a group is sharing plates and trying bites of many different dishes.

RESTAURANTS DRAW THE LINE ON SUBSTITUTIONS AS DINERS PUSH MENU LIMITS

Solo diners who still want to sample a variety of items without having an overwhelming amount of food on their table may be able to do so by simply asking their server if they can place a half-order, Food & Wine reported.

Opinions are divided online about whether this is an acceptable request, with some believing that it’s no big deal while others say it’s not worth it.

"Don't even bother, order the regular meal. And when it comes, you eat what you want of it, and anything that you have left over, get a to go box and take it home," one person wrote on Quora.

CLICK HERE TO 

Many restaurants don’t appreciate when an adult orders a smaller portion size, the commenter added, saying, "they consider it to be a waste of their cooking time to make small portions for an adult."

Plus, they noted, it doesn't hurt to have leftovers.

Some chefs are happy to serve smaller portions to a solo diner because they want them to have a positive dining experience and be able to try many different dishes without wasting as much food, Food & Wine noted.

"It never hurts to ask!" another Quora user said, with the caveat that certain dishes are more easily re-portioned than others.

"Whether or not you are successful in your request depends on a few things. If the dish is pre-proportioned, then it’s not likely," they noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

For example, if an entree contains a half lobster tail, it’s probably not likely that the kitchen will scale that component down, the commenter continued, adding that restaurants may refuse to serve whole fishes and meats, portioned desserts or pizzas in smaller sizes.

The important thing for diners to remember, they said, is that they will probably pay full price for a dish even if it’s a half-sized portion, because it takes an equal amount of time and effort to make.

One Reddit user agreed that the portion sizes of certain dishes are more easily adjusted than others.

"I think it’s easier with pasta dishes because they can portion out the amount of pasta, sauce, garnish, etc and keep selling the rest. Not so easy with a piece of protein (1/2 steak, 1/2 fish filet, 1/2 burger) because those are generally pre-portioned for service," they said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Another person noted that they wanted a smaller portion to reduce food waste — and a smaller bill would be nice, too.

"I hate wasting food, but if I eat the full portion I’m overeating and will feel sick. I’d love to do a half portion for a slightly cheaper price and not overeat or waste food," they said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

One Redditor shared that they were pleasantly surprised when a restaurant they dined solo at charged them half of the menu price for a half-sized portion.

World.title: Hakeem Jeffries calls Trump chief of staff Stephen Miller a ‘stone-cold racist,’ refuses to sit down with him
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., declared firmly on Saturday that he will not sit down with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — calling Miller a "stone-cold racist" while mulling over who his conduit to the White House will be.

Jeffries, who is set to become House speaker in January, made the remarks during a recent podcast interview with The New York Times, in which he discussed ways he plans to work with the Trump administration to move forward legislation for the American people. When asked whether he imagined sitting across from Stephen Miller, Jeffries firmly said, "No," and disparaged the White House official.

"I've made it clear that Stephen Miller is a stone-cold racist. Why would I deal with him at this point in time?" Jeffries said.

TRUMP'S MOVE FROM WILES TO MILLER SIGNALS MAJOR TACTICAL SHIFT FOR GOVERNING WITHOUT CONGRESS

Jeffries, who has historically been an outspoken critic of Miller, said he cannot meet with someone who has carried out such a violent immigration agenda.

"This is the architect, the architect of Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine. And there's cruelty associated with that. There's chaos. In fact, there's death associated with what's taking place," Jeffries said.

In response to Fox News Digital, White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended Miller's track record.

"Unlike the hardcore, partisan Democrats who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C., and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance," Rogers told Fox News Digital.

JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

When President Donald Trump appointed Miller, Jeffries also blasted the president’s move as an "irresponsible decision" and condemned the chief of staff for his movement to "brutalize and kill American citizens," referencing the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good during immigration enforcement actions.

Trump defended the deportation agenda of his chief of staff pick at the time, telling Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America" that, "The one thing with Stephen – he was very strong on the border."

"So, he called him a racist. But we had to be strong," Trump continued. "They allowed 25 million people and killers, murderers. They allowed drug dealers and rapists into our country."

The president also lauded Jeffries as a "very smart" and "reasonable guy."

"What he did is pretty spectacular with getting that position," Trump said. "And it’s nice – first Black person in that position. It’s a big deal."

THE MISTAKE NEWLY-ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN'T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS

Jeffries insisted to The New York Times that his refusal to meet with Miller was "not a boycott," and expressed that he was willing to have an open communication line with Trump, just not Miller.

"I think practically speaking, one, I can communicate directly with the president," Jeffries told The New York Times. "I mean, everybody seems to have his number, but the president is not a hard person to reach."

Jeffries also said he can take his issues to Vice President JD Vance, explaining that in prior administrations, engagement between congressional leaders and the White House oftentimes happened via Cabinet secretaries or vice presidents.

"I wouldn't say I like any of the Cabinet secretaries within the Trump administration at this particular point in time," Jeffries said, adding that he has spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

The New York Democrat declared he will "maintain a willingness" to work with politicians across the aisle to get things done for the American people.

Jeffries’ office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

World.title: Week 12 AP Top 25 Poll sees Big Ten powers rightfully punished while Longhorns jump the Crimson Tide
World.content:
After the Week 11 AP Top 25 poll was an anomaly, with the top nine teams going unchanged from the week prior, we returned to our regularly scheduled programming of utter chaos in college football and a lot of moving pieces in the newest edition of the AP Top 25 poll.

The Big Ten suffered some untimely cannibalization in Week 12, with Indiana, UCLA, and Ohio State all going on the road and losing, and all three teams were punished rather harshly as a result.

The SEC scoreboard featured nothing but chalk this past weekend, but with the Big Ten producing a mess, Texas has entered the Top 5 again, which can't be sitting all too well among Alabama fans.

GEORGIA HAS TOP COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF SEED IN SIGHT WITH DOMINATING ROAD WIN OVER NO 21 SOUTH CAROLINA

Week 12 AP Top 25 Poll

Georgia Utah Notre Dame Miami (FL) Texas Alabama Tennessee Wake Forest Texas Tech UCLA BYU Indiana Iowa Oregon USC Arizona Houston Louisville Oklahoma Florida Liberty Boise State Ole MIss Missouri Ohio State

With voters being forced into putting out a fresh set of rankings every week for three consecutive months, they appear to have found their stride, at least as best they can. Remember, voters are spread out all around the country, in different time zones, making it physically impossible to watch even the extended highlights of every meaningful game on the slate.

With that in mind, there isn't a whole lot to get too worked up about when it comes to the upper echelon of this week's rankings.

Punishments of UCLA and Indiana feel just right

UCLA has been a great story this season, and the sport is better when the Bruins are relevant, but they've undoubtedly felt like the team primed for a slip-up, and that coming to a Michigan team that is inept on offense is pretty peak college football.

The Bruins tumbling from No. 4 to No. 10 after having their unbeaten season ruined in Ann Arbor is fair. They're still a one-loss Big Ten team, and one-loss Big Ten teams deserve to remain inside the Top 10 this season.

LANE KIFFIN TAKES THE SIDE EXIT AS TENNESSEE SENDS LSU HOME AND MOVES TO THE DOORSTEP OF CFP

Indiana went from a one-loss Big Ten team to a two-loss Big Ten team after an unsuccessful trip to Washington. The Hoosiers may only have one meaningful win all season – against USC in Week 11 – but their two losses have come by a combined seven points. Plus, Ohio State was still Ohio State when Indiana lost at home to the Buckeyes in October.

Everyone would rank the Hoosiers ahead of Iowa, Oregon, and USC in the Big Ten, which is exactly what the AP voters did this week.

Longhorns get a three-spot boost for beating...Arkansas

The Longhorns dominated a 4-6 Arkansas team 45-3 on Saturday, and it was exponentially more impressive than Alabama's 47-0 win. It's incredible that sentence is factual, but it is, seeing as how Alabama's shutout came against FCS Chattanooga.

FIFTH-RANKED TEXAS DOMINATES ARKANSAS AS ARCH MANNING IS HEATING UP AHEAD OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

Texas, Alabama, and Tennessee all sit at 9-2 on the season, and the Longhorns getting inside the Top 5 after UCLA and Indiana fell is inarguable. The Longhorns beat Tennessee earlier in the year, and the schedule broke with Alabama's cupcake game coming in the penultimate week of the season, hence the inside move on the Crimson Tide.

A week ago, the Longhorns were No. 8 while Alabama was a spot ahead.

Voters are still clueless about the Bottom Five

The AP Poll is irrelevant due to the College Football Playoff Rankings ruling all, meaning the back end is even more pointless, but it gives college football fans something to argue about and argue we will.

Last week, voters elected to keep Ole Miss ranked at No. 25 after losing to Oklahoma. Florida was also ranked No. 23 a week ago. The Sooners beat both the Rebels and Gators earlier in the year, but did not have a number next to their name in Week 11.

Suddenly, a week too late, Oklahoma has surged to No. 19 ahead of the Gators and Rebels.

We can't just pick on the SEC teams when it comes to the back end of this week's poll, because what on Earth is Boise State doing at No. 22?

The Broncos lost 22-20 at home to what was a 5-5 San Diego State team on Saturday night for their second loss of the season.

Liberty, at No. 21, is the lone non-Power Four team that should be inside the Top 25, but we as a society decided long ago that 'the little guy' has to be shown preferential treatment, and internal fighting among voters may have broken out if only one Group of Five team had a number next to its name this late into the season.

World.title: DK Metcalf disqualified from Steelers game for unsportsmanlike penalties including poking opponent's facemask
World.content:
DK Metcalf is clearly frustrated about this season because he's not producing as expected and on Sunday we saw what could be a full manifestation of that frustration when he was disqualified from the game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

The incident happened in chapters on consecutive Steelers' drives and culminated with 4:58 left in the third quarter when Metcalf seemed to poke the facemask of Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

DK METCALF WILL NOT FACE CRIMINAL CHARGES FOR VIRAL ALTERCATION WITH LIONS FANS

This fracas was away from the play and even after the play was over. But officials caught it, and disqualified Metcalf for picking up his second unsportsmanlike conduct penalty of the third quarter.

Officials called Metcalf for an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty because, they said, he was taunting DeJean. The Eagles contend Metcalf poked DeJean in the facemask.

The previous possession by the Steelers offense, Metcalf had gotten into a kerfuffle with DeJean and been flagged for his first unsportsmanlike conduct penalty.

We have no idea what led to this little brouhaha between Metcalf and DeJean. On the first play, Metcalf turned a block of DeJean into a push, during which he grabbed DeJean by his neck and then the front of his collar.

DeJean (6-foot and 198 pounds) then grabbed the bigger Metcalf (6-4 and 235) around his collar and the two men started pushing on each other.

But Metcalf was apparently very hot because he could be seen jawing at DeJean even as other Eagles and, eventually, Steelers players joined the fray.

(By the way, NFL moments like this are a sportswriter's dream because they allow for the use of words such as kerfuffle, brouhaha and fracas).

Anyway, as the two men were locked onto each other's collars, officials joined the tussle and pulled each player away.

Except that when the game umpire stood between Metcalf and his ability to rejoin the rumpus, he put a hand on Metcalf's chest.

And Metcalf swiped it away – which is surely about to get the NFL's attention beyond the disqualification.

Anyway, Metcalf was penalized for unnecessary roughness as his first offense.

So Metcalf went to the locker room with more personal foul penalties (2) than catches (1), and he cost the Steelers more yards by penalty (19) than the yards he contributed via his catch (1).

NFL SUSPENDS BUFFALO BILLS SAFETY CJ GARDNER-JOHNSON AFTER GROTESQUE SPITTING INCIDENT

Metcalf is supposed to be Pittsburgh's top receiver but had only 35 catches for 432 yards and 2 TDs in nine games coming into Sunday's action.

One more thing: Metcalf has something of a history as a hothead.

During the 2025 NFL season, Metcalf was suspended for two games without pay by the NFL for initiating a physical confrontation with a fan during a Week 16 game at Ford Field against the Detroit Lions on December 21, 2025.

World.title: Democrats win the largest House majority since 1992
World.content:
Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats.

It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian, and four races are yet to be called. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats.

The second-largest House majority for Democrats this century came in 2008, when the party won 257 seats.

The party cemented control of the chamber not only by winning competitive races in battleground districts, but also by winning in deeply Republican areas that voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago.

In 2024, Trump won Foxx’s district by almost 18 percentage points, per an NBC News Decision Desk analysis.

Now, Hubbard is projected to win North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District by a fraction of a percentage point following a recount that Foxx requested after Election Day.

Earlier Sunday, Foxx called Hubbard to concede, according to a source familiar with the call.

In a post on X, Hubbard wrote: “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process. Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.”

Foxx isn’t the only North Carolina Republican who lost in what was considered to be a solidly GOP seat heading into Election Day. Democrats flipped seven Republican seats in North Carolina, the most of any state in the nation.

In the state’s 9th Congressional District, Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda II defeated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, who this year chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. Elsewhere in the state, Democratic Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP Rep. Addison McDowell.

Trump won Hudson’s district by 16 percentage points in 2024 and McDowell’s district by 17 percentage points that year.

World.title: Delta restores system after nationwide flight delays as Thanksgiving travel begins
World.content:
Delta Air Lines said it restored an automated system Sunday afternoon after a problem with it delayed flights nationwide as Thanksgiving travel got underway.

A of 4 p.m. ET, more than 1,100 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 36 had been canceled, according to FlightAware.

The airline, which has 5,000 Delta and Delta connection flights scheduled for Sunday, said 70% of the delays and cancellations are connected to the automation issue. It attributed the rest to bad weather and other air traffic control restrictions in New York and elsewhere in the Northeast.

The system calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff.

The Federal Aviation Administration briefly halted Atlanta-bound flights Sunday morning, then allowed them to depart at staggered times. The delay program applied to Delta and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson from the contiguous United States. The FAA had projected delays of 57 minutes on average and lasting up to 1 hour and 51 minutes.

At 11:26 a.m. ET, the agency lifted the delay program.

Delta said it was rebooking passengers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed. Passengers whose flights were canceled could get a refund if they chose not to travel.

Hartsfield-Jackson said the disruption was limited to Delta and did not affect airport operations broadly. The airport urged travelers to check their flight status with their airline and arrive at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.

Sunday’s disruption followed a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 caused by a technical issue with the FAA’s air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend.

A separate system outage delayed United Airlines departures on Nov. 16, disrupting crew communications and the airline’s ability to send pilots final aircraft weight data, according to the union representing United pilots. United said it resolved the issue that day.

World.title: COP31 climate talks break down after angry dispute over fossil fuels
World.content:
International climate talks in Turkey broke down Sunday after the European Union and other nations rejected a draft agreement that had cut all references to fossil fuels.

Negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya fell apart two days after the United Nations’ COP31 conference was meant to end, after delegates from 196 countries and the European Union struggled to agree on new pledges for climate action and how to deliver on previous promises.

COP31 President Murat Kurum said Sunday that there would be no new climate agreement draft after a fourth draft was rejected.

“There is nothing to do. We did all that we could,” said Kurum, who is host nation Turkey’s environment minister. “​We will not ​be carrying out ​work on a new ⁠text in an environment ⁠where there ​is no consensus.”

He later added that he had wanted a a “much stronger outcome” from the summit.

Chris Bowen, COP31’s president of negotiations, told reporters that there were “unbridgeable red lines” in the discussions.

“The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory,” the Australian minister said. “Things that were manageable in the past, in previous COPs like the last two where people wanted certain words mentioned but didn’t get them, it became a red line this time,” Bowen added.

The latest draft agreement, released on Sunday, had set out proposed measures for countries to accelerate climate action, but the 12-page document drew immediate criticism over its failure to mention a move away from fossil fuels, a key demand of the E.U. and other nations.

Irish minister Darragh O’Brien, representing the E.U. in Antalya, said the bloc “strongly objects” to the deal, which he called “greenwashing.”

“These decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change,” O’Brien said. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels.”

Panama also rejected the deal, saying it didn’t go far enough, as did the Marshall Islands, a low-lying Pacific nation that faces an existential threat from sea-level rise.

Kate Hughes, the spokesperson for the United Kingdom delegation, called the draft text the “lowest common denominator.”

All countries had to agree on the text for it to pass. The talks were the longest in COP history, surpassing the delay in negotiations at COP25 in Madrid.

The summit began on Nov 9. A first draft was circulated a week later and mentioned “fossil fuel” or “fossil fuels” six times. But a second draft, published Thursday, had removed all references, to the anger of many countries.

The conference officially ended on Friday without an agreement. Members have continued talks in a bid to find a resolution, but a fourth draft released Sunday still contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia and India have pushed back on including any reference to the words in the text, amid concerns that phasing out fossil fuels, central to their economies, could pose a financial risk.

The United States, one of the largest emitters of greenhouse gases, is officially absent from the conference, having withdrawn from a series of international climate commitments under President Donald Trump.

The latest draft started by “recalling the United Arab Emirates Consensus in its entirety,” a reference to COP28 in the UAE, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away” from fossil fuels in energy systems.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said the world was “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

“We love the petroleum guys,” he told a press conference on Wednesday. “We can’t live without them, and they are so smart, they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa called COP31 the “worst ever.”

“The collapse of climate talks at COP31 in Antalya needs to be a wake-up call for the world,” he wrote in a statement. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.”

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.”

“But this setback does not change the facts,” he posted on X. “There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

The latest draft also acknowledged that the goal set by the 2015 Paris Agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius is going to be missed.

As warming goes beyond 1.5 C, the impacts of climate change, including extreme heat and other weather events, are expected to ramp up significantly.

As the talks break down, Kurum could choose to convene a follow-up meeting or delay decisions until next year’s conference, hosted by Ethiopia.

Talks last failed at COP6 at The Hague in the Netherlands in 2000.

World.title: Princeton neuroscientist detained by ICE at D.C. airport after leaving conference
World.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested a Princeton University Ph.D. student at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Thursday as she was preparing to fly back to New Jersey after presenting her research at a conference, her adviser said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year neuroscience student from China, has had an asylum application pending for 10 years after her family came to the U.S. when she was 14, according to her attorney, Kerry Doyle. The Department of Homeland Security said Xie was in the country illegally, which Doyle disputed, saying she had permission to live, work and study in the country while her case was pending.

“Her arrest and detention is without legal basis as ICE and DHS are fully aware,” Doyle told NBC News.

DHS said in a statement about her arrest that Xie was admitted to the United States temporarily in March 2016 and was required to leave by Sept. 15 of that year. The agency said she stayed past that date.

“Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States,” the statement said. “To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States.”

Xie, 24, was being held at the Caroline Detention Facility in Bowling Green, Virginia, according to a detainee search on ICE’s website.

Doyle filed a habeas corpus petition in federal court in Virginia challenging the legality of Xie’s arrest. She argued that ICE had no grounds to arrest Xie without a warrant because Xie was not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

Doyle said people with pending asylum cases “have permission to be here” while their cases are decided.

“It’s their over-the-top enforcement used as a way to scare people,” Doyle said. She called Xie’s arrest “an incredible waste of time and resources — to what end?”

Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., on July 30. Kevin Carter / Getty Images file

The Trump administration has detained asylum-seekers and others with pending immigration applications as part of its broader immigration crackdown.

In its statement on Xie’s arrest, DHS repeated a warning it issued in recent press releases, saying it was working to prevent people it considered to be in the country illegally from flying domestically.

Xie’s adviser, Carlos Brody, described the research she presented at the conference in an emailed statement.

“There, Eva described her work discovering and researching an unexpected link between how brains make decisions and how they navigate through space,” Brody said.

Brody said Xie mentors undergraduates and sent messages to colleagues from the detention center “to make sure that her experiments could move forward and the grant applications she is part of could be submitted.”

“Eva is a gentle, kind, caring person who is contributing enormously to the United States,” Brody added. “She belongs back home in Princeton, doing the science that she loves, and helping our country excel and grow.”

Princeton’s graduate school dean, Rodney D. Priestley, said that Eva’s arrest “is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community.”

“The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s attorney did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

According to Xie’s professional biography page, she graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024 with degrees in computer science and mathematics. She was helping to plan a cognitive computational neuroscience conference in the U.K. in 2027, according to the page.

World.title: Democrats reach historic House majority not seen since 1992
World.content:
Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House on Sunday, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Trump's first midterm in 2018. It's an election sweep unseen since 1992 for either party, creating not only vast opportunities for Democrats to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Hubbard led Foxx by 330 votes following a recount, according to the North Carolina Board of Elections.

"House Democrats have just secured the largest majority any party in Congress has held this century. BOOM," Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, of New York, wrote on X Sunday afternoon.

The milestone in the 435-member House exceeded Democrats' own expectations, and they could still gain a few more seats with four other House races remaining outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The blue wave, or as some have called it, "blue tsunami," sets up a divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address the high cost of living while also confronting Mr. Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

In an interview on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Jeffries repeatedly emphasized the need for action, saying, "Can you imagine how angry the American people will be with Washington if, over the next two years, we fail to do anything about affordability, fail to do anything about healthcare, and fail to do anything about immigration?"

Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and war with Iran and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Mr. Trump.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats in their House races, according to CBS News exit polls. This was the second straight election most voters told CBS News inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters also backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

Newly elected members of the U.S. House of Representatives pose for a family photo on the steps of the US Capitol in Washington, D.C., on November 12, 2026. Jim WATSON /AFP via Getty Images

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Mr. Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr. Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.

The New York Democrat called the big numbers "a mandate for change."

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr. Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."

A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democratic Rep. Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

World.title: Ossoff's broad and decisive Senate win fuels 2028 speculation
World.content:
Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state.

Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028.

Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five.

Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg.

"I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done."

"Ossoff Lotería" campaign merchandise from the GALEO Impact Fund, a Georgia-based Latino political advocacy group that endorsed Sen. Jon Ossoff's 2026 reelection bid.

Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too.

"He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'"

It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution.

"Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere?

"I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated.

Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors.

All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare.

"Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school."

In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point.

Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows.

Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center.

He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris).

Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points.

Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin.

And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier.

A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement.

Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022.

The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier.

In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory.

Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations.

Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia.

"Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work.

Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach.

"His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won."

In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024.

In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election.

States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup.

In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition.

Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like.

"He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said.

World.title: Army plans to carry out detonation at Iowa plant despite indefinite pause
World.content:
The U.S. Army says it plans to move forward with the detonation of several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on or by Tuesday, according to a new court filing. It will do so despite a federal court order that paused the detonation plans indefinitely, which the Army said it does not need to follow because of the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

In federal court records filed late Saturday, the Department of the Army said it plans to use an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion to the Environmental Protection Agency's permit. The government argues it needs to perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion.

On Friday, a federal court suspended the U.S. Army's plan to detonate the explosives containing lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa, after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

The Army originally scheduled two controlled explosions for Friday. The Army then delayed them until Monday before the court stepped in.

The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted an emergency motion to pause the demolition after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.

The military said on Friday it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said.

A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 19, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In its filing on Saturday, the government warned that it must conduct the controlled explosion by Tuesday because the temperature is expected to drop below 30 degrees in the next several days. It says the lead azide has deteriorated and that crystals in the waste could break as temperatures drop.

"A controlled detonation allows the Army to implement measures to minimize the risk to the public, including the risk from the ejection of partial unexploded ordnances that can explode later from the Facility," the court filing says. "The Army intends to act consistent with the terms of the Emergency Permit and its mitigation measures even if not in effect. That includes mitigation measures to minimize the risk of the dispersal of lead dust. In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion."

In response to the Army's filing, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed a motion Sunday seeking to supplement their emergency request to block the planned detonation.

The filing includes three expert and local government declarations challenging the Army's assessment of the risk of delaying the detonation, as well as concerns about public notice and potential health and environmental impacts.

In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration, saying "this emergency is of the Army's own making."

"The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

World.title: Delta Air Lines hit with delays after baggage network system issue
World.content:
A systemwide network issue affecting Delta Air Lines' baggage system that forced teams to manually process bags, resulting in nationwide delays during a busy holiday travel weekend, has been fixed, the airline said Sunday.

The airline said in a statement that the automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations is now working, several hours after it forced a temporary ground delay program to be issued at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport — Delta Air Lines' mega hub — to manage traffic backups caused by the system outage. The ground delay, which has been lifted, impacted only Delta's flights.

"Delta apologizes to customers for the delay in their travels today," the airline said. "Delta is rebooking customers to the next best itinerary and providing meals and hotel rooms where necessary. For customers facing a canceled flight and don't wish to travel, refunds are being given."

Delta warned that while teams are focused on completing the 500 Delta and Delta Connection flights scheduled for Sunday, cancellations would be a last resort if all other options have been exhausted.

According to FlightAware, Delta Air Lines currently has more than 1,600 delayed flights, as of 3:50 p.m. EST. The airline said about 70% of these delays are connected to the automation.

"The remaining are attributable to inclement weather and ensuring ATC programs in NYC and the U.S. Northeast," the airline said.

United Airlines had a similar issue last Monday that forced the airline to hold departures for about 90 minutes.

AAA projects nearly 6 million people will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving this week.

World.title: Russian warship struck by suspected Ukrainian drones at Libya naval base
World.content:
A Russian warship was struck by a suspected Ukrainian drone at a naval base in Libya's Benghazi, Libyan officials said. It marked the latest attack in the North African nation tied to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The strike at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette, and ignited a fire at the facility, two Libyan military officials said.

They said that several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship from a base run by Ukrainian forces in western Libya, according to an initial investigation into the attack. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, they said.

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Satellite imagery appeared to show a boat on fire at the Benghazi port on Sunday, and images captured several hours later appeared to show the same boat partially submerged, CBS partner BBC News reported.

A combination of satellite images shows a Russian corvette and the northern port area before (above) and after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base, with the latter image showing the vessel capsized, in Benghazi, Libya, on Nov. 21 and 22, 2026. Vantor/Handout via REUTERS

Libya has been divided since a NATO-backed uprising toppled longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, who was later killed, in 2011. A U.N.-supported government is based in Tripoli and a rival administration is located in the east. The oil-rich nation remains a focal point for a long-running rivalry between Russia and the West.

The eastern Libya-based government said in a statement that the strike on Sunday caused an explosion and fire at the base, which was later extinguished.

The vessel had docked at the base for refueling and supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said, without providing details on the vessel or its cargo.

A joint investigation was launched with Russia to "uncover the circumstances of the attack, its source, and the party behind it," the statement said.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack. There was no immediate comment from either Russia or Ukraine.

On Sunday evening, local media said that another sea drone hit a commercial vessel off the port of Benghazi in a separate attack. No further details were given. The Almasar satellite television channel said that naval and air forces destroyed at least 12 other sea drones off the Mediterranean city.

The western Libyan government expressed concerns about "dragging Libyan ports and civilian facilities into external conflicts," in an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine.

"The government reaffirms its categorical rejection of turning Libya into an arena for international conflicts or a theater for external powers to settle scores," it said in a statement.

In March, Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya under a covert deal struck a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in a suspected sea drone attack near Maltese waters, Libyan officials said at the time.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, operated mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also at other military facilities in the capital, Tripoli, and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press.

World.title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeats Rep. Virginia Foxx in House race
World.content:
Washington — Chuck Hubbard defeated Rep. Virginia Foxx, CBS News projected 19 days after Election Day, adding to Democrats' sizable majority in the House next year.

Hubbard, 64, is a former journalist who took on Foxx for a second time after falling short by almost 10 points in 2024. This cycle, he became the latest Democrat to overcome expectations and flip a House seat.

Foxx, who chairs the House Rules Committee, has represented the Tar Heel State in the House since 2005 and is the longest-serving member of the state's congressional delegation. Her loss comes as Democrats saw a slew of wins throughout the country, with key victories delivering them majorities in both chambers in the new Congress. And the dynamic was especially acute in North Carolina, where Democrats flipped several House seats and a Senate seat. Heading into Election Night, the Cook Political Report rated Foxx's seat as likely Republican.

Hubbard said Foxx called to concede on Sunday, after a recount had been conducted in the tight race.

"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," Hubbard wrote in a post on X. "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

With the victory, Democrats have secured 258 seats in the House, marking the largest majority either party has won in the lower chamber in a general election in three decades.

World.title: Natural gas pipeline fire in Alabama lights up night sky
World.content:
A fire on a natural gas pipeline lit up the night sky in rural Alabama late Saturday with a towering column of orange flame, prompting the operator to shut down part of the line but causing no injuries, the company said.

The cause of the fire is under investigation, and customer deliveries were not impacted, Southern Natural Gas Company said in a statement Sunday.

Photos and videos posted on social media appeared to show flames rising dozens of yards above the trees near Ward, with smoke billowing into the air. People said on social media that the fire was visible from miles away across the state line in Mississippi.

Southern Natural Gas told The Associated Press that it "experienced a natural gas release and fire" on the segment of the pipeline at around 11:30 p.m. CST Saturday. Emergency responders and company personnel secured the area and the blaze was extinguished, the company said. The impacted part of the pipeline was shut down and depressurized.

A still image from a video provided to CBS News by Kimberly Terrell shows a gas pipeline fire in Ward, Alabama. Kimberly Terrell

CBS News has reached out to the company for more details.

Pleasant Hill Volunteer Fire Department said on social media that its firefighters, along with several other volunteer fire departments, responded to the blaze after midnight to assist Sumter County officials after "a major pipeline explosion that caused a secondary brush fire."

The Sumter County Emergency Management Agency did not immediately respond to a voicemail seeking information.

Ward is an unincorporated community located near the Mississippi state line. The mayor of nearby York urged residents on Sunday to remain calm and avoid the affected area.

Mayor Renee Ward Pringle said in a social media post that the city of York's gas facilities are not believed to be affected.

World.title: Full transcript of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 22, 2026
World.content:
On this "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" broadcast, moderated by Margaret Brennan:

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent

Brad Smith , Microsoft president and vice chair

, Microsoft president and vice chair House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York

Click here to browse full transcripts from 2026 of "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

MARGARET BRENNAN: I'm Margaret Brennan in Washington.

And this week on Face the Nation: A surge of technology outages hit government agencies and major corporations.

Plus, what does the global AI arms race mean for the U.S. economy? Wall Street is bracing itself for Monday's market opening after last week's brutal sell-off, as concerns about artificial intelligence continue to rattle investors.

We will have an exclusive interview with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the president of Microsoft, Brad Smith, whose company was at the center of one of those outages in recent weeks.

Our panel of experts, former CISA Director Chris Krebs, former Department of Homeland Security official Samantha Vinograd, and cybersecurity expert Dmitri Alperovitch, will break down the risks, the consequences, and what's next.

Then: After a historic trilateral meeting with two of America's biggest rivals, President Trump returns to questions about Iran, technology instability, and the looming Democratic takeover of Congress. Will he be open to working with the incoming speaker of the House?

(Begin VT)

DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): He's a smart guy. He's a streetwise guy, and he's smart. If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too.

(End VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will ask Hakeem Jeffries what's at the top of his agenda.

It's all just ahead on Face the Nation.

Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation.

We have a lot to get to today, and we begin with the secretary of the Treasury, Scott Bessent.

It's good to have you here, and in person, sir.

SCOTT BESSENT (U.S. Treasury Secretary): Margaret, good to see you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, there were thousands of customers across America who, when they went to some of the biggest banks, had issues this past week with tech outages, and it caused a bit of a panic, with people pulling out cash.

In this age of AI, what should Americans be prepared for, and should they worry about their financial institutions?

SECRETARY SCOTT BESSENT: It's a good, good question, Margaret.

And, no, they shouldn't. The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades. They experience attacks every day, every week, every month. And they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy.

What we are seeing, as they – because of the SI, as they go into patch their security systems, the patches may cause a glitch, which is what happened last week. J.P. Morgan went in. And I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine. Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.

MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

Well, there's other concerns about AI, as you know. And we've seen in the stock market anxiety, a real sell-off over the past week. Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the central bank of AI, since it uses its cash to finance things like data centers and essentially boost demand for its own sales. We have a graphic there sort of showing the gist of that.
