World.title: COP31 climate talks collapse after member states reject deal for not mentioning fossil fuels
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Climate talks collapsed on Sunday at COP31 in Turkey, ending the longest ever UN climate summit with no deal to show for it.

For more than two weeks, representatives from nearly 200 countries, scientists, businesses and more gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for this year's COP31 conference. The annual UN climate change conference brings together member states to negotiate — and ideally commit to — climate policies that aim to curb global warming. It's the main vehicle through which countries co-ordinate climate action.

But this year, no agreement was met — despite extending heavily into overtime this weekend following Friday's deadline — after the European Union and others rejected the draft put forward by Turkey and Australia.

"There is nothing to do, we did all that we could. Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision and we will respect their decision," said Turkey's COP31 president Murat Kurum. "There will be no new text from now on."

The lack of a deal means there will be no new action on climate disaster and adaptation financing for developing countries hardest hit by the impacts of climate change as the world is expected to overshoot the 1.5 C target set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, nor any further attempts to rein in the main human drivers of the climate crisis.

It's the first time UN climate talks have failed since 2009, when the conference was held in Copenhagen for COP15.

WATCH | Ex-minister McKenna says any UN climate deal must address fossil fuels: Any UN climate deal must address fossil fuels, says ex-minister McKenna after talks fail | Duration closed caption 9:22 Climate talks collapsed on Sunday at COP31 in Turkey after multiple members said the proposed agreement didn't go far enough, in part because the text contained no mention of fossil fuels. Former minister of environment and climate change Catherine McKenna said the outcome is disappointing but 'in a way it's a better decision [because] we cannot go on where we can't recognize the problem at climate negotiations.'

Fossil fuels weren't mentioned in final draft

Multiple members said the proposed agreement didn't go far enough to match the gravity of the climate crisis — in part because there was no mention of fossil fuels anywhere in the text, despite scientific consensus that they drive global warming.

"At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls short," said a joint European Union statement , delivered by Ireland's Environment Minister Darragh O'Brien and Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.... And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels."

Jeanne-Marie Huddleston, Canada's chief climate negotiator, expressed "deep disappointment" that a consensus could not be reached.

Former environment minister Catherine McKenna told CBC News Network following the conference that there is "no way" to have a COP agreement that doesn't mention fossil fuels.

"You need to mention the problem if you're going to actually get to solutions," she said.

Kurum voiced his disagreement with the decision, saying "you should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase."

Oil-producing nations like Saudi Arabia reportedly lobbied to leave out mentions of fossil fuels and instead pushed for the deal to focus on carbon capture and storage technologies.

WATCH | Big emitters profiting off of the climate crisis, says UN chief: Big emitters 'profiting' from the planet's destruction: UN chief | Duration 0:46 United Nations Secretary General António Guterres took aim at 'big emitters' and the fossil fuel lobby at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31), calling for drastic emissions cuts to keep global warming below the 1.5 C limit set by the Paris Agreement by the end of the century.

A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit he was surprised that member states voiced resistance to the technology, which is heavily pushed by industry lobbyists.

"If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important, it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions ... will be taken off the table," he said.

Environmentalists have long voiced concerns about overreliance on the tech, saying it could prolong global reliance on fossil fuels. Experts have also warned that carbon capture, while important, can't roll back global warming on its own.

Russia was also against mentioning fossil fuels in the agreement.

Panama said it rejected the deal because it failed to acknowledge the scale and urgency of the climate crisis, while Norway's Climate Minister Sigrun Gjerløw Aasland said the draft "takes us backwards."

Climate finance another sticking point

Developing countries, many of which are already struggling with the worst effects of global warming, said the deal didn't allocate enough money to adequately respond to the climate crisis.

"Climate finance must be fully mobilized to drive needed scale and speed in mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer, capacity building and loss and damage," the Philippines delegation said. "A target without means is a promise without a pathway."

Kenya echoed the concern and said Africa wasn't adequately represented.

WATCH | Who pays for the aftermath of climate disasters: Who pays when climate disasters strike? | Duration closed caption 2:51 Nepal has become the first country to have funding provisionally set aside from the UN's Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage following devastating flooding. But Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and the fund has set aside just millions. From the Himalayas to the COP31 climate summit, can the international community deliver the help vulnerable countries need?

"Africa is not named. The decision rightly speaks of least developed countries and small island states, but not once of Africa's special needs and circumstances," said Kenya's delegation. "Those who took the lead in emissions must take the lead in support. We ask our partners to bring the finance that makes this ambition possible."

Reactions from others trickling in

Reactions from officials, activists and experts already started flooding the internet early Sunday, with many supporting the EU's decision to reject the deal.

"Countries from across regions were right to reject the colossal betrayal that the COP31 co-presidencies tried to pass off as climate action," wrote Amnesty International climate justice policy adviser Ann Harrison. "They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use."

The UN Secretary General António Guterres wrote on X that he's "deeply disappointed" that COP31 ended without consensus.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But the setback does not change the facts," he wrote. "The take-home message from COP31 is clear: The world must do much more to confront the climate crisis."

WATCH | Greta Thunberg at COP31 says planet is being killed: 'The planet is not dying, it is being killed' - Thunberg at COP 31 | Duration 0:55 Speaking at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on Thursday, Swedish activist Greta Thunberg says genocides and ecocides were coming all along, and that basic needs might soon become luxuries. This is the first UN climate change conference Thunberg has attended in five years.

This year, the stakes were high

Notably, this year's summit was the first to take place after the UN's environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 C — a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify, including through heat waves, floods and droughts.

But it's also marked by competing priorities that threaten to sideline climate action. The collapse this time is against the backdrop of competing crises, including wars and public outcry over the cost of living, that have distracted political attention from the problems of a warming climate largely caused by human activity.

What's next for COP31?

That's it for COP31. The annual summit requires consensus when finalizing agreements. That means: no consensus, no deal. Existing frameworks and agreements established in previous years are still in effect.

The next UN climate summit will take place next year in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

World.title: Tenants in Madrid say Toronto-based Brookfield is pricing them out of formerly public housing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At a Madrid apartment complex just outside the city's centre, red maple leaves hang upside down in windows along with defiant posters urging Canadian investment money to get out of their neighbourhood.

"They are pushing us out of our houses," said Rafael Cuadrado, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

The main target of the residents' wrath is Toronto-based Brookfield Corporation.

A sign on a window of a Madrid apartment accuses Toronto-based Brookfield of treating tenants unfairly. In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield said it complies with all 'applicable Spanish tenancy legislation, including statutory tenant protections and extension requirements.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

One of Canada's premier financial and investment institutions, Brookfield owns 900 units in Cuadrado's residential complex, along with approximately 4,100 others around the Spanish capital.

Cuadrado and other residents accuse Brookfield of planning to let their leases expire and then flip their homes for market prices that few here can afford. He says several of his neighbours have already received notices from Brookfield's management company informing them their tenancies will not be extended.

CBC News has seen one letter sent to a tenant who was told their expiring lease would not be renewed and they would have to turn over the keys to their apartment.

It's not illegal, but the residents say it's unfair.

"Our daughter came here when she was two years old. This is our first house ... so this is our life," Cuadrado told CBC News in his living room.

Many of the residents are long-time tenants who moved into the buildings when they used to be part of Madrid's public housing stock. Most pay rents well below the current market rate, as a succession of lease extensions and government-mandated rent caps have kept their outlay relatively low.

Raphael Cuadrado lives in a Madrid apartment complex owned by Brookfield, one of Canada's top investment firms. He and other residents fear the company plans to flip their units when their leases expire. (Jason Ho/CBC)

Cuadrado says he pays 930 euros a month for his 800-square-foot, three-bedroom apartment. The unit would likely fetch about 1,500 euros on the open market.

"Why do we have to leave our house because there is a big investment company coming from abroad to get a profit [from] us?" he said. "No way."

WATCH | Clashes in Spain as thousands protest nation's housing crisis: Clashes in Spain as millions protest nation's housing crisis | Duration closed caption 2:13 Spain saw widespread disruption Wednesday, including clashes with police in Barcelona, as millions protested the country's housing crisis. The demonstrations come one month after the death of an 87-year-old pensioner who had been evicted from her home.

'Vulture funds'

Anger over housing in Spain has hit a breaking point.

The eviction of Madrid resident Maricarmen Abascal in late September, after the 87-year-old woman was unable to pay a hefty rent increase, sent protesters into the streets. Authorities evicted her on the back of a stretcher and she died in hospital a few weeks later.

Her eviction prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an election for Nov. 29, with housing the central issue.

Spain's public unions, which allied with the tenants, are casting money from institutional investors, such as pension plans, as one of the primary villains. And some of them are Canadian.

"'Vulture funds' are what they call them," said Alicia Del Rio, who is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid (Madrid Tenants Union), one of the country's most prominent advocates for renters.

Del Rio blames a succession of cash-strapped Spanish governments for laying out the welcome mat for foreign investors, who she says have in turn treated Spanish residential properties as a commodity to be flipped, with little regard for the people living in them.

Alicia Del Rio is with Sindicato de Inquilinas de Madrid, Spain's most prominent tenants union. (Jason Ho/CBC)

"[The government] gave the message, 'Welcome to Spain, this is going to be your paradise.'"

Canadian owners

Canadian retirement funds and investment firms are designed to seek out safe returns — wherever they can find them. And Spain is seen as an attractive place to grow that money.

Along with Brookfield, Canada Pension Plan Investments has a roughly 900-million-euro portfolio ($1.4 billion Cdn) in the Spanish housing sector, although it's focused on student housing rather than residential homes. It owns approximately 13,000 dorm-type beds across Spain and Portugal, concentrated in cities with large universities.

In a statement to CBC News, CPP said its investments help "expand the overall supply of housing available to students without removing existing homes from the conventional residential market."

HOOPP — Health Care of the Ontario Pension Plan — owns approximately 700 million euros ($1.1 billion Cdn) worth of Spanish properties, including 27 residential buildings and 2,300 Madrid homes.

The Spanish tenant unions haven't raised any specific concerns about HOOPP's activities or its properties.

Whether foreign investment firms are cornering the country's housing market has become one of Spain's most fiercely debated issues.

Numbers from the Bank of Spain say institutional investors control only a tiny share — roughly two per cent — of the country's total housing stock.

The tenant unions, however, say the fact that many of those properties used to be public, non-market housing for middle- or lower-income families matters far more than their share of the national total.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears at a campaign rally in Palma de Mallorca on Nov. 14, ahead of the Nov. 29 general election. (Francisco Ubilla/Reuters)

They also claim that the concentration of apartments in central areas of cities gives companies like Brookfield outsized power to drive up rents across entire neighbourhoods.

Brookfield used to be chaired by Prime Minister Mark Carney, but he had left the company more than a year before it bought the Spanish homes in March 2026 from U.S. private equity giant Blackstone.

Blackstone held the buildings for 13 years. Residents claim Brookfield's intention is to sell the apartments once their existing leases finish.

Residents of the Madrid building told CBC News that when Brookfield eventually puts their apartments on the open market, they believe they could fetch upward of 600,000 euros apiece — a price few of them can pay.

"It is a constant anguish that is affecting our mental health," said Yutzy Fany Vargas Jimenez, who has lived in the complex for 20 years.

Engaging residents

In a statement to CBC News, Brookfield says any allegation that it is forcing people out of their homes is false.

"We comply with all applicable tenancy laws and tenant protections, and allegations that we terminate rental contracts in breach of these protections are inaccurate," said the statement.

None of the residents that CBC News spoke to had suggested Brookfield had cut short an existing lease. Rather, their concerns were about what will happen when their current tenancy contracts expire.

"We are working closely with our local operating partner, to engage with residents and address their concerns, while continuing to invest in the maintenance and quality of these homes and providing opportunities for residents who wish to become homeowners," the Brookfield statement continued.

The company didn't explicitly address whether it plans to terminate leases when current contracts expire, as the residents claim. However, the company did say it will review individual tenancy matters on a case-by-case basis.

Residents of a Madrid apartment complex say Brookfield intends to force them out of their homes when their leases expire. The company told CBC News that all of its rental arrangements in Spain 'reflect the applicable Spanish legal framework, including statutory requirements governing lease duration.' (Jason Ho/CBC)

Election issue

The cost of housing has become a central issue in Spain's upcoming election, although the roots of the problem can be traced back almost two decades.

Sara Herrero, vice-dean for academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid business school, says after the 2008 global financial crisis, Spain was broke and its government turned to private capital to bail it out.

"The situation was really horrible," Herrero recalled, as governments and municipalities were forced to unload real estate they had on their balance sheets.

She said at the time, international funds were among the only buyers willing to inject billions of euros into the Spanish economy, helping banks clean up their toxic debt.

"What if they didn't come? What would have happened with these many residential houses if these supposed 'vulture funds' didn't come to Spain?" she said.

"They were doing a legal thing."

Sara Herrero is vice-dean of academic planning and financial management at EAE Madrid, one of Spain's top business schools. (Jason Ho/CBC)

Soaring prices

But recently, property values in the country have soared, rising 34 per cent in the past five years.

"The problem is the basic economic problem of supply and demand," Herrero said. "It's the perfect storm of low salaries, high population growth and high taxes."

The Bank of Spain also estimates upward of 300,000 homes have been converted to short-term tourism rentals, further displacing long-term tenants.

The left-wing government of Prime Minister Sanchez is trying to harness the housing anger to help with his re-election bid — even though the price hikes have all happened under his watch.

People in Madrid take part in a 24-hour nationwide general strike on Nov. 11 demanding wages that allow access to what demonstrators say is decent housing. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

Sanchez even appeared to give tacit support to the unions leading the general strike, as he passed tenant-friendly decrees that would likely be reversed if he fails to get re-elected.

His opponents on the political right, the People's Party and the far-right VOX, accused Sanchez of creating the crisis by passing legislation that made it hard for landlords to stay profitable, thereby discouraging new supply.

The latest opinion polls in Spain continue to favour a right-of-centre coalition taking power after Nov. 29, although they also indicate Sanchez's party has shown some recent momentum.

Tenant Raphael Cuadrado says he has repeatedly written to the Canadian Embassy in Madrid, hoping someone there can help residents who are worried about their future.

So far, he says he has not received a reply.

"This is day-by-day fighting, and this is not a life," he said.

In a statement to CBC News, Global Affairs Canada said any questions about Brookfield and its activities in Spain should be directed at the company.

World.title: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebecor Inc. CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus Corp. amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.

"Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning.

The Montreal-based telecom, media and entertainment company said on Monday that it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations and that the Vancouver-based corporation is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month.

Quebecor's move comes three years after the federal government approved Rogers Communications' acquisition of Shaw Communications on the condition that Freedom Mobile be sold to Quebecor to preserve a four-player market.

Péladeau told CBC chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that his company has been servicing Freedom Mobile and the Canadian market "pretty efficiently, and our results talk by themselves. We look forward to being able to continue to do the same with the Telus assets."

WATCH | What Quebecor's Telus bid means for your phone bill: Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill | Duration closed caption 4:07 Quebecor has launched a massive $31-billion bid to take over Telus, a move that would crown it Canada’s largest telecom company — and potentially shrink the wireless market back down to three major players in B.C. The CBC’s Lien Yeung breaks down why Telus is pushing back and what this blockbuster merger could mean for your monthly phone bill.

Asked how a merger of this size would help with Canadians' wireless costs, Péladeau said prices continue to fall after his company acquired Freedom Mobile.

"Our earnings are growing, our free cash flow is growing," he said. "Why would you change a successful strategy?"

According to Canada's annual telecom report , consumer prices for cellular services declined in recent years but ticked back up in 2025. Canada still had some of the highest wireless prices compared with other developed countries.

Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. With its $14.77-billion market capitalization and Telus's $21.72-billion market cap, the potential deal would make Quebecor larger than Rogers or Bell by that metric.

Péladeau also framed the proposed bid as a way of protecting Canada's sovereignty, noting Elon Musk's satellite internet provider Starlink services parts of the Canadian market and is likely hungry to expand its operations.

"[Starlink's] business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said, adding that Netflix "destroyed a Canadian industry" despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).

Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, with a $14.77-billion market capitalization. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Telus says it has formed a special committee to review the offer and determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has discovered a number of "significant risks," John Manley, the chair of Telus's board of directors, said in a statement on Monday issued by the company.

Telus also takes issue with how the Quebecor proposal values the company.

Manley said Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns while exploring alternatives.

The federal perspective so far

In its news release on Monday, Quebecor acknowledged that Canada's Competition Bureau — along with other authorities, such as the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada — will need to approve the deal.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.

WATCH | NDP Leader Avi Lewis calls on Competition Bureau to block Telus sale: 'This is the last thing we need': NDP asks feds to block Quebecor's Telus bid | Duration closed caption 10:03 NDP Leader Avi Lewis joins Power & Politics after Montreal-based telecommunications company Quebecor announces its $31-billion bid to acquire competitor Telus. Critics of the potential deal are calling on the federal Competition Bureau to block the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

Carney declined to comment directly on Quebecor's proposal but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players. He didn't elaborate further.

Péladeau said he doesn't think anyone would disagree with Carney's comments, noting that even if there are three Canadian companies, there will still be other competition, like Starlink.

On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party has not yet seen the proposal but would study it and base its judgment on the principle of lowering prices for consumers.

Poilievre also criticized Carney's comments, saying he has never seen "any economist anywhere in the world say that oligarchies ultimately bring prices down.... Once again, Mr. Carney favours the corporate power brokers over the consumers."

NDP Leader Avi Lewis has called on the Competition Bureau to cancel the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

"We already pay some of the highest cellphone prices in the world," he said. "I just think it's so obvious to the vast majority of people who are suffering under this cost-of-living crisis that this is just yet another thing where the big boys just ... swallow up another company."

World.title: Why the U.S. midterms might have ended JD Vance's presidential hopes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the most significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's U.S. midterm elections.

His chances of becoming the Republican candidat e in two years may have suffered a more recent blow, as reports suggest U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president.

"Despite years of work to keep his feet glued to Trump’s MAGA coattails, [Vance] is probably losing any semblance of hope that he’ll get to be a GOP frontrunner in 2028," New York Intelligencer staff editor Chas Danner wrote in an article under the headline "JD Vance’s presidential dream is being snuffed out."

"At the beginning of the year, Vance was widely seen as the GOP’s presumptive 2028 nominee. He may end the year as the presumptive also-ran, if that."

Over at the conservative magazine National Review, senior writer Noah Rothman also weighed in on what he views as Vance's diminishing political fortunes, saying, "Those who invested in JD Vance ’s political stock ... may be looking to offload their holdings."

Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate.

However, since the midterms, Vance's aspirations "have suffered, because he's Donald Trump's vice-president," said Michael Traugott, a research professor emeritus at the University of Michigan's Center for Political Studies, in an interv iew with CBC News.

Exit polls suggested Republicans lost the election over issues relating to inflation and the cost of living, government corruption and the war in Iran.

"The problem is that the vice-president can't separ ate himself very easily from the administration's policies," Traugott said.

Donors express concerns about Vance

According to the Wall Street Journal, after the Democrats' success in taking the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms, some Republican donors began making calls to senior party members a nd expressing concerns that they couldn't back Vance, because he's too tied to an unpopular administration.

This illustrates the challenge Vance faces: Do Republican primary voters want a candidate who has broader support among the general public but isn't directly connected to the president, or will they only support someone who has Trump's endorsement?

There are reports that Trump has grown frustrated with Vance's position on Iran. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters.

Trump hasn’t endorsed Vance or anyone else. Reports have also emerged recently that Vance himself is not so sure about a run, particularly in the wake of the Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.

In Republican primaries, Trump still commands a lot of votes and a lot of respect, Martin Cohen, a political science professor with James Madison University, told CBC News.

"I would definitely think that the front-runner would be the candidate with Trump's endorsement, if he does give one," he said.

Vance blamed Iran war for midterm losses

That means Vance will have to get his boss's approval, as well as the support of the MAGA base, while "trying to distance himself a little bit, at least," Cohen said.

Vance's attempt to distance himself from the administration may have already begun, with possible consequences. Following the midterms, Vance, in a lengthy post on X, levelled much of the blame for Republican losses on the war in Iran.

"If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest."

Vance, who according to reports has for a while privately expressed reservations about the war, has simultaneously argued that there's "no daylight" between him and the president on Iran.

WATCH | JD Vance blames Iran war for midterms. Is he really blaming Trump?: JD Vance blames Iran war for midterms. Is he really blaming Trump? | Duration 1:12 U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blamed deep Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war, in a lengthy online post on Wednesday. U.S. President Donald Trump also acknowledged the impact of the Iran war, suggesting voters were frustrated by high gas prices caused by the conflict.

In response to the X post, Trump agreed Iran may have been a factor in the midterm losses. But he also insisted that invading Iran was the right policy decision.

Trump told reporters that Vance's post should have added, "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."

Soon after the X post, the vice-president, who had been leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, was taken off the file.

Posting on Truth Social, Trump said his administration no l onger needed a deal with Iran and that he wanted Vance to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

Abe Greenwald, the executive editor of Commentary magazine, called Trump's sidelining of Vance a " remarkably skillful work of public humiliation."

Karen Beckwith, a political science professor with Ohio-based Case Western Reserve University, said in an email to CBC News that Trump's removal of Vance from any responsibility for negotiating or interacting with Iranian counterparts "undermines Vance as a potential presidential nominee in 2028."

Meanwhile, Fox News host Brian Kilmeade lashed out at Vance after his interview with Kilmeade's colleague Laura Ingraham, in which Vance said there were some who want the Iran war to go on indefinitely.

Kilmeade rejected that assertion, calling it "another straw man" argument from Vance, while adding that "he never should have been vice-president."

Trump reportedly frustrated with Vance

Beckwith said this could leave Vance without any substantive achievements on which to campaign for the 2028 nomination — unlike potential opponents like Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Republican governors and senators.

Asked about his social media post about Iran at a news conference on Friday, Vance, flanked by both Trump and Rubio, said the president makes the decision, that the president has said he would attack Iran again and that it's his job to support the president.

Vance's comments followed a New York Times report earlier this week that Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how Vance has framed his assessment of what went wrong in Iran, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran.

Accordi ng to the Times, Trump has instead been praising Rubio, a strong supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, as a potential presidential candidate.

While Trump may have soured on Vance, he reportedly has been praising U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, right. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

While past polls have shown Vance as the leading Republican candidate for 2028, a recent poll from Emerson College had Rubio as the top choice.

Presidents in recent history, dating back to Ronald Reagan, have all publicly endorsed their vice-presidents who sought to be their party's candidate for the presidency. That includes Joe Biden's endorsement of Kamala Harris in 2024, despite Biden having been pressured by members of his own party to not run for second term.

"I don't think that Donald Trump is g oing to be shy about endorsing somebody," Traugott said. "Ordinarily, we would think the vice-president would have an advantage ... so the fact that he may be souring on this relationship is very important. Even if they were to say that [Trump] was remaining neutral, that would be a slap in the face of that."

Yet some political observers are cautious about writing Vance's political obituary just yet. Republican strategist Mark Bedn ar told CBC News that V ance has developed good connections to a large donor base within the Republican party over the past couple years.

Meanwhile, Republican strategist Barrett Marson told CBC News that Trump may have actually done Vance a favour by taking him off the Iran file.

"That is an absolute blessing. The less one has to do with this immensely unpopular war, the better you are off politically."

Marson added that there's still a lot of time before 2028, meaning things could improve to Vance's benefit. For example, gas prices could come down significantly, interest rates for homes could drop and voters could start to view the economy in positive terms.

"Two years is just an eternity," Marson said. "Especially in Donald Trump's America."

World.title: Will Canadian workers refuse to handle Israeli goods? Why unions increasingly say they should
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions and workers are preparing for potential battles with their employers.

The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents more than three million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be "hot cargo" and calling for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. The CLC also resolved to cut ties with the Histadrut, Israel's largest trade union organization.

The move followed similar resolutions passed by numerous local and provincial labour groups over the past year, including the Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador labour federations.

Next week, the B.C. Federation of Labour will vote on a resolution that would "support affiliate locals and unions in refusing to engage with" Israeli goods and specifically ask the B.C. government to stop importing and selling Israeli wines.

A BCFL spokesperson said in an email that the union does not comment on resolutions before delegates have had a chance to debate them.

The movement to isolate Israel with economic pressure is growing as its deadly strikes on Gaza continue after a ceasefire deal was signed more than a year ago. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, while Israeli officials say five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

"I think the vast majority of union activists have come to see that this is a situation where people of conscience, and workers of conscience, need to do what they can to oppose Israeli crimes and our complicity in them," said Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee that pushed for the resolutions across Canada.

A report by the UN 's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory including East Jerusalem and Israel stated last month that Israel has continued to commit genocide since the ceasefire. Israel dismissed the charge as part of a "misinformation campaign."

Israel is facing accusations of genocide before the International Court of Justice, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is wanted on an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.

Union says Palestinian workers made request

Levangie, a member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Atlantic in Halifax, says the Canadian government is not doing enough to stop the flow of weapons to Israel, or the import of products manufactured in illegal settlements in Palestinian territories, so it "falls on Canadian workers" to ensure they are complying with their obligations under international law.

Levangie visited the West Bank as part of a union delegation in September and October, where he met with Palestinian groups, including trade unions, who have asked unions in the West to take on this work.

"We're honouring a request that was made by Palestinian workers," he said.

"In that way, it's very similar to the South African context of the 80s and 90s, where South African trade unions, South African civil society organizations, were asking for us to isolate apartheid South Africa until the freedom struggle was won."

Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee, says workers want to comply with international law. (Submitted by Kevin Levangie)

Canadian dockworkers, postal workers and retail workers joined international campaigns declaring South African goods as hot cargo in the 1980s to pressure the country's government into ending apartheid.

Canadian workers also took hot cargo actions to protest Argentina's human rights abuses and suppression of trade unions in 1979 and joined a trade union boycott of Indonesia in 1999 to protest the country's military occupation of East Timor.

Canadian unions have not acted on the CLC resolution, though workers in other countries have taken action.

Italian workers staged a day-long general strike last month, blocking roads, causing rail delays and cancellations and disrupting airports to protest Israel intercepting an aid flotilla that was carrying food to Gaza.

Canada's unions did not participate in a global day of strike on Oct. 30, which saw efforts to disrupt weapons transfers to Israel as part of a broader anti-war protest at 113 ports across 22 countries.

Critic says Israel singled out

The CLC's resolution has created tension within the labour movement, according to Kim Kazur, labour consultant and adviser with the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee advocacy group.

A retired Ontario Public Service Employees Union member, Kazur says she feels unions are unfairly singling out Israel on the world stage and the resolutions are a way to "hide behind" what she views as "Jew hate."

Kazur says unions should "stay in our lanes" and not contribute to "divisive political ideology," adding workers could end up putting themselves at risk of being fired.

"The idea of a union encouraging its members to do some type of disobedience is not OK," she said.

Levangie denied accusations of hate and noted Labour for Palestine regularly collaborates with advocacy group Independent Jewish Voices in its organizing work.

"We in Labour for Palestine are strongly opposed to antisemitism and all other forms of hate," he said.

Advocates say they want to end Canada's involvement in manufacturing F-35 parts that could end up on Israeli jets. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)

Workers could face discipline

Levangie acknowledges a concern about discipline or retaliation by employers if workers refuse to handle certain goods — from components of F-35 fighter jets that are manufactured in Canada, to oranges shipped from Israel to Canadian grocery stores — but says the declaration of hot cargo is the labour movement's "greatest power."

The tactic is often used in the context of labour disputes, says Andrew Stevens, an associate professor at the University of Regina's school of business.

The BCFL issued a hot cargo edict on Nov. 2 — in solidarity with striking Trigon employees with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 523 — ordering workers not to handle Trigon coal and petroleum products.

Moving to concrete action can be complicated, however, especially on a heated political issue.

"If an individual worker engages in this, I think people are going to see it as insubordination, which means that they could be subject to discipline up to and including termination of employment," Stevens said.

If two or more workers deliberately refuse orders to unload goods or procure services, he says that would be deemed an illegal strike.

WATCH | CBC investigates allegations against Israel: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

Stevens says workers will need strong support from their unions and labour organizations if they plan to carry out the CLC's resolution on the ground.

"Its strength is really going to be premised on the support from the unions themselves," he said.

CBC News has reached out to the CLC for comment but has not heard back.

World.title: A small latte and a chat, please: Why this B.C. café owner put conversation on the menu
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Amrin Satani knows what it’s like to feel alone.

When she came to Canada from India in 2011, she didn’t know anyone. It was a quiet time in her life, she said.

"I know how it feels to have so much in your heart and not have anybody to share that with," she said.

That experience is why she started a business dedicated solely to making sure others have someone to talk to.

According to the Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA), 13 per cent of Canadians aged 15 and up say they are often lonely. While it affects all demographics, the association says loneliness can affect youth, seniors, people with disabilities and those suffering from addiction in particular.

Shane Trudell, a registered clinical counsellor and the clinical director of Nightingale Counselling in Vancouver, said few people seek mental health support specifically for loneliness, but it does often come up during appointments.

He estimates about one-third of the population suffers from loneliness — but it can be tough for people to realize.

"When you’re hungry for food, you learned a long time ago how to be aware of that and to go get a meal," he said. "With loneliness, most people are not aware of it. They feel this social hunger and they don’t know it’s something they should go and fix."

And, he said, the cure for loneliness isn’t one-size-fits-all.

For example, you may be busy at home but in need of connection with people outside the house, he said. Or, you may be dating and meeting new people all the time, but really seeking someone to know you more deeply.

Humanity Café

Satani had always wanted to help others; she planned to study medicine when she first touched down in Canada.

It turned out health care wasn’t for her. But that itch to help people remained.

In 2025, she opened You N Me' (Humanity Café) in New Westminster, B.C.

There, customers have the option to order a drink, something to eat and a conversation.

Amrin Satani chats with a customer at her café in New Westminster. (Submitted by Amrin Satani)

"It's for the days when you feel very happy, or you're feeling lonely, or you want to vent out, you want to celebrate a win, or simply you're just not feeling yourself," she said. "You want just another company and you feel that at least I had somebody whom I can just sit with or have coffee with."

Satani sits with customers who ask for a conversation whenever she can.

"I love it. It has no money attached to it. It has no finance attached to it. It has no tip attached to it, but I think it's the best thing people can buy here at the café."

While everything, including connecting with others, often happens online nowadays, Trudell said he’s encouraged by the concept of Satani’s café.

"I love that it’s something that’s in person," he said. "There’s kind of a high bar for entry. A person has to be willing to say, 'Hey I’d like to order a conversation.' You’re more likely to get people who are going to benefit from the experience."

World.title: Satellites are constantly photographing Earth. A Waterloo student has compiled the pictures into one spot
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Satellites are constantly photographing Earth, and a new website designed by a University of Waterloo student is making these photos more accessible to the general public.

Armaan Gupta is a computer science student. As a project one weekend, he decided to make a website, Watched.Earth, when he found out some of his friends were unaware that satellites are perpetually taking pictures of Earth.

When a user clicks on the website they are greeted with an interactive globe. Users can type in an address and will be taken to that place on Earth. The website shows how many satellites passed by over the past seven days, and any publicly available satellite photos. There is also a "surprise me" option, which takes users to a random place on Earth.

A time-lapse feature shows photos from the past 10 years of a specific area. Gupta says the time-lapse feature helps highlight the scale of destruction in war-torn areas.

WATCH | UW student creates website that shows time-lapse satellite images: UW student creates website that shows time-lapse satellite images | Duration 1:20 Armaan Gupta is a computer science student at the University of Waterloo. He recently created and launched the website Watched.Earth that shows publicly available satellite photos from anywhere on Earth, along with a 10-year timelapse of any location.

Gupta says seeing the progression of destruction in a war-torn area, such as Gaza, Ukraine or South Sudan can be eye-opening for people around the world.

"We always hear about these kinds of things, but it's never really brought to our attention the scale of the destruction. Like, I can't remember the last time it was made like so easily to see exactly how the shape of a particular war zone country has changed throughout the years," Gupta said.

Watched.Earth shows how many satellites passed over an area within the last seven days, along with the recent publicly available photos taken by these satellites. (Watched.Earth)

Although all the photos on Gupta's website are publicly available, he says compiling the photos from websites like NASA and other space agencies into one place makes them more accessible.

"I think that we should make it more accessible to the public that ... like 6,000 satellites are taking images of you every few hours. And so I think that kind of information should be accessible to everyone," said Gupta.

Not for professional analysis

Although the website is helpful for raising awareness about countries experiencing war, or just a spot for a curious person to go, the resolution of the photos are not clear enough for professional analysis, according to one expert.

Nathaniel Raymond is the executive director of the Humanitarian Research Lab at the Yale School of Public Health.

His team investigates war crimes and mass atrocities by analyzing satellite imagery, primarily from Google Earth and other high-resolution data sources.

Raymond says Watched.Earth allows the general public to access low-resolution imagery from one interface and "allows them to interact with it in a general way, but not to the degree you would if you were analyzing it to detect change."

He says when using Watched.Earth, it can be difficult to make out alleyways between buildings or distinguish between structures.

However, the imagery that his team uses has a very high resolution that allows them to tell the difference between models of cars.

"In the case of Sudan, we can see dead bodies on the ground," he said.

Despite the low resolution of most of the images on the website, Raymond says it is useful as an awareness-raising tool for the general public.

"It is important that platforms like this exist to allow members of the public to begin to gain familiarity with what can and cannot be seen at different resolutions, and to begin to understand how in conflict areas, damage happens over time at scale," he said.

A photo of Gaza on the left taken by a satellite Dec. 8, 2015, as shown on Watched.Earth's time-lapse feature. The photo on the right shows the same view of Gaza taken on Nov. 10, 2026. (Watched.Earth)

Gupta says he's received a lot of feedback from users asking for higher resolution photos. He says he's currently in the process of communicating with more satellite organizations to try and gain access to their data.

According to Raymond, higher resolution imagery is often highly access controlled, and isn't updated as regularly as lower resolution satellites.

World.title: Elite B.C. snowboarder's injury highlights financial strain of Olympic dreams
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A debilitating injury that an elite B.C. snowboarder sustained while representing her country has highlighted the financial challenges of pursuing an Olympic dream.

Prince George's Meryeta O'Dine took home a pair of bronze medals in snowboard cross at the 2022 games in Beijing, and travelled to Italy to compete in the 2026 Milano-Cortina Olympics.

But she suffered a fractured ankle in a devastating crash during a snowboard cross training run in February and was unable to compete.

First aid workers treat Meryeta O'Dine after a fall during training at the 2026 Winter Olympics. (Submitted by Meryeta O'Dine)

"I was home by the time my event was happening," O'Dine said. "It was horribly upsetting."

Adding to the heartbreak of missing the competition was financial strain.

O'Dine said she was unable to fulfil contracts and attract future sponsors, and was injured badly enough she couldn't work for five months.

Meanwhile, travel, training and rehab bills have piled up.

"I'm essentially kind of in crisis mode right now," she said. "It's more than what I currently have in my bank account, and the bills I have coming up."

O'Dine said people often don't realize that most competitive athletes, outside of the high-paying professional leagues, are already scrambling to make ends meet.

Canadian Olympic snowboarder Meryeta O'Dine is seen dressed for competition. (Submitted by Meryeta O'Dine)

Big money sponsorships are hard to come by unless you top the podium, while international travel and a weak Canadian dollar make training and competition expensive, she said.

"Genuinely, I've never had a year where I haven't ended my season in debt, because things always cost a little bit more than we are expecting them to," O'Dine said.

Nationwide issue

Advocates have long raised concerns about funding for Canadian athletics.

Can Fund, a charity that helps financially support Canadian athletes, says almost two-thirds of applicants to its program work part-time jobs, on top of their training, just to get by.

It says three in five of those athletes are in debt and live with a negative net income.

"The average athlete goes $30,000 to $80,000 in debt," said Can Fund founder Jane Roos.

A former athlete herself, Roos said she started the program after suffering an injury as a way to help other competitors.

"I've never met an athlete who wants a handout," she said. "But let me tell you, when they win the medals, we sure claim them as our own and we tell the world how happy we are, and proud of them we are.

"And you know what? You can't be the best in the world at anything without support, right?"

In July, the federal government announced it was adding $3 million to the Athlete Assistance Program (AAP), which provides a monthly living and training allowance to about 1,900 qualified athletes.

The funding will see monthly support for senior athletes increase by 5.5 per cent to $2,300 per month.

WATCH | Additional $60M in sports funding: Feds announce additional $60M in sports funding | Duration closed caption 1:28

New funding from Ottawa

Last month, Ottawa unveiled about $60 million in supplemental funding for 62 governing sports bodies, part of a new five-year $660-million sport funding package, including a $2.86-million boost to the Canadian Snowboard Federation.

At the time, Snowboard Canada CEO Dustin Heise described the new funding as "transformational."

O'Dine said she wouldn't be able to compete without the funding she receives from the AAP, and is grateful for the increase.

But she said it's still not enough to cover her travel and out-of-country training expenses, and is currently fundraising to keep her dream alive.

Meanwhile, she isn't letting funding challenges get in the way of her passion for snowboarding.

She's currently in Austria training.

"I don't think I've ever been so excited for a season," she said. "The training just this past week on snow has been absolutely incredible."

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.
