Costa Rican law allows pension operators to invest up to 50% of ROP funds in international markets, a limit Supen described as a way to diversify portfolios and reduce the concentration of risk. The cap is a ceiling, and not every operator holds that much abroad. Over longer periods the funds remain in positive territory. Supen reported nominal ROP returns through October 2026 of 10.85% over three years, 6.69% over five years and 8.63% over 10 years. The regulator cautioned that those figures do not represent any individual saver’s return this year.

Supen advised workers to review their account statements regularly and to judge fund performance over three-, five- and 10-year horizons rather than reacting to short-term swings. The pressure on the dollar has drawn heavy intervention from the Banco Central de Costa Rica. The Central Bank bought $39.65 million in stabilization operations on Friday alone to limit the decline. Through Nov. 20 it had bought $261.3 million in stabilization operations this month, the highest monthly total of 2026, ahead of the $259.1 million it bought in February.

Analysts see little short-term relief. Economist Pablo González of brokerage Mercado de Valores said that as long as dollar supply keeps outpacing weak demand, a major change in the trend is unlikely, and he noted that early December often brings additional downward pressure. That outlook is in line with earlier forecasts that the dollar would keep falling through year-end.

The stronger local currency cuts both ways. It makes dollar-priced goods cheaper in colones, but it reduces the colón income of anyone paid in dollars, from exporters to retirees living on foreign pensions, who already face some of the highest retirement costs in Latin America.

The currency hit to pension statements comes as Costa Rica also debates the future of its main public pension, with a proposed overhaul that could require 30 years of contributions instead of 25. For most savers, Supen’s message is one of patience. Pension savings are built over decades, and exchange-rate moves can reverse, as they did in 2022, when the dollar climbed from about 640 to about 691 colones in the first half of the year.

World.title: Chunox man charged after police say suspected crack found in clenched fist
World.content:
Chunox man charged after police say suspected crack found in clenched fist

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Yhair Edvaldo Tun, 23, a construction worker of Chunox Village, Corozal District, with possession of a controlled drug.

The arrest was made around 12:10am on Saturday, November 21, by a joint police special operations team on mobile patrol along San Antonio Road in Orange Walk Town.

According to police, an officer’s attention was drawn to a man walking quickly away from an alley known for drug peddling.

The patrol stopped. An officer identified himself and informed the man that he would be searched for illegal drugs and firearms.

Police say the man’s left hand was closed in a fist. When he was told to open it, officers saw a buff coloured substance suspected to be crack cocaine.

He was arrested and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station, where the substance was weighed in his presence. It amounted to a gross weight of 0.16 grams.

Tun was formally arrested and charged at 1:10am.

Police say he was cautioned and chose to remain silent.

World.title: San Lazaro man charged with driving under the influence after pickup seen swerving
World.content:
San Lazaro man charged with driving under the influence after pickup seen swerving

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Cesar Cowo, 48, a self employed resident of San Lazaro Village, Orange Walk District, with driving a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

The arrest was made around 12:40am on Saturday, November 21.

According to police, officers on mobile patrol between San Lazaro and Yo Creek villages noticed a white Toyota Tacoma pickup approaching from the opposite direction and swerving on the road.

The officers pursued the vehicle and signalled the driver to stop. He complied.

Police say the driver had a strong smell of alcohol on his breath and was seen staggering when he exited the vehicle.

He was arrested, cautioned and informed of his constitutional rights, then escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

At the station, he agreed to provide a urine sample. Police say the specimen was split in two, with one portion given to him and the other sealed in an evidence bag in his presence.

Cowo was formally charged and chose to remain silent.

He was granted police bail and is to appear in the Orange Walk Magistrate’s Court on Monday, November 23.

World.title: Elhart White remanded after police find 9mm pistol in SUV; claims he gave two strangers a ride
World.content:
Elhart White remanded after police find 9mm pistol in SUV; claims he gave two strangers a ride

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 26-year-old Ladyville man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after police allegedly discovered an unlicensed 9mm pistol inside his vehicle during a checkpoint along the Philip Goldson Highway.

Elhart Ernest White, a resident of the Mitchell Estate area, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Belize City on Tuesday, November 17, charged with keeping a firearm and ammunition without a gun licence.

Police say that around 9:15 a.m. on Monday, November 16, officers conducting a checkpoint between Miles 8 and 9 stopped a black Nissan Rogue travelling toward Ladyville without licence plates.

According to police, an officer approaching the vehicle allegedly observed White, who was wearing a Rangers security company uniform, remove a green object resembling a firearm from his waist and place it inside the vehicle’s centre armrest.

A subsequent search reportedly uncovered a green and black Tisas 9mm pistol fitted with a black extended magazine. White was unable to produce a firearm licence and was detained.

During his arraignment, White pleaded not guilty to both charges and offered an explanation for the weapon’s presence. He told the court that he had given two young men a ride from the Belama area to the highway near Renur before continuing toward Ladyville, where police stopped him and discovered the firearm.

However, due to the nature of the firearm-related charges, the Senior Magistrate did not grant bail, and White was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until February 1, 2027.

World.title: Trial Farm man charged after punching his 65 year old father in the eye
World.content:
Trial Farm man charged after punching his 65 year old father in the eye

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Nassir Anthony Carlos, 28, a labourer of Trial Farm Village, Orange Walk District, with the crime of harm.

The charge stems from a report made by his 65 year old father.

The father told police that around 10:30pm on Thursday, November 19, he was at home when his son arrived smelling strongly of alcohol and went to his bedroom.

About ten minutes later, he said, he heard his son’s voice raised in an argument with his common law wife. The woman came out of the room and sat beside the father on the sofa.

According to the report, the son then approached in a manner that led the father to believe he intended to assault the woman.

The father said he stood up, tried to calm his son and lightly pushed him. He alleged that his son then punched him in the right eye.

The son reportedly collected a bag and left the house. The father called 911, and police responded.

On Friday morning, the father was examined at the Northern Regional Hospital, where a doctor certified his injuries as harm. He requested court action.

Police detained Carlos around 5:30am on Friday. He was later formally arrested and charged.

Police say he was cautioned and chose to remain silent.

World.title: Man charged after partner says he slapped her during argument with mother in law
World.content:
Man charged after partner says he slapped her during argument with mother in law

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Rufino Moralez Jr., 25, a labourer of San Jose Village, Orange Walk District, with the crime of harm.

The charge follows a report by a 26 year old woman, who told police she was slapped in the face by her common law husband during a family argument in San Pablo Village.

The incident happened on Friday, November 20, around 5:30pm. The woman said she was in her kitchen when an argument began with her mother in law over her children, and that her partner intervened and told her to stop arguing with his mother before striking her.

A doctor certified her injuries as harm.

Police say Moralez was located the same day, informed of the report against him, cautioned and detained. He was advised of his rights in custody.

Officers then obtained a warrant and formally arrested and charged him.

Police say he remained silent when charged.

World.title: Lord’s Bank man narrowly dodges jail for alleged rock attack; Was already on prison bus when surety arrive to sign bail
World.content:
Lord’s Bank man narrowly dodges jail for alleged rock attack; Was already on prison bus when surety arrive to sign bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 53-year-old Lords Bank resident accused of threatening another man with a large rock narrowly avoided being sent to the Belize Central Prison after his surety arrived just as he was being transported from court.

Anthony Austin Garbutt Jr. appeared before a Magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, November 18, charged with aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument.

The charge stems from an incident on Monday, November 16, at a property on Willow Street in Lords Bank, where Garbutt allegedly assaulted another man with a large rock.

Garbutt, who was unrepresented, pleaded not guilty. With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

His bail conditions prohibit him from interfering with the complainant, his family members or any prosecution witnesses.

However, Garbutt nearly ended up behind bars when court proceedings concluded before anyone arrived to sign his bail. A commitment warrant had already been prepared, and he was being escorted to the Belize Central Prison when his surety arrived at the courthouse on Coney Drive.

The prison bus was stopped, and Garbutt was brought back to court to complete his bail arrangements, allowing him to avoid being remanded.

He is scheduled to return to court on February 4, 2027.

World.title: “Shut up”: Woman says partner slapped her during family dispute in San Pablo
World.content:
“Shut up”: Woman says partner slapped her during family dispute in San Pablo

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police in the Orange Walk District are investigating a report of domestic violence in San Pablo Village.

A 26 year old woman visited the Trial Farm Police Sub Station and reported that she was assaulted on Friday, November 20.

She told police that around 5:30pm, she was sitting in her kitchen when her mother in law began arguing with her over her children.

According to the report, her common law husband intervened and told her to shut up and stop arguing with his mother.

She said the argument continued, and that he then raised his right hand and slapped her on the left side of the face, causing pain.

The woman was issued a medico legal form. A doctor certified her injuries as harm.

Police have not yet announced any arrest or charge in the matter.

World.title: Trial Farm man charged after woman says she was punched in her own bed
World.content:
Trial Farm man charged after woman says she was punched in her own bed

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Orange Walk police have charged Efrain Munoz, 43, a driver of Trial Farm Village, with the crime of harm.

The charge follows a report made by a 43 year old woman on Thursday, November 19.

She told police that around 7:30am that day, she was on her bed at home when her common law husband arrived, apparently under the influence of drugs or alcohol.

According to the report, he grabbed her right hand and punched it several times, causing her pain.

The woman requested court action. She was issued medico legal forms, and a doctor certified her injuries as harm.

Munoz was detained. On Friday, November 20, police obtained a warrant and formally arrested and charged him.

Police say he was cautioned and chose to remain silent.

World.title: IShowSpeed tests himself against Usain Bolt in new video
World.content:
The trend continued on the Jamaica leg of his Caribbean tour in April, where he participated in a relay at the National Stadium.

This meeting with Bolt, however, he describes as a lifelong dream

“This episode is so important to me. Like, my name literally has Speed in it. Obviously, I take every episode I do very seriously. But this one, I’m taking it more to the heart. I’m training so I can impress Usain Bolt, the GOAT,” he said.

He added, “My whole life I’ve been waiting for this moment. I still picture that little boy on his…on his mom’s computer, at my mom’s house, watching Usain Bolt run, watching his highlights, watching his sprints…So, I got to make that little boy happy,” he shared.

Boldon and Bolt were both present for the one-man race, in which Speed attempted to beat his training time of 10.72, passing on encouragement and guidance.

The sprinting sensation ribbed Speed even as he gave advice.

“You guys think track and field, easy,” Bolt joked, but admitted that he was genuinely impressed with the efforts from the youngster

“[He has] competitive mindset that’s why he’s pissed,” Bolt shared after one failed attempt ending in a time of 10.50.

“I think overall, he might be disappointed. But if you ask any track person, it’s impressive,” Bolt added.

When questioned on whether Speed was in Bolt’s league, the sprinter responded: “No, no, no. That’s a different story,” with a laugh.

For Speed, who eventually hit 10.35, his excitement at being guided by Bolt was immense

“This is a very exciting day for me, man. It’s like I was playing baseball with my dad, you know, like the classic,” the streamer said.

Speed expressed excitement for the journey, acknowledging Bolden’s caution that the work will be extremely difficult.

World.title: Opposition senator questions Government’s commitment to accountability
World.content:
In this video grab Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson makes her contribution to the debate on the asset tax in the legislature.

Opposition Senator Kisha Anderson has accused the Government of practicing accountability “only when it is convenient, when the questions are comfortable or when the answers are favourable”.

Anderson made the accusation Friday, during her contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Nation Debate in the Senate.

“Every Jamaican has the right to ask, ‘Weh di money deh?’, and every government has a responsibility to provide an honest answer and to account for its decisions, expenditure and performance,” said Anderson. She noted that while elections give governments the authority to govern, “what they do not give governments is the authority to operate without scrutiny”.

“The Jamaican people do not surrender their right to ask questions when they cast their ballots. Neither do they relinquish their right to know how their taxes are being spent, whether public commitments are being honoured, or whether the decisions taken in their name are improving their lives,” Anderson remarked.

She argued that accountability is not a foreign concept that Jamaica must now discover, the country having demonstrated, through experience, what can be achieved if it is taken seriously. The JMMB Director pointed to 2013 when the public debt stood at 147 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) and the steps taken, with the involvement of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and bipartisan support in the Parliament, to turn the situation around.

About the state of affairs in 2013, Anderson said, “I will not debate how we got there, as I know we all know that since independence both political parties have held state power.

“So in 2013 Jamaica had been to the IMF before, we had signed past agreements, but this time something had to be different. In May of that year when the IMF approved the 4-year Extended Fund Facility for Jamaica, it came with accountability – clear targets, strict reporting requirements and consequences for failing to meet our commitments”.

Anderson highlighted that requirements for public disclosure allowed Jamaicans to know whether their government was doing what it had promised, “And importantly, we strengthened accountability through legislation”. In this regard, she pointed to the reinforcement of the fiscal rules in 2014, establishing the framework for reducing public debt to 60 per cent of GDP by 2025/26.

Said Anderson: “The IMF programme changed the terms of accountability in effect from ‘trust us’ to ‘show us’ and accountability did not stop there. As a responsible Jamaican collective, we were mature enough under the leadership of Dr Peter Phillips at the Ministry of Finance to establish the Economic Programme Oversight Committee (EPOC)”.

Anderson told her fellow lawmakers that EPOC was part of the then Government’s commitment to transparency, led by the independent private sector. She noted that it brought together representatives from business, trade unions, civil society and the State with a straightforward mandate to monitor whether the Government was meeting its targets and report its findings to the Jamaican people, plainly and regularly.

“Every quarter, EPOC reported publicly on performance relative to target and any risks that existed. EPOC engaged with the Jamaican people and in one such engagement with residents in Swallowfield, (now) Government Senator Keith Duncan said, ‘To have oversight means that you hold the Government, any Government, to do what dem supposed to do.’

“Any Government; EPOC was not a partisan instrument. It began under one administration and continued under the next,” Anderson highlighted.

She reminded that in 2016, Prime Minister Andrew Holness re-established EPOC and told its members that it was “‘very important that the Government be kept on its toes.’”

She cited that even after the IMF arrangements ended, the Government signed a memorandum of understanding to keep EPOC in place because Jamaica had recognised the value of independent oversight.

The Opposition lawmaker also noted that EPOC’s responsibility for monitoring Jamaica’s fiscal rules passed to a permanent statutory body in 2024 with the establishment of the Independent Fiscal Commission. She said temporary oversight became part of Jamaica’s permanent institutional framework, demonstrating how accountability can turn commitments into measurable results.

Anderson also pointed to other examples of accountability, highlighting that a company listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange that raisees money from the Jamaican public must publish its unaudited results within 45 days of each quarter.

“It must file audited accounts within 60 or 90 days of its financial year-end, and a full annual report, including management’s explanation of the numbers, within 120 days.

“If a company expects to be late, it must explain why and indicate when its reports will be submitted. And if it fails to report, trading in its shares can be suspended until it complies. The Exchange exercises this power and publishes monthly regulatory reports identifying companies that are late,” said Anderson.

“Should a Government that spends hundreds of billions of the people’s dollars be held to a lower standard?” she asked.

She added that, “If these reporting standards and consequences are good enough for the shareholders of a listed company, surely they should be good enough for the shareholders of Jamaica: its citizens, the Jamaican people”.

World.title: JPL matches postponed over unpaid referee fees
World.content:
FIFA referee Daneon Parchment (right) looks on as Montego Bay United’s Demario Phillips receives treatment in a Jamaica Premier League game against Harbour View at the Montego Bay Sports Complex on September 23, 2024 during the 2024-25 season. (Photo: Paul Reid)

All Jamaica Premier League (JPL) matches scheduled for this weekend have been postponed amid an ongoing dispute over unpaid referee fees, with negotiations continuing between the league’s organisers and the referees’ association.

According to sources, the referees’ association is still owed millions of dollars.

Discussions are ongoing and the parties are hoping to reach an amicable agreement that would settle the outstanding balance, establish payment dates and allow referees to return to the pitch.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Fragile cash
World.content:
A vendor displays torn $100 and $500 bills to the Jamaica Observer.

Vendors, cab drivers, bus conductors, and other Jamaicans whose livelihoods depend heavily on cash transactions say they are taking losses as some of the country’s most frequently circulated banknotes succumb to tearing and fading, prompting concerns about their durability.

The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ), acknowledging the problem, says it is exploring ways to make the notes more resilient.

“It’s too easy to tear, man; soon as you draw them so they split… I’m not comfortable with them,” long-time Coronation Market vendor Nadine Campbell told the Jamaica Observer.

“I have [so] much in my drawer, about $5,000 [worth of] $100, $50, all of them, I just throw them down,” Campbell added.

The polymer notes now in circulation were introduced in 2023, replacing cotton-based $50, $100, $500, $1,000, and $5,000 denominations, incorporating new designs and enhanced security features. The roll-out also saw the introduction of an entirely new $2,000 denomination.

At the time, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke said the upgraded notes have the latest in material technology for greater durability, which reduces the frequency of replacement. That would have a positive impact on the BOJ’s annual spend of about $1.4 billion every year to print banknotes.

Additionally, the new notes have specific markers to facilitate ease of use by visually impaired people.

However, Jamaicans who engage in cash-heavy transactions daily are now doubtful about the notes’ longevity.

“If there’s a little tear, nobody wants it, [and] it washes out easily,” shared a vendor who identified herself as Denneshia.

“It is easy to slide out of your pocket; I don’t like them. But we have to use them because… we have to use them,” she added.

Andrew, who loads taxis plying the Price Rite/Whitehall route, had several $50 and $100 bills with microtears along the edges in his hand when the Sunday Observer spoke to him in Half-Way-Tree.

“They are quick to tear and, as you get a tear on it, it rips off completely,” he said.

In June 2026 the central bank, in an interview with the Observer, had maintained that the new notes far outlast the old cotton-based currency

— up to three years compared to 1.5 years.

When contacted for this story, the BOJ declined to comment on the complaints. However, it did admit that the lower denomination notes, including $50, $100 and $500 bills, are coming back to the bank damaged more frequently than higher denomination notes.

Almost a quarter, around 22 per cent, of the notes in these denominations that it processes are deemed unfit for recirculation.

But anecdotal evidence suggests the number could be higher, as a familiar refrain among vendors and customers with whom the Sunday Observer spoke is that they don’t return the most damaged notes.

Some, like a cab driver who identified himself as Prince, showed the newspaper their stash of damaged notes.

This is not good, look at this,” Prince said, flipping through a wad of torn bills, mostly $50 and $100 notes.

Similarly, more than half of the vendors and customers who spoke to the Sunday Observer said they have damaged bills collecting dust at home.

One vendor, who identified herself as Grace, said she had taken the torn notes to a bank to have them replaced. But that effort failed as the bank refused to take them.

“When I bring it to the bank, they told me to go and find the other piece if there’s another piece to find, but they’re not changing it,” Grace said.

That, she insisted, was opposite to her experience with the former cotton-based notes. “We always could bring them to the bank as long as they have on the serial number,” Grace explained.

She said the serial numbers are visible on the damaged $500, and $1,000 bills she had, but she has since thrown them away “because we don’t know what to do with them”.

A vegetable vendor, Gem, who said she has been selling in Half-Way-Tree for more than 15 years, told the Sunday Observer she has her own collection of damaged notes.

“As you quint [blink] they tear,” she said. “The amount that I’ve gotten I have to carry them and put down at my house, because sometimes how people ginnal you and give you, you don’t even notice. Some of them you can use a piece of tape and it’s good to go, but others…”

“Maybe one day when I am broke and don’t have any money I can draw back for them and carry them to the bank,” Gem added, laughing.

A driver who travels through Spanish Town, Frankie, maintained: “Once they have a rip, that’s it; they don’t have any value unless you take them back to the bank.”

Despite the complaints, the bills seem almost impossible to rip. Jamaica Observer reporters who tried various methods to tear a $100 bill found that it merely bent and wrinkled.

When the Sunday Observer contacted De La Rue, the British company that manufacturers the notes, an employee explained that it would be very difficult to comment without knowing the state of the notes beforehand, including how old they were and how they had been used.

However, the employee said: “If you have to work really hard to destroy the notes and then you are seeing some that are damaged, it suggests that the notes have two very different histories.”

The BOJ has blamed rough handling, including stapling and graffiti, for the state of some of the bills.

It also said in June, that while replacement rates have dropped across all denominations, it is working with the manufacturer to “identify ways to further improve durability, particularly for the lower denominations”.

The Sunday Observer then asked De La Rue whether any changes have been signed off on with BOJ regarding the notes; if so, when are they due to begin production, and whether Jamaicans could expect any tangible changes, for example, a different feel or thickness. However, the manufacturer said it was not able to comment on any conversations it had with any central bank.

In the meantime, Jamaicans who use the lower denominations the most say it’s costing them money.

“It is a loss for me, because when a passenger gives me a torn note I have to just fold it up and put it somewhere; I can’t even pass it on,” said Prince.

Another issue that several bus conductors and drivers on the Spanish Town to Kingston route pointed out was that the notes tend to stick together when they get damp or moist, leading them to give away more bills than they intend.

They explained that this regularly causes conflicts between commuters and conductors.

Similar concerns were shared by a Coronation Market vendor who identified herself as Dimples.

“It is nice, but when it is wet it can be a little tedious because it sticks together… it poses a problem because suppose a shopper comes, and they come thinking it’s one note and… pass it on to me, and I give you the change, and you go to someone else thinking you have the other money, which you don’t; it’s gonna cause a problem… there’s a little friction, and we don’t really want that,” she said.

Regular consumers had fewer issues with the currency, though they still shared complaints about it tearing.

One customer in Coronation Market was complaining about the very issue when the Sunday Observer visited.

Displaying her $500 bill with a small piece missing from the edge, she said: “I don’t have a problem with the money, but there are times when you come and you will give someone, say, $1,000 or $2,000, and they tend to give you back money that is torn. And then now when you try to spend it, nobody will take it, and that is where I have a problem,” she said.

Another customer explained that she loves the fact that the notes can stand up to water, especially with accidental washing.

“So when you check the pocket now after the clothes dry, you find the money, and it’s still all right. It’s not crushed up… So you can use it again. The only problem with it, when it tears, you have a problem, because nobody want to take it from you. But I think it was a good switch. I appreciate it,” she explained.

World.title: Safety sells Jamaica
World.content:
CHANG... my job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang has declared that Jamaica’s continued success in tourism depends heavily on maintaining a safe environment for both visitors and residents, insisting that the country’s natural attractions mean little if people are afraid to enjoy them.

“Safety is part of the product. The most beautiful beach in the world means nothing if people are afraid to walk on it. My job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach,” Chang said to applause last Thursday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated Sandals South Coast in Westmoreland.

The hotel, which reopened to guests on Wednesday after sustaining extensive damage during the passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, was restored over a compressed 10-month period by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects.

Chang said the Government’s investments in national security, coupled with the efforts of the security forces, were helping to create an environment in which tourists could move beyond hotel compounds and experience the wider Jamaican community without fear.

He said the ultimate goal was for visitors to feel comfortable travelling to nearby communities, visiting beaches and local attractions, and interacting with residents.

“[We want guests to] begin to feel free to go on the road and walk, take a taxi, go down to Whitehouse, go down to the beach, down to the fishing beach, buy some fried fish, and jump on any taxi and come back to the hotel without feeling fear,” he said.

“We have made significant progress, and as the ministry responded, with the support of the prime minister, we have made the investment in our security, and our police have responded,” Chang added.

He stressed, however, that safeguarding the tourism industry also means protecting the thousands of Jamaicans employed in the sector, particularly in the communities where they live.

The minister said hotel workers sometimes face criminal pressure as they return home at weekends, despite the industry’s move away from paying salaries in cash.

“Our security forces have delivered a sharp reduction in murder, and we will not ease up. We will keep strengthening policing in our resort areas and the communities where hotel workers live,” Chang assured.

He acknowledged that unemployment and other social challenges continued to contribute to criminal activity, adding that the police were also having to contend with domestic violence and less serious offences that could escalate into deadly confrontations.

Pointing to the impact of increased investment in policing, Chang highlighted an 82.14 per cent reduction in homicides in Westmoreland, which he said had previously recorded more than 100 and, at one stage, over 140 murders annually.

“Today, we have 25 for the year,” he said, while commending the work of the police leadership, including head of the Westmoreland division, Senior Superintendent Othneil Dobson.

Despite the significant decline in murders, Chang cautioned that domestic and interpersonal violence remained a troubling source of killings across the country, requiring more targeted interventions alongside conventional crime-fighting measures.

Describing the trend as “an unfortunate part of the social scene today”, he said the Government was developing a range of interventions involving communities, schools, and the police to address the problem and encourage behavioural change.

He said the police had established the Community Security and Safety Branch, while the Government intended to roll out a major anti-violence programme aimed at encouraging people to report domestic disputes before they turned fatal.

“We intend to embark on a major programme

— anti-violence

— to provide an opportunity for domestic disputes to be reported to the police early, and to avoid the fatal outcome,” Chang said.

He also disclosed that the Government had established approximately 20 domestic violence centres, with men accounting for about 30 per cent of those seeking assistance.

“Not sure what it’s saying

— men reporting threats of violence

— but we are getting responses, and we intend to expand those centres and ultimately begin to get the kind of behavioural change we want in that sector,” the minister added.

World.title: A separate Grammy category for dancehall?
World.content:
Since the nominations in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on November 16, there has been some uproar across social media platforms by fans and some members of the entertainment fraternity alike about the non-inclusion of some notable albums by dancehall artistes.

Some of the albums include God and Time by Vybz Kartel, Eminence by Beenie Man, Heights of Fire by Capleton, Forever Reign by Masicka, NPT by Alkaline.

Some have even suggested a bias towards dancehall artistes.

The 2027 reggae Grammy nominees are Too Too Bad by Buju Banton, The Art of Acceptance by Protoje, Supernova by Runkus, Exile by Chronixx, Brightside by Ziggy Marley, and Lottery by Shaggy.

There has been a call for a separate category for dancehall artistes, while others have argued that renaming the category to Best Reggae/Dancehall Album would suffice.

A few months ago, the JUNO Awards (Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys) announced the renaming of its Reggae Recording of the Year category to Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year for the 2027 staging.

The reality, some say, is that there are not sufficient releases each year by dancehall artistes to argue for a separate dancehall category in the Grammys. The Best Reggae Album category, instituted in 1985, was allegedly on the chopping block a few years ago due to the low number of submissions. This year, the number improved to 119, compared to 73 last year.

Recording artiste, producer, and music executive Ce’Cile, who is a registered member of the Recording Academy, says the Grammys aren’t obligated to do anything to drown out the noise created each year after the nominations are announced.

“They [Grammys] are not obligated to do anything. They gave us a category, and it would be nice to have an additional dancehall category, but there are many other genres that are still not a part of the Grammys,” Ce’Cile told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

She also argued that there hasn’t been the same enthusiasm and support for local award shows.

“The Grammys can do what they want to do. How many of us within the industry are voting members? We don’t even support our local award shows.”

Well-known entertainment attorney and music business consultant Lloyd Stanbury doesn’t support renaming the Best Reggae Album category. Instead, he supports the idea for a separate category for dancehall.

“The dancehall music genre, although born out of the reggae music genre, has evolved and grown to establish itself globally as yet another distinct music genre coming out of Jamaica. Dancehall music has earned and deserves its own standalone category in the Grammys. What is needed is more membership representation in the Recording Academy of both reggae and dancehall creatives to lobby and advocate for change.

“I think we will see more qualified submissions from both reggae and dancehall when Jamaican music creatives take their activities as serious business, inform themselves, and create support teams with qualified personnel,” the respected music industry insider told the Observer.

Music producer, artiste manager, publicist and podcast host Ralston Barrett, who has more than 30 years of experience in the industry and has represented Grammy-nominated and Billboard-charting acts, concurs with Stanbury that a separate dancehall category is needed.

“I think dancehall is more vibrant than reggae right now, so I expected to see more dancehall artistes nominated. To me, it’s a slap in the face to dancehall music. Buju Banton is the only nominee I’d put squarely in the dancehall camp. Some people would include Shaggy, but his music blends dancehall, reggae, and other genres. I was hoping to see Masicka, Vybz Kartel, and Alkaline among the nominees, and I would have liked to see Capleton nominated too,” said Barrett.

Barrett continued: “I’d like to see two separate Grammy categories: Best Reggae Album and Best Dancehall Album. Right now, I don’t think we have the numbers to make a strong case for that, though. Our industry needs to get more organised and united, do more to strengthen both genres, and encourage more eligible Jamaican music professionals to join the Recording Academy as voting members. Putting dancehall by itself could encourage more submissions. A category of our own would give artistes even more reason to submit.

“We also need more dancehall artistes making strong albums. Once the album is done, you still have to market it, network, and get people to hear it. When an artiste wins, people are quick to curse the artiste or the team. Give them credit for putting in the work. And where are our own award shows in Jamaica? We should be honouring our music and the people who make it right here at home,” he charged.

Music executive, Grammy-nominated producer, and former chair of the Grammy reggae committee Cristy Barber poured cold water on the assertion that no dancehall artistes were nominated this year.

“Although some of the predictions that were spoken about were not among the six nominees this year, there are three deejays nominated — Buju, Shaggy and Runkus — this year. So there is a dancehall presence. Hard-core, crossover, however you see it, they are still dancehall. So, renaming the category probably won’t change the problem some have with the title just being reggae. But the Academy looks at the category as all-inclusive — reggae and dancehall,” Barber reasoned.

Dancehall artistes who have won the Best Reggae Album award over the years include Shabba Ranks, Beenie Man, Sean Paul, Buju Banton, and Shaggy.

World.title: ODPEM chief saw trouble long before audit
World.content:
Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management head office at Haining Road in St Andrew.Photo: Joseph Wellington

INTERNAL Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) correspondence seen by the Jamaica Observer show that Director General Commander Alvin Gayle had long held concerns about several of the issues raised by the auditor general in a report tabled in Parliament last Tuesday.

In its report the Auditor General Department said its team members who inspected warehouses holding Hurricane Melissa relief supplies found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables, and 15 unopened containers that had not been recorded in ODPEM’s inventory, exposing serious gaps in how the agency accounted for and safeguarded donated goods.

The report also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were not included in the donation schedules maintained by ODPEM.

The auditor general also raised concerns about the conditions in which relief supplies were being stored, given the presence of insects on the packaging of some consumable items.

Additionally, the inspection exposed a basic problem with the agency’s record-keeping. ODPEM did not provide auditors with store records showing the quantities of goods that should have been in Warehouse 3. This meant the auditors could not compare what they physically counted with the supplies recorded as received since November 2025 or those distributed during the period under review.

Sunday Observer sources have since pointed to repeated efforts by Gayle to address the issues before the auditor general’s report.

These include a memo dated June 22 in which Gayle wrote to the entity’s then logistics manager seeking urgent information on the agency’s readiness for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

In the memo Gayle pointed to a previous correspondence one month earlier in which he had already requested the information which had not been submitted by the logistics manager.

“Reference is made to my memorandum dated May 21, 2026, directing the completion and submission of the Hurricane Inventory Template to facilitate the consolidation and verification of the office’s operational readiness inventory for the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season.

“A review of your submission has revealed that the information provided was materially incomplete and required significant intervention by the Office of the Director General to address critical gaps. This situation is both disappointing and unacceptable,” said Gayle in the June memo.

He pointed out that the initial response from the logistics manager failed to adequately capture or provide the required information relating to all Starlink devices, including their current locations, operational status, assigned custodians, deployment details, and other relevant tracking information;

Gayle added that the logistics manager failed to provide generator inventories, including donor information, generator capacities, current locations, operational status, and additional information required under the General Stores section, including inventory balances, stock status, and other supporting details necessary for effective operational planning and reporting.

“The purpose of the exercise was to provide the Director General’s Office with a comprehensive and accurate inventory position. It is therefore unacceptable that such fundamental omissions were not identified and addressed prior to submission. The information requested falls squarely within your remit and should already have been known, maintained, and readily available through established inventory management processes and systems.

“The fact that the Office of the Director General found these significant gaps in the records that have been provided by you demonstrates a serious deficiency in the preparation, verification, and quality assurance of the submission,” added Gayle.

He directed the logistics manager to immediately review the inventory management and reporting processes within the Logistics Unit and provide a written report to include: The reasons for the incomplete submission; the measures being implemented to ensure inventory records are maintained accurately and in real time; the quality assurance mechanisms that would be instituted to prevent a recurrence of this issue and; any outstanding inventory information that remains to be verified.

“The maintenance of accurate inventory records is a fundamental operational requirement, particularly in the context of disaster preparedness, emergency response, donor accountability, and audit compliance. I expect immediate corrective action and sustained improvement in this regard. Please treat this matter with the urgency and seriousness it warrants,” said Gayle.

Days later Gayle again wrote to the logistics manager expressing concern about the receipt, storage, issue and status of the generators donated by the Government of Mexico to Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The ODPEM director general demanded details on when the generators were received, amount issued and how many were still in storage.

By August an obviously frustrated Gayle wrote to the logistics manager expressing displeasure over the management of the department and his failure to maintain proper records of the supplies and donated items donated to ODPEM.

“These matters fell directly within the core responsibilities of the logistics manager, particularly the maintenance of accurate and up-to-date inventory records, the proper accounting for equipment and supplies received and distributed during disaster and relief operations, and the preparation and maintenance of records showing the final disposition of items donated by local and international partners.

“ODPEM’s mandate requires the organisation to maintain effective systems for the management, control, and accountability of resources entrusted to it in support of national disaster preparedness, emergency response and relief operations. Proper accountability for these resources is therefore fundamental to the effective discharge of that mandate and to safeguarding the wider public interest,” said Gayle to the logistics manager who resigned from ODPEM in August.

World.title: HORSE POWER
World.content:
Constable Achasha Madden of the Mounted Troop Division shows her affection for Behave after visting Caymanas Park for the first time on Saturday, November 7. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

There is life after racing — and at Caymanas Park, it is a life worth living.

That was the powerful message on Saturday, November 7, as the Racehorse Retirement Programme took centre stage, celebrating almost 500 horses that have been retired from racing in the past five years and given a second career, a new home, and a new purpose.

This year’s showcase featured two of the programme’s key retirement partners — the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) and the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Mounted Troop Division — along with the launch of a new QR code that takes the public directly to the Racehorse Retirement webpage.

The page is a one-stop hub for the programme. It lists the names of the almost 500 horses retired from Caymanas Park in the past five years, provides access to the horse ownership transfer form, shares testimonials on race horse retirement, and carries media articles on the programme’s work.

For Sergeant Everal Alexander of the Mounted Troop Division, retired race horses are not just animals — they are partners in service.

The Mounted Troop is the oldest division in the entire Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), and at present it has 15 equines, ranging in age from two years old to 24 years old.

“We have a veteran in TJ, from a race horse. He’s pretty much retired. So what we do there is pretty much ceremonial duties, regular mounted patrol, school visits — it’s really the lighter side of policing,” Alexander explained.

Alexander said that getting a race horse ready for that lighter side takes patience and skill.

“We normally take them onto the street because some are not used to vehicle traffic, some are not used to noise, and so we use different apparatus like flags. What we do is to take a horse out of its competitive spirit and into a slower, calmer spirit that can be manoeuvred safely through traffic and crowds, in schools and on parade.

“We are members of the retired race horse association, so when a horse is not competitive enough to win, sometimes we are fortunate when we get them, and we just automatically transition into what we do there,” Alexander told the Sunday Observer.

The need, he added, is growing.

“The programme is good and we are on the hunt for more horses because the ones that we have are pretty much aging, so we need to replenish the stock. Wherever we can get those horses, we do most greatly appreciate it,” he said.

The Mounted Troop is also breaking new ground in its own ranks. In 2025, it trained 17 persons at the National Police College of Jamaica — including five females, the first time that has ever happened in the constabulary. At present, out of a cohort of 18 riders, six are female.

Derrick Deslandes, president of CASE, said that retired race horses, have become a critical part of teaching and learning.

“We teach agriculture, and its equine science course focuses on horses and so part of our programme is to expose the students to the horses.

“The programme has been around for quite a while, but we have always done equine sciences. We have just brought in the animals so the students can actually work with the animals directly,” Deslandes told the Observer.

The partnership with Caymanas Park, he said, works for everyone.

“So the horses are finished racing and you may not have the time to feed them and the cost to feed them, so institutions like mine will take them. And we’ll grow them out and raise them and they’ll become part of our programme, our teaching and learning programme,” Deslandes said.

CASE currently has 11 or 12 horses from the programme, but like the police, it is always looking to replenish as horses age or pass on.

“We’re also looking to do a programme to train young people to ride horses. We are looking to establish a programme to train people in Portland to ride horses,” Deslandes revealed.

And fittingly, it was also revealed that the Richard Azan-trained Mojito — one of the most popular horses of his generation — is now preparing for his own next chapter. He will be a stable pony at his barn in 2027.

World.title: Global climate talks have collapsed. Here’s what just happened.
World.content:
Missing the 1.5C target, the Paris Agreement’s most ambitious aim, loomed large in Turkey. Many nations cited the impending overshoot as justification for agreements to make deeper cuts to pollution, take stronger action to prepare for disasters and increase financial support for poorer countries.

But countries rich in oil and gas resources fought to keep any mention of fossil fuels — the main cause of global warming — out of the final text, while wealthy nations were reluctant to commit to specific funding goals.

U.N. Climate Change executive secretary Simon Stiell speaks to media after the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya on Nov. 22, 2026. | Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images

The final impasse that brought down the talks revolved around the future of energy. A coalition of 130 countries, led by the European Union and small island states, demanded the COP31 text include a reference to a three-year-old commitment to phase out fossil fuels. But that was too much for some petrostates. Even recommitting to this earlier agreement was a red line for countries such as Saudi Arabia.

Another point of conflict was a paragraph in earlier drafts of the deal that appeared to put contentious carbon capture technologies on equal footing with clean power sources such as renewables. The anti-fossils coalition wanted those references deleted, arguing they catered to Riyadh’s interests to prolong the use of oil and gas.

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia pushed back. “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5 degrees within reach, and yet called carbon capture, utilization, and storage technologies greenwashing,” said country negotiator Mohammad Ayoub.

In a fractious final plenary session, the EU and small islands, alongside the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland, several Latin American nations and a group of the world’s poorest countries, rejected the deal drawn up by Turkey and Australia, the conference co-hosts.

World.title: Global left rallies in Paris to make ‘not so radical’ case for taxing billionaires
World.content:
The gathering drew lawmakers from the U.S. Congress and opposition leaders from Italy, Germany, Britain and the Netherlands, united in the belief that taxing the super-rich could help the left regain the political initiative.

Their pitch was that Zucman’s proposed annual minimum tax of 2% on billionaires’ wealth is a modest measure that most voters already support — and a potent answer to the far right.

“It’s the status quo which is radical,” said Zucman, who cites polls that put support for his tax in France at 86%.

“Remigration will not make your life better, but redistribution will,” said Elly Schlein, leader of Italy’s Democratic Party.

The summit ran for almost 12 hours in a hall the size of a small community theater that was packed for much of the day. Proceedings spilled into corridors and side rooms, where politicians and union leaders from the U.S., Europe and Latin America met between panels.

The event also marked the launch of the Paris Manifesto, a declaration against “international oligarchy” that pairs a minimum tax on the ultra-rich with protections for journalists and a new ownership model for AI companies. More than 100 researchers have signed it, including Nobel Prize-winning economists Joseph Stiglitz, Esther Duflo, Paul Krugman and Daron Acemoglu.

World.title: Cyprus expels Russian diplomats on suspicion of espionage
World.content:
They added that the two diplomats were forced to leave Cyprus last week and were suspected of working for Russian intelligence under diplomatic cover. The men were in contact with Cypriot citizens who had access to confidential information, the officials said.

POLITICO contacted the Russian Embassy in Cyprus for comment on the matter but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

Moscow was once considered a primary source of foreign direct investment for Nicosia and the Mediterranean island previously served as a banking hub for Russian investors, from arms dealers to gambling firms.

But in recent years, EU sanctions, regulatory pressure and shifting geopolitical alignment have forced Nicosia to move away from these kinds of investments. Cyprus, an EU member, has backed the bloc’s escalating sanctions against Russia in the wake of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

European countries have expelled more than 700 Russian officials from diplomatic establishments since Russia began its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

World.title: COP31 : l’accord capote sur fond de désaccord sur les énergies fossiles
World.content:
Près de 200 pays ont débattu sur différents aspects de la transition énergétique, et notamment l’impossibilité de limiter le réchauffement climatique à long terme à 1,5 ° au-dessus des niveaux préindustriels.

Alors que les négociations touchaient à leur fin, les parties n'ont pas réussi à surmonter leurs divergences. C'est la première fois en 17 ans, à Copenhague, que les négociations de la COP n'aboutissent pas à un accord.

“Il est inacceptable que nous ayons une décision-cadre qui ne fasse aucune référence aux combustibles fossiles […] C’est pour cette raison que l’Union européenne s’oppose fermement à ce texte”, a déclaré le ministre irlandais du Climat, Darragh O’Brien, s’exprimant au nom de l’UE.

Le Panama a qualifié cet accord de “revers”. Les Iles Marshall ont déclaré qu'accepter cet accord reviendrait à une trahison. “Nous n'accepterons pas un résultat qui compromettrait notre sécurité et menacerait notre avenir”, a déclaré la négociatrice Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

La ministre britannique de l'Energie, Miatta Fahnbulleh, qui dirigeait la délégation de son pays à la COP, a déclaré : “La situation exigeait une ambition audacieuse, et nous avons travaillé sans relâche pour tenter de parvenir à un consensus. Il est extrêmement décevant que nous n'ayons pas réussi à y parvenir.”

“Ce texte nous ramène en arrière. Il efface toute mention de la sortie des énergies fossiles, relègue la science au second plan et laisse croire que des technologies dont le déploiement à grande échelle reste incertain suffiront à régler le problème”, regrettait Monique Barbut, ministre de la Transition écologique un peu plus tôt dans la journée.

World.title: Climate deal crumbles amid fossil fuel rows
World.content:
Nearly 200 nations were locked in intense debate over issues involving energy transitions and how to respond to the reality that the world will miss its most urgent climate target — to limit long-term global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

As talks sped toward a conclusion, they were unable to bridge the divides. It is the first time in 17 years that COP talks have failed to reach agreement.

“It is unconscionable that we will have a cover decision that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transition away from fossil fuel, and it is for that reason that the European Union strongly objects to this text,” said Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU.

Panama called the deal a “setback.” The Marshall Islands said accepting the deal would be a betrayal. “We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future,” said negotiator Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner.

The U.K.'s Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who led her country's COP delegation, said: “The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”

Fossil fuel silence

The inability to land a deal on a deeply divisive text illustrates how fraught the talks have become, at a time when the world’s climate targets are drifting further out of reach and energy price shocks, war and inflation are testing governments’ willingness to embrace new pledges.

World.title: ‘Brexit is done’: Theresa May tells Burnham to move on
World.content:
Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership. On Friday, he proposed an “informal brainstorming process” to explore the future relationship, without explicitly putting rejoining on the agenda.

His European relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told POLITICO on Friday that the government would take its time setting out those options, given the divisive nature of the debate.

May said she was “slightly aghast” at the prospect of further negotiations over EU membership, warning that such talks would consume time across government, from the prime minister to officials.

She also accused Burnham of patronizing voters who backed leaving in the 2016 referendum.

“He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer,” she added.

May campaigned to remain in the EU but became prime minister after the referendum, promising to carry out the result. She resigned in 2019 after repeatedly failing to get her Brexit deal through Parliament.

World.title: All flights to and from Brussels, Charleroi airports canceled Monday amid strike
World.content:
Charleroi's management criticized Skeyes for the short notice of the action, saying the company had informed it of the disruption less than 36 hours in advance, despite the airport having prepared to operate normally.

In a statement Saturday, Charleroi accused air traffic controllers of showing a "completely cavalier attitude" toward airlines, passengers and airport staff.

It said thousands of travelers and some 3,400 people working at Charleroi would be affected, and called on Belgian authorities to develop a coordinated plan to prevent recurring disruptions.

“Skeyes has been informed that a group of air traffic controllers will participate in the national strike on Monday, November 23," the agency said in a press release, adding, "Staffing levels will be insufficient to ensure the management of normal air traffic under optimal safety conditions during this period. Consequently, Skeyes is compelled to temporarily suspend the affected services."

Monday's protest is organized by Belgium's main trade unions against spending cuts and economic reforms pursued by Prime Minister Bart De Wever's government.

Public transport across Brussels is also expected to be disrupted.

Passengers have been advised to check with their airlines before heading to either airport.

Tommaso Lecca contributed to this report. This story has been updated.

World.title: 14 missing after Russian strike as Zelenskyy presses US over Patriot missiles
World.content:
He urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s partners through NATO’s PURL program, which allows allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said earlier this month that deliveries under the program, including Patriots, were continuing.

Russia launched 186 drones overnight, including 72 jet-powered models, Ukraine’s air force said. Ukrainian defenses shot down or disabled 161, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations.

Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked 20 Ukrainian regions over the past week, launching around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles.

Many were ballistic missiles, including North Korean-made weapons, he said, accusing Moscow of helping Pyongyang improve their accuracy.

World.title: Morocco: A surreal sculpture park turns the world upside down
World.content:
One of its most striking attractions, The House Fallen from the Sky, was created in 2010 as a tribute to the artist's grandfather. Resting on its roof at a 17-degree angle, the house contains inverted furniture, windows and bathroom fittings, creating a disorientating experience for visitors. Elsewhere, enormous chairs, tables, notebooks and wardrobes invite guests to rediscover the world from a child's perspective.

 

The park also features farmers and gardeners with oversized pumpkin and plant-shaped heads, giant ants surrounding a mud-built structure, and colourful architectural installations. Fourtou says these unusual combinations of human and botanical forms are designed to provoke curiosity and unease, while his oversized household objects recreate the sensations he experienced as a young child exploring his great-grandmother's home. The artist began transforming the site in 1999, before opening it to the public in 2024. Today, Ramakech attracts around 5,000 visitors annually. For Fourtou, the sculptures are less about nostalgia than exploring emotions, family relationships and the memories that shape our understanding of the world.

World.title: Midterms: US Democrats secure biggest House majority in decades
World.content:
The Democrats have won at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, gaining 44 from Republicans in its strongest general election performance since 1992.

 

The latest victory came in North Carolina, where Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated veteran Republican congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Four House races have yet to be decided, with contests in Minnesota and Tennessee still awaiting a result and two Louisiana races heading to runoffs in December.

The result surpasses the Democrats' gains in the 2018 midterm elections, when they picked up 40 seats during Trump's first presidency. Republicans are now set to hold no more than 177 seats, leaving them with one of their smallest House delegations in decades.

The Democratic wave extended across traditional Republican strongholds, the Midwest and the East Coast, reflecting widespread voter frustration over the cost of living, the war in Iran and allegations of corruption surrounding the Trump administration.

Democrats will also control the Senate, where they have secured 56 seats, giving the party its strongest position in Congress in more than a decade.

An ambitious agenda — and high expectations

With control of both chambers from January, Democrats are preparing an ambitious first 100 days focused on household finances, healthcare and government accountability.

Their priorities include reversing Republican cuts to Medicaid and restoring Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired under Republican control. The party also intends to use congressional investigative powers to scrutinise Trump's administration, including the financial interests of the president and his family.

Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, is expected to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes on 3 January 2027.

Unlike outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who struggled to manage a razor-thin majority, Jeffries would have considerable room to accommodate disagreements between progressive and moderate Democrats.

Nevertheless, the scale of the victory has raised expectations that the party will produce tangible results.

“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” Democratic congressman Jason Crow of Colorado told the Associated Press, pointing to Americans struggling with healthcare costs, economic insecurity and immigration enforcement.

Progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez described the election result as “a mandate for change”, while centrist Democrat Tom Suozzi argued that the party should devote most of its attention to affordability rather than investigations.

Confrontation with the White House

The Democratic takeover threatens to significantly constrain Trump during the final two years of his presidency.

Congressional committees are expected to launch investigations into the administration, potentially issuing subpoenas and demanding testimony from senior officials. Jeffries has also declined to rule out a third impeachment attempt against Trump.

The White House has responded aggressively, suggesting that some proposed investigations could amount to criminal misconduct — a claim that has intensified tensions over Congress's constitutional oversight responsibilities.

Republicans, meanwhile, face a difficult period of rebuilding. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chosen to lead the party's diminished House minority, has pledged to fight for American families and regain political ground ahead of the 2028 elections.

For Democrats, however, the immediate challenge is turning an overwhelming electoral victory into effective government. Their substantial congressional majorities offer an unusual opportunity to advance legislation, but Trump's continued control of the White House means major bills could still face a presidential veto.

Fact is: The midterm elections have fundamentally shifted the balance of power in Washington.

World.title: Finland confirms Russia is towing drone-hit cargo ship after Baltic Sea attack
World.content:
A Russian cargo ship hit by drones in the Baltic Sea is being towed out of Finnish waters by Russian rescue vessels after catching fire and drifting into Finnish territory, according to Finnish authorities.

 

Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a post on X that the Sparta II, which had posed a serious threat, had left Finnish waters. He added that "the consequences of Russia's war of aggression are also being felt in our neighbouring regions" and reaffirmed Finland's commitment to maintaining stability and security in the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian-flagged vessel, Sparta II, was reportedly struck by two drones on November 21 while sailing in the eastern Gulf of Finland, west of Gogland Island. The ship caught fire and lost its ability to manoeuvre before drifting into Finnish territorial waters. Its 16 crew members were evacuated, while Finnish and Russian rescue teams worked to contain the blaze.

The attack sparked a fire aboard the ship, forcing its 16 crew members to evacuate. One crew member reportedly sustained minor injuries.

By November 22, Russian vessels had begun towing the damaged ship away from Finnish waters following an emergency response involving maritime authorities from Finland, Estonia and Russia.

Although the immediate danger appears to have been contained, the incident raises broader questions about the security of Russian shipping, the vulnerability of Baltic maritime routes and the possibility of further military escalation near NATO territory.

A Russian military-linked vessel under attack

The Sparta II is a 121-metre cargo ship operated by Oboronlogistika, a Russian logistics company associated with the country's Ministry of Defence.

The company provides transportation and logistical support for Russian state operations, making its vessels potentially significant assets within Russia's broader military supply network.

At the time of the attack, the ship was travelling from St Petersburg toward Kaliningrad, Russia's heavily militarized exclave on the Baltic Sea, situated between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.

Kaliningrad occupies a particularly important position in Russia's military strategy. The territory hosts major naval installations and other military infrastructure, while its geographic separation from mainland Russia makes maritime transportation an important logistical connection.

The cargo carried by the Sparta II has not been publicly established. Finnish authorities indicated that military equipment could not be ruled out, although no definitive confirmation of such cargo was available.

The vessel is also subject to US sanctions, reflecting broader Western restrictions targeting Russian entities connected to military and logistical activities.

Suspected Ukrainian involvement

Finnish military officials reportedly assessed that Ukraine was likely responsible for the drone attack.

However, Ukrainian authorities had not publicly confirmed responsibility in the reporting available at the time. The identity of the attacker, the operational objectives and the precise circumstances surrounding the strike have not yet been independently established.

If Ukrainian involvement is confirmed, the incident could represent a notable development in the maritime dimension of the Russia-Ukraine war.

World.title: Germany tests Kamikaze drones and AI targeting technology in Lithuania
World.content:
Germany's armed forces have begun testing kamikaze drones and artificial intelligence-assisted targeting technology in Lithuania, marking another step in the Bundeswehr's efforts to modernize its military capabilities amid continuing security tensions between NATO and Russia.

 

The trials, conducted at the Rūdninkai military training area near the Belarusian border, involve loitering munitions developed by German defence technology companies Helsing and Stark Defence. The weapons are designed to identify and strike battlefield targets, including armoured vehicles, while potentially offering greater flexibility than conventional precision-guided weapons.

According to Reuters, the tests form part of the multinational Freedom Shield military exercise, which brings together approximately 3,800 personnel from eight NATO countries.

The exercise also provides German forces with an opportunity to evaluate how artificial intelligence can improve battlefield reconnaissance, target identification and military decision-making.

A new generation of battlefield weapons

Often referred to as kamikaze drones, loitering munitions are unmanned aircraft designed to remain airborne while searching for or waiting to engage a target. Once an attack is authorized, the drone flies into its target, destroying itself in the process.

Unlike traditional missiles, which are generally launched toward a previously designated target, loitering munitions can provide military operators with additional time to observe battlefield developments before committing to an attack.

During the Lithuanian trials, German troops tested drones against simulated armoured targets. The aircraft were equipped with inert warheads, allowing military personnel to evaluate their performance without using live explosive payloads.

The Bundeswehr is examining how such systems could complement existing artillery, reconnaissance platforms and armoured formations.

The technology has attracted increasing attention following its extensive use during the war in Ukraine, where both Ukrainian and Russian forces have employed attack drones against tanks, artillery positions, supply vehicles and other military targets.

Their widespread deployment has demonstrated how relatively inexpensive unmanned systems can threaten costly conventional equipment.

However, the conflict has also exposed significant limitations, including vulnerability to electronic interference, communication disruptions and increasingly sophisticated counter-drone defences.

Artificial intelligence enters the targeting process

Alongside the drone trials, German military personnel also evaluated Clarity, an AI-supported military intelligence and targeting platform developed by Helsing.

The software is designed to process battlefield information from multiple sources, potentially including drones, surveillance systems and other military sensors.

By analysing large volumes of information, AI-assisted systems can help identify potential targets and provide commanders with a more comprehensive picture of battlefield activity.

Traditional targeting procedures may require information to pass through several stages of analysis and communication before a military unit can respond. AI-assisted software could reduce some of these delays by identifying relevant information and presenting it to military personnel more efficiently.

Lithuania becomes a strategic testing ground

The decision to conduct the trials in Lithuania reflects the country's growing importance in NATO's eastern defence strategy.

Lithuania borders Belarus, a close ally of Russia, and Russia's heavily militarized Kaliningrad region. Its geographic position places it near one of the alliance's most strategically sensitive areas.

Germany has committed to permanently stationing a combat brigade in Lithuania, representing a significant development in its military posture.

The formation, known as Panzerbrigade 45, is expected to reach full operational capability by 2027, with approximately 5,000 military personnel and supporting civilian staff.

The brigade is intended to strengthen NATO's ability to defend Lithuania and reinforce the alliance's deterrence posture along its eastern frontier.

Testing emerging military technologies in the country allows German forces to evaluate equipment in an operational environment relevant to their future responsibilities.

The wider Freedom Shield exercise also includes conventional military activities such as manoeuvre operations, electronic warfare and cooperation between different branches of the armed forces.

Together, these activities reflect NATO's efforts to integrate traditional military formations with emerging technologies.

A changing security environment in Europe

The trials are taking place against the backdrop of continuing concern among European governments about Russia's military capabilities and the long-term security of NATO territory.

European defence officials have repeatedly emphasized the need to improve military readiness, expand ammunition production and strengthen the alliance's ability to respond to potential threats.

Russia, meanwhile, has rejected accusations that it intends to attack NATO territory and has criticized the alliance's military expansion near its borders.

The opposing positions have contributed to a security environment in which military exercises, force deployments and weapons development carry increasing strategic significance.

The future of European warfare

Germany's drone and AI trials in Lithuania illustrate a wider shift in military thinking across Europe.

Future battlefield effectiveness may depend not only on tanks, artillery and aircraft, but also on the ability to connect sensors, autonomous or remotely operated systems, artificial intelligence and human decision-makers.

The Bundeswehr's experiments represent an attempt to understand how these technologies can operate together in realistic military conditions. Whether the tested systems ultimately deliver the expected operational advantages remains to be demonstrated.

The Bundeswehr itself has acknowledged that battlefield drone success rates can be significantly lower than footage of successful strikes might suggest.

World.title: Marc Márquez wins eighth MotoGP title in Portugal, surpassing Rossi's record
World.content:
Marc Márquez clinched his eighth MotoGP world title this Sunday by being crowned world champion at the Portuguese Grand Prix, held at the Portimão circuit.

 

The Spanish Ducati rider finished in eighth place, a result that was enough to secure the championship mathematically and thus move past the seven premier-class titles of Italian rider Valentino Rossi

Márquez needed to finish at least ninth to guarantee the title without depending on other results. In the end, he took the flag in eighth after Brazilian Diogo Moreira crashed on the final lap.

The race win went to Italian Marco Bezzecchi, on an Aprilia, ahead of his teammate Jorge Martín and fellow Spaniard Raúl Fernández, who completed the podium.

The championship is the tenth motorcycle world title for the rider from Cervera, who also won one in 125cc and another in Moto2. With this total, he overtakes Rossi's nine championships, seven of them in the premier class, and draws level with Italian Giacomo Agostini in the all-time ranking of premier-class titles.

The triumph is particularly significant in view of the difficulties he has faced during the season. At the end of May, after the Italian Grand Prix at Mugello, Márquez found himself 102 points behind the then leader, Bezzecchi.

Marc Márquez, alongside former motorcycle racer Giacomo Agostini, after the end of the Portuguese Motorcycle Grand Prix on 22 November 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

A crash in the sprint race at the French Grand Prix, in Le Mans, forced him to undergo surgery, which also meant he missed the following round in Montmeló. His comeback was hampered by injuries, but from the Hungarian Grand Prix onwards he began a fightback that allowed him to claw back ground and take the lead at Misano.

After wrapping up the championship, Márquez dedicated the victory to his fans and described the title as "very special", referring to the years of work, injuries and recoveries he has had to go through to get back to the top.

World.title: French interior ministry rocked by probe into prefect's leaks to National Rally
World.content:
Five months before the French presidential election, the Interior Ministry is in turmoil. Hugues Moutouh, prefect of Centre-Val de Loire, is suspected of having passed confidential information to the National Rally.

 

On Saturday, the senior official announced that he had asked to be relieved of his duties.

In a statement, shared by the X account of the prefecture based in Orléans, Hugues Moutouh denounced a "campaign of destabilisation" that "goes far beyond" his own case and would target the institutions as well as the prefectural corps. "Through me, it is the very authority of the state that people are trying to attack", he said.

"This offensive comes at a time when some people are methodically working to weaken our institutions, to delegitimise those who embody them and to challenge the very foundations of the republican order", the prefect added.

"Calling me a mole is vile"

At the same time, in an interview with the weekly Journal du dimanche (JDD), published online on Saturday evening, Hugues Moutouh said he was "the victim of a manhunt".

"I have always served the state of one country, France, which I love deeply. Portraying me as a henchman in the pay of a party is odious, calling me a mole is vile," he said.
