World.title: Polish Supreme Court rejects government’s position on Constitutional Tribunal
World.content: Why are you seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s rule-of-law crisis has taken another twist, after the Supreme Court (SN) issued a resolution effectively opposing the government’s position towards another top court, the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), and endorsing that of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. The SN found that TK rulings are only valid if issued by judges the president has sworn in and that they take effect even if the government refuses to publish them. Nawrocki has refused to swear in five TK judges, while the government has refused to publish 85 previous TK rulings. However, the government’s justice minister argues that the new SN resolution is itself invalid because it was issued by judges who were appointed unlawfully. Połączone izby Sądu Najwyższego o wyrokach Trybunału Konstytucyjnego jako podstawie wznowienia postępowaniahttps://t.co/DzgL6aDTGK pic.twitter.com/GpiGbWMvNn — Sąd Najwyższy (@SN_RP_) November 18, 2026 On Wednesday, the SN issued a resolution in response to questions over the validity of rulings issued by the TK. It found, among other things, that a valid TK ruling can only be issued by a panel of judges who, after being elected to the tribunal by parliament, have “taken an oath before the president, that is, in his presence”. Those latter words relate to a key dispute that has arisen around the TK. The government’s majority in parliament has this year chosen eight new TK judges, who would now form the majority on the 15-seat tribunal. However, Nawrocki has refused to receive the oath of five of those judges, citing concerns over the method of their appointment or their qualifications. Those five judges have instead arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies before a notary and then forwarded their oaths to the presidential chancellery. They and the government argue that this meets the requirement for them to take up their seats. However, Nawrocki and the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former government, reject that position and say that the judges cannot take up their seats on the court until the president receives their oath in person. The Supreme Court has now effectively endorsed their stance. Meanwhile, the SN also addressed another contentious issue. Since March 2024, the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – has refused to publish any of the 85 TK rulings issued in that time. That is because, under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, three judges were unlawfully appointed to the TK. The current government argues that TK rulings only take force when published in the official Journal of Laws. Indeed, so did the former PiS government when, in 2016, it refused to publish TK rulings that contradicted its judicial policies. However, the SN has now deemed that valid TK rulings enter force even if not published. “In a situation where the body responsible for publishing TK rulings fails to fulfil this obligation…these abuses by the executive power cannot affect the universally binding force of TK rulings,” said SN judge Aleksander Stępkowski, quoted by the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily. However, the validity of the SN’s resolution is itself contested as it was issued by judges whose own status is questioned. That is because they were appointed to the court through the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS) after it was overhauled by PiS in a manner that brought it under political control and rendered it invalid, according to Polish and European court rulings. The current government has generally rejected decisions issued by such “neo-judges”, as it calls them. And that position was reiterated on Thursday by justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who wrote that “the neo-judges in the Supreme Court have adopted a so-called resolution”. “Any decision issued with the participation of even one person appointed through the politicised National Council of the Judiciary after 2017 is a non-existent judgement,” he added. Neosędziowie w Sądzie Najwyższym podjęli nibyuchwałę połączonych trzech izb (III CZP 41/26), uznając, że nieopublikowane rozstrzygnięcia Trybunału Konstytucyjnego mają moc powszechnie obowiązującą, a za wyrok TK można uznać tylko taki wydany przez osoby, które złożyły ślubowanie… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 18, 2026 The SN’s resolution comes as the TK itself is embroiled in a crisis. At the end of October, the eight new TK judges chosen by parliament this year took control of the tribunal and announced that its chief justice, Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, supported by Nawrocki and the SN’s chief justice, Zbigniew Kapiński (also a “neo-judge”), has rejected that move as an illegal “coup d’état” and claims he is still in charge of the tribunal. However, police have prevented him from entering the building. On Wednesday, just as the SN was issuing its resolution, the eight government-backed TK judges announced that they had lifted Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution at the request of Żurek. World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Looking for a Team Challenge in Prague? This Venue Has 25 Different Tests
World.content:
Looking for something to do in Prague beyond the usual sightseeing?

TEPfactor offers an indoor adventure combining physical challenges, puzzles and teamwork, just a short walk from Wenceslas Square.

Located at Vodičkova street, the 1,500-square-metre venue takes inspiration from the TV show Fort Boyard.



Its main attraction features 25 challenges testing participants’ strength, logic, dexterity, patience and ability to work together.

Visitors compete in teams of two to six people, tackling a series of tasks that require both physical effort and problem-solving skills. The main game takes approximately three hours, making it an option for groups of friends, families and visitors looking for an alternative to traditional tourist activities.

For those seeking something more intense, TEPfactor also operates Fear House, a horror-themed attraction with several levels of difficulty. Options range from group experiences to more demanding individual challenges.

The most intense version, Hardcore + Kidnapping, includes a staged kidnapping scenario and must be arranged in advance.

The venue also caters to organised groups. Schools can book activities designed to encourage communication and cooperation, while companies can use the challenges for team-building events. Birthday celebrations, stag and hen parties and private gatherings are also among the available options.

Beyond the adventure games, TEPfactor offers event space for larger gatherings. Facilities include a theatre-style room with a stage, sound equipment and the option to arrange a DJ and catering.

Additional entertainment can include pub quizzes, stand-up comedy, mobile casino activities and theatre performances.

Reservations can also be made through its online booking system.

World.title: Prague Pride to Host Studio 54-Inspired New Year’s Eve Party
World.content:
Prague Pride will celebrate the arrival of 2027 with a Studio 54-inspired New Year’s Eve party at Slovanský dům, bringing disco music, drag performances and LGBTQ+ matchmaking.

The event, titled Disco Royale, will take place on December 31, 2026, from 8 p.m. until 4 a.m. at Empire Hall in Slovanský dům, Prague 1.



Organisers are promising a night inspired by the legendary New York nightclub Studio 54 and the disco era of the late 1970s.

Guests are encouraged to dress accordingly, with sequins, satin, colourful suits, platform shoes and extravagant accessories all part of the suggested dress code.

The programme will combine live entertainment with music and activities throughout the evening. A queer and drag cabaret will feature performances by Radek Horáček, Hugo Seneši, Lukas Illusion, Rudy Daddy, Melancholia Blackbile and Barbora Elz.

Music will be provided by DJ Jan Witek, who will play a mix of disco classics by Donna Summer, ABBA, the Bee Gees and Chic, alongside modern disco-house and contemporary party tracks. DJ Koko will also join the line-up.

Beyond the dance floor, visitors can take part in LGBTQ+ matchmaking activities, including a Traffic Light Dating System and an interactive game designed to help guests meet new people. A Studio 54-themed photo booth and a New Year’s raffle are also planned.

A dedicated chill-out area will offer a quieter space away from the music, while the bar will serve a signature New Year’s Eve cocktail.

Tickets are available in two categories. Basic admission costs 890 CZK and includes a welcome drink, a complimentary snack and access to open seating in the main hall and lounge area.

VIP tickets cost 1,390 CZK and include guaranteed table seating, access to a second-floor balcony and the same welcome refreshments.

Tickets are available through December 30, or until the event sells out. Proceeds from ticket sales support Prague Pride’s work with LGBTQ+ people in Czechia.

World.title: Black Friday in Czechia: When to Shop and How to Spot Fake Discounts
World.content:
Black Friday will officially fall on November 27 this year, but shoppers in the Czech Republic will not have to wait until the final Friday of November to find deals.

Major retailers have already turned the traditional one-day sale into a weeks-long campaign, with promotions appearing in several rounds throughout the month.

While stricter consumer protection rules have made misleading discounts harder to advertise, shoppers still need to be careful. Some retailers continue to use pricing strategies that make reductions look more attractive than they really are.



When does Black Friday 2026 start in Czechia?

Black Friday 2026 takes place on Friday, November 27. Originally an American shopping tradition held the day after Thanksgiving, the event has gradually become one of the biggest retail campaigns in Europe.

In the Czech Republic, however, the sales period now extends well beyond the official date. Many retailers begin advertising discounts in early November, gradually introducing new offers under campaigns commonly marketed as Black Week or Black Month.

The extended shopping period also serves a practical purpose. Spreading orders across several weeks helps online retailers manage warehouse operations, deliveries and payment systems, avoiding the logistical pressure that would come with concentrating all purchases into a single day.

The country’s biggest retailers are following slightly different approaches.

Alza.cz typically divides its Black Friday campaign into several stages, with different product categories and limited quantities of discounted items introduced throughout November. The final round is expected to coincide with the week of November 23–29.

Datart also rotates its promotional selection during the month. Its offers cover everything from large household appliances to smaller electronic devices, with discounts available both online and in its physical stores.

Allegro, which has incorporated the former Mall.cz into its marketplace, uses a different approach. Its platform features daily promotions from a large number of independent sellers, with special offers continuing throughout November and reaching their peak on November 27.

Notino focuses its Black Friday campaign on selected brands and promotional discount codes. Its broader offers are concentrated around the main Black Friday shopping period.

Black Friday or Cyber Monday when should you buy?

The official Black Friday date is not necessarily the best opportunity to make every purchase.

Cyber Monday, which falls on November 30 in 2026, follows the Black Friday weekend. Originally introduced as an online equivalent of traditional in-store sales, it has become another important date for retailers, particularly those selling electronics and IT equipment.

For some products, waiting until Monday could pay off. Retailers may review their weekend sales figures and introduce additional reductions on items that have not performed as expected. Televisions, laptops, monitors and computer components are among the categories worth monitoring.

How to recognise artificial discounts

Although Czech consumer protection legislation has introduced stricter rules on how retailers advertise price reductions, promotional labels do not automatically mean a product is being sold at its best price.

Under the European Omnibus Directive and the related amendment to the Czech Consumer Protection Act, retailers must generally display the lowest price charged during the 30 days preceding a price reduction.

This requirement is intended to prevent sellers from temporarily increasing prices before a sale and then advertising a seemingly substantial discount against the inflated amount.

Nevertheless, consumers should not rely exclusively on the percentage displayed next to a product.

Independent price-comparison services and historical price-tracking tools can help establish whether an offer represents a genuine saving. Checking how much an item cost in the weeks before Black Friday is often more useful than comparing its current price with the original recommended retail price.

World.title: Prague Has 2,600 Homeless People, but Shelters Cannot Keep Up
World.content:
Around 2,600 people are living on the streets of Prague, according to estimates by the non-profit organization Naděje.

While the city and its municipal districts provide various forms of assistance, social workers say existing shelters and day centres are struggling to meet demand.



Prague’s support system includes overnight shelters, emergency accommodation, low-threshold day centres, professional counselling and temporary housing programmes. The city also operates hostels, provides grants to municipal districts for homelessness-related projects and works with non-profit organizations.

One of the main forms of assistance is provided by social curators, municipal employees who work directly with people living on the streets. Prague 1 and Prague 2 both employ their own teams.

Prague 2 established a food bank distribution point in the courtyard of the New Town Hall (Novoměstská radnice). People in need can collect food and basic hygiene supplies there.

Social services struggle to meet demand

Despite these initiatives, the capacity of Prague’s existing facilities remains a major concern.

Aleš Strnad, head of services at Naděje’s Prague branch, said the number of places available in day centres and overnight shelters was insufficient.

According to Strnad, opposition from local residents is one of the main obstacles to opening new facilities. He pointed out the contradiction between resistance to new centres and public complaints about the growing number of people living in poor and unhygienic conditions on the streets.

The city also introduces additional measures during the winter months. From December until the end of March, its humanitarian programme allows people experiencing homelessness to spend the night in heated facilities free of charge.

World.title: Prague’s First Christmas Market Opens at Náměstí Míru With Higher Prices
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas market season began on Friday, November 20, with the opening of the traditional market at Náměstí Míru.

Visitors can expect higher prices this year, with food and drinks costing around 10% more than in 2025.

It will operate daily from 10 am to 8 pm until December 24. The layout remains largely the same as last year, although the Christmas tree features several new decorations.



Security measures have also been introduced at the entrances, where reinforced concrete barriers have been installed to protect visitors.

Vendors have agreed on a common price for mulled wine, which now costs 90 CZK for a 200 ml cup, up from 80 CZK in 2025.

Prices for other food and drinks vary depending on the stall. Visitors will find the following options:

– Trdelník – 130 CZK

– Grilled sausage – 140 CZK

– Chocolate-covered strawberries – 180 CZK

– Fish soup – 85 CZK

– Hot waffles – 160 CZK

– Crêpes – from 120 CZK

– Carp fish fingers – from 159 CZK

– Lángos – from 120 CZK

– Mead (200 ml) – 120 CZK

– Hot slivovitz – 100 CZK

– Hot chocolate – 130 CZK

– Cheese sticks – 180 CZK

The remaining Christmas markets across Prague will open gradually in the coming weeks.

The city’s two largest markets, located at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, are scheduled to open on Saturday, November 28.

These central markets will also stay open longer than the others, continuing until January 6, 2027, reflecting their popularity with international visitors and tourists.

World.title: Smartwings Could Adopt Ryanair Model Under New Owner Pegasus
World.content:
Smartwings could move closer to the business model used by Ryanair following its acquisition by Turkish airline Pegasus Airlines.

The new owner plans to expand the Czech carrier’s fleet and route network, while potentially reducing its reliance on travel agencies and tour operators.

Pegasus completed its acquisition of Smartwings and Czech Airlines (ČSA) on October 1, 2026. The Smartwings brand will remain in place, as will its headquarters in Prague, but changes to its commercial strategy are expected.



Smartwings may rely less on travel agencies

One of the potential changes concerns how Smartwings sells its tickets.

The Czech airline has traditionally depended heavily on charter flights arranged through travel agencies and tour operators, including Blue Style, Čedok, Exim Tours and Fischer. It has also recently extended its cooperation agreement with German travel group TUI.

Pegasus has experience moving away from this model. Originally established as a charter airline in the 1990s, it switched to a low-cost business model, focusing increasingly on direct ticket sales.

Smartwings could follow a similar direction, although Pegasus has not yet announced a detailed restructuring plan.

Additional services are another important part of the low-cost model. During the first nine months of 2026, they accounted for 36 percent of Pegasus’ revenue, generating approximately €31 per passenger. At Ryanair, ancillary services represented around 32 percent of revenue in the last financial year, or roughly €24 per passenger.

Smartwings already charges extra for services such as seat selection, checked baggage, onboard refreshments and booking changes.

Pegasus plans more aircraft and destinations

Expanding the route network is another priority. Under its winter 2026 schedule, Smartwings operates direct flights from Czech airports to 39 destinations, alongside services from Poland, Slovakia and Hungary.

The airline has recently added scheduled connections to Bergen, Venice and Lisbon, while increasing flight frequencies to Porto, Bilbao and Toulouse.

Pegasus has also identified opportunities to expand into the Middle East, North Africa and markets including Armenia, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan.

World.title: Michelin Guide Adds Four New Starred Restaurants in the Czech Republic
World.content:
The Michelin Guide has expanded its selection in the Czech Republic, awarding stars to four new restaurants.

The latest edition brings the country’s total to 13 Michelin-starred establishments, while 27 restaurants have received the Bib Gourmand distinction for good food at reasonable prices.

The new selection was announced at a gala ceremony, marking the second year of the Michelin Guide’s official presence in the Czech Republic.



All nine restaurants recognised in the inaugural edition have retained their distinctions, while four newcomers have joined the list.

Among the new one-star recipients is Zlatá Praha, located on the rooftop of the Fairmont Golden Prague hotel. The restaurant continues the tradition of the former establishment at the same location, previously housed in the InterContinental Hotel.

Another newcomer is Reason, a restaurant on the top floor of the Masaryčka building in central Prague. Designed by Zaha Hadid Architects and developed by Penta, the building offers panoramic views of the city. The restaurant is led by chef Jan Horák.

The third new addition is Taro, a contemporary Vietnamese restaurant inside the Dunaj Palace on Národní třída. The restaurant was founded by brothers Khanh Ta and Giang Ta.

The fourth newcomer is Salabka, a fine-dining restaurant in Prague’s Troja district. The establishment combines a restaurant with its own winery, distillery and accommodation. Its kitchen is led by chef Petr Kunc.

Papilio retains its two Michelin stars

The Czech Republic’s only two-Michelin-star restaurant remains Papilio, led by chef Jan Knedla. Located in Vysoký Újezd, near Beroun, the restaurant focuses on seasonal ingredients sourced from local farms and a contemporary interpretation of Czech cuisine. Knedla’s cooking also draws on memories of his childhood.

Several other restaurants retained their one-star distinctions, including Field, led by Radek Kašpárek, and Entrée in Olomouc, run by Přemek Forejt, known to Czech television audiences from MasterChef.

The selection also includes Essens, located in Hlohovec in the Lednice-Valtice area and headed by chef Otto Vašák, as well as La Villa in Zlín.

Last year’s edition brought particular attention to restaurants outside Prague, a development that also surprised Michelin inspectors. In the capital, the previous selection included Field, Štangl, Levitate, La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise and Casa De Carli.

A total of 27 Czech restaurants received the award this year, including 11 new additions.

World.title: Snakes in Lake Balaton: what foreign swimmers need to know before getting in
World.content:
I had already been in the water once that afternoon at Zamárdi, just the warm, shallow stretch of Lake Balaton’s southern shore where you can walk fifty metres out and still have the water barely reach your waist. Then I went back for a second swim, looked down near the edge, and froze. A snake was gliding right past me.

Written by Tselmeg Khosbayar

Coming from Mongolia, seeing a snake casually swimming in a lake is not something your brain is prepared for. Lakes back home simply do not come with surprise reptiles. I was so shocked I pulled out my phone, filmed a few seconds of it, and threw it on TikTok as a joke. Honestly, I didn’t expect anyone to care, so watching it blow up caught me off guard.

The comments split right down the middle. Foreign viewers reacted with the exact same panic I felt on the beach. Hungarians, meanwhile, were mostly amused and some telling me there was nothing to worry about, others asking why I was swimming in a natural lake if I expected a swimming pool. They had a point. Still, for anyone living in or visiting Hungary from places without freshwater reptiles, spotting snakes in Lake Balaton is a rite of passage nobody warns you about.

If you issed it – Warning: Lake Balaton could split into three separate bodies of water by the end of the century

Why Snakes Live in Lake Balaton

Many tourists see Balaton primarily as a summer beach destination, but it’s important to remember that it’s actually Central Europe’s largest freshwater lake and a big ecosystem. With its shorelines, warm shallow waters, and mass of small fish and frogs, it creates a perfect habitat for water snakes. You’re most likely to catch a glimpse of them on quieter beaches, near stone breakwaters, or around reed beds, particularly in early summer or during late afternoons. In busier areas like Zamárdi or Siófok, the heavy foot traffic typically keeps them away from crowded swimming spots, although you might still spot one wandering close to shore from time to time.

Are They Dangerous?

Luckily, no. The snakes swimmers spot in Balaton are almost always grass snakes (vízisikló) or dice snakes (kockás sikló).

Grass snake. Source: depositphotos.com

Neither of them is venomous, and they have zero interest in bothering swimmers. In fact, they are often more frightened by splashing swimmers than we are of them. When a snake swims near the shore, it is usually either hunting for small fish or swimming from one patch of reeds to another.

Both species are protected under Hungarian law, meaning that harming or attempting to capture them is illegal and can result in significant fines.

What to Do If You Spot One While Swimming

If you find yourself knee-deep in Balaton and notice a snake gliding through the water, there’s no need to panic, although a startled reaction is understandable.

Maintain your distance and allow it to pass; snakes are swift swimmers and will quickly disappear into the reeds if left undisturbed.

If you are uncomfortable, stay away from the reeds and stick to open, sandy, or grassy municipal beaches where the bottom is clear and foot traffic keeps wildlife away.

Don’t try to poke, grab, or scare it off. Even harmless snakes can spray a pretty nasty-smelling fluid if they feel cornered, and messing with protected animals can get you fined.

Embracing a Different Kind of Lake Culture

That whole TikTok moment taught me something simple about Hungary: locals see Balaton as real nature, not a giant chlorinated pool. Once you know the snakes won’t hurt you, going back into the water is no big deal. Still, I always check the water near my feet before stepping in now.

World.title: Hungary–China education cooperation strengthens as Chinese university delegation visits Budapest
World.content:
Hungary–China education cooperation took another step forward on 18 November 2026, when a delegation from Sanming University in China’s Fujian province visited Budapest for high-level discussions on academic partnerships, artificial intelligence, innovation and economic collaboration. The event brought together representatives of Hungarian and Chinese academic, business and diplomatic circles, highlighting the growing importance of educational ties between the two countries.

The meeting was organised by the Europe–China Economic, Trade and Innovation Association, a Budapest-based organisation dedicated to promoting cooperation between China and European countries.

According to the Hungarian Chinese-language newspaper Xin Dao Bao, the delegation was led by Chen Lieping, Party Secretary of Sanming University, who emphasised the importance of expanding practical cooperation in higher education, technological innovation and industry-oriented training.

Hungary–China education cooperation enters a new phase

The Budapest discussions focused on strengthening existing academic relationships and identifying opportunities for further collaboration between universities, research institutions and businesses.

Chen Lieping highlighted the longstanding connections between Hungary and Sanming, a city in China’s southeastern Fujian province.

Chen Lieping, Party Secretary of Sanming University. Source: xindb.com

These ties extend beyond education. Sanming maintains a sister-city relationship with Budapest’s 15th district, while Mingxi County has established a partnership with the Hungarian town of Velence.

The Chinese community in Hungary has also played an important role in developing business relationships and facilitating cultural exchanges between the two countries.

Sanming University, which specialises in applied higher education, aims to strengthen its international partnerships while preparing students for the changing demands of the global economy.

Artificial intelligence partnership with the University of Miskolc

One of the most significant developments discussed during the meeting was Sanming University’s cooperation with Hungary’s University of Miskolc.

According to the Chinese delegation, a joint undergraduate programme in artificial intelligence received official approval in May 2026, and its first students have already enrolled.

The initiative represents an important milestone in educational cooperation between Hungary and China’s Fujian province, particularly in emerging technologies.

For international readers, the University of Miskolc is one of Hungary’s established public universities, with a strong tradition in engineering, technology and applied sciences.

The partnership reflects a broader trend in Hungary–China relations, in which academic institutions are increasingly exploring opportunities for joint training, research and technological development.

Another initiative highlighted during the discussions was the establishment of a Hungarian Studies Centre in June 2026, developed jointly by Sanming University and Shanghai International Studies University.

The centre aims to support academic research, cultural exchanges and institutional cooperation while improving mutual understanding between Hungary and China.

Budapest association seeks to connect universities and businesses

Chen Shiquan, president of the Europe–China Economic, Trade and Innovation Association, welcomed the visiting delegation and stressed the importance of building practical bridges between the two countries.

Originally from Sanming and having lived and worked in Hungary for many years, Chen spoke about his personal commitment to strengthening bilateral relations.

He highlighted the potential for cooperation in education, technological development, business investment and cultural exchange.

Chen Shiquan, president of the Europe–China Economic, Trade and Innovation Association. Source: xindb.com

The association intends to use its established network of Hungarian and Chinese business representatives, universities and community organisations to support future projects.

Particular attention was given to connecting academic training with industry requirements, enabling students and researchers to gain practical international experience.

Sanming’s industrial strengths, including equipment manufacturing, advanced materials, electronics and tourism, were also presented as potential areas for further cooperation.

Stronger ties between Hungary and China’s Fujian province

The discussions took place against the background of expanding economic and educational relations between Hungary and China.

Hungary has become an important European destination for Chinese investment, particularly in manufacturing, electric vehicles and battery-related industries. University partnerships can complement these economic connections by encouraging research collaboration, knowledge exchange and the development of specialised skills.

Participants in the Budapest meeting expressed their commitment to maintaining contact and exploring additional projects involving universities, businesses and local communities.

The delegation also included senior representatives of Sanming University’s academic administration and faculties.

The programme concluded with an exchange of commemorative gifts, symbolising the participants’ intention to continue developing institutional and personal relationships.

The meeting demonstrated how Hungary–China education cooperation is increasingly moving beyond traditional academic exchanges towards more practical partnerships involving technology, innovation and economic development.

World.title: Debrecen could face water shortages in summer 2027 as factories increase demand
World.content:
Debrecen, Hungary’s second-largest city, could face serious water supply difficulties as early as summer 2027 because of the growing demands of major industrial plants, according to documents obtained by local news outlet Debreciner.

Could Debrecen residents run out of water next summer?

The findings raise concerns that the city may struggle to provide enough water for both factories and residents during periods of peak consumption.

An investigation by Debreciner, based on documents released following a public information request, suggests that municipal and state-linked organisations have been aware of the potential problem since early 2026. The newspaper argues that residents were not informed of the findings, despite the implications for the city’s future water supply.

A study by Debrecen Infrastructure Development Ltd (DIF), a company owned by the local authority, found that five major industrial investments could require an additional 11,264 cubic metres of water per day during peak periods in 2027 compared with 2025. This includes the first phase of Chinese battery manufacturer CATL’s factory, but excludes its planned second phase.

Existing supplies already under pressure

The DIF’s calculations used a daily supply of approximately 12,000 cubic metres from the Keleti Main Canal, provided by the Tiszamenti Regional Waterworks (TRV) in 2025. The company also considered an increase in this supply to 22,000 cubic metres per day.

Even with that additional capacity, the calculations showed a shortfall of 1,264 cubic metres per day during peak periods in 2027, based on the industrial developments already included in the assessment. The figure does not account for the planned second phase of CATL or any growth in residential water consumption.

The DIF warned that summer demand could be difficult or impossible to meet with the available resources. Its managing director, Ferenc Kun, wrote that Debrecen had already faced a precarious situation during heatwaves in 2025, before the major new factories were operating. The city’s reservoirs had to be filled to capacity in advance and were almost completely emptied by the end of the hottest periods.

Kun described this as a risky and unsustainable arrangement during prolonged heatwaves, when the city consumed more water than the system could replenish.

CATL’s second phase could require even more water

The documents also reveal the scale of the planned expansion. The Debrecen CATL plant reportedly requested cooling water of 4,450 cubic metres per day for its first phase, while the second phase is expected to require 5,406 cubic metres daily. The latter figure is higher despite the second phase still being in preparation.

The DIF concluded that supplying the expansion would require further increases in water deliveries from the TRV. However, the national water utility had already told the National Investment Agency (HIPA) in March that increasing capacity beyond 22,000 cubic metres per day would not currently be feasible. Even after additional infrastructure investment, the maximum achievable supply was estimated at 30,000 cubic metres daily.

That would provide an extra 8,000 cubic metres compared with the current capacity, only moderately more than the combined additional requirement of 6,670 cubic metres for CATL’s second phase and the shortfall identified in the DIF study.

Residents’ future needs were not included

Debreciner also highlighted that the assessment did not include rising household demand, even as new residential areas are being developed to accommodate the growing workforce. Climate change and increasingly severe summer heat could further increase domestic consumption.

The newspaper reported that the South Korean EcoPro plant may also require an additional 3,000 cubic metres of treated wastewater daily from 2028. Meanwhile, water extraction from the Keleti Main Canal was restricted during the summer of 2026 because of low water levels in the Tisza.

The findings do not establish that household taps will run dry in 2027. They do, however, point to a potentially serious mismatch between available supplies and projected demand. Debreciner has also questioned how much Debrecen’s mayor, László Papp, knew about the assessments. The mayor previously said he had learned of the relevant correspondence only through the newspaper’s reporting.

World.title: Lake Balaton in winter? Here are 13 restaurants and cafés that stay open
World.content:
Think Lake Balaton is only worth visiting in summer? Think again. While many beach bars, restaurants and seasonal businesses close their doors after September, the Hungarian seaside has plenty to offer during the colder months, too. From traditional Hungarian dishes and local wines to speciality coffee and lakeside dining, several restaurants and cafés continue welcoming guests throughout winter.

The challenge is knowing where to go. Opening hours can change considerably between November and March, and some places only operate at weekends. Fortunately, there are still plenty of options if you know where to look.

On the southern shore, Mala Garden in Siófok is one of the safest choices, staying open every day throughout the year. Its menu offers an unusual change from traditional Hungarian winter food, with Thai soup and Peking duck among the options. Meanwhile, Kistücsök Food & Room in Balatonszemes, one of the region’s best-known restaurants, continues serving guests daily, with a seasonal menu celebrating local ingredients, including venison and vegetarian dishes.

Those looking for something more traditional can head to Anno Taverna in Balatonszárszó, where the old-fashioned interior and house pasta with porcini mushrooms create a cosy atmosphere. At Rádpuszta near Balatonlelle, visitors can enjoy bográcsgulyás, a hearty Hungarian beef goulash prepared in a traditional kettle over an open fire.

The western side of the lake is another good option, particularly around Hévíz, where the famous thermal lake attracts visitors throughout the year. Kocsi Csárda serves traditional Hungarian specialities daily, including venison stew with dödölle, a regional potato dumpling. At Brix Bistro, guests can try a more modern take on lángos, the popular Hungarian deep-fried flatbread, topped with truffle cream.

Winter also brings its own culinary experiences to the northern shore. At Laposa Borterasz in Badacsony, visitors can enjoy local wines while looking out over the quieter lake, while Káli Fecske in Salföld focuses on seasonal game dishes. Those with a sweet tooth should not miss Apátsági Rege Cukrászda in Tihany, where the lavender cream slice is a particularly tempting choice.

However, planning ahead is essential. Some restaurants only open from Friday to Sunday, Christmas opening hours can differ, and online listings do not always reflect the latest winter schedules.

Planning a winter trip to Lake Balaton? Our sister publication, Hungary Insider, has compiled a guide to 13 restaurants, cafés and wine terraces that remain open between November and March. The full article includes their exact winter opening hours, locations, recommended dishes and practical advice to help you plan your visit.

World.title: Budapest airport bus fleet gets major upgrade: All 24 new 100E express buses now in service
World.content:
Budapest’s 100E Airport Express now has its complete fleet of 24 brand-new articulated buses, each fitted with dedicated luggage racks. The new vehicles are designed to make journeys between the city centre and Budapest Ferenc Liszt International Airport more comfortable and convenient for passengers.

The rollout, which began in early November, has now been completed, with all 24 buses entering service on the 100E route.

Operated by ArrivaBus on behalf of the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK), the MAN Lion’s City 18C articulated buses feature a dedicated luggage area inside the passenger compartment, just before the second set of doors. This allows travellers to store their suitcases and larger bags more conveniently, helping keep the aisle clear.

Depending on luggage size, the racks can accommodate between 15 and 25 suitcases or large backpacks at a time. The new buses also come with several modern features aimed at improving passenger comfort and safety.

These include:

Fully low-floor design , making boarding and alighting easier.

, making boarding and alighting easier. Modern passenger information systems , providing travel updates on board.

, providing travel updates on board. On-board CCTV cameras , helping improve passenger safety.

, helping improve passenger safety. Advanced safety features, including blind-spot monitoring to assist drivers.

All 24 vehicles now operate on the 100E Airport Express, which connects the city centre with Budapest Airport. The buses previously used on the route have been reassigned to other services across the capital. According to the BKK, this means the fleet upgrade could also improve comfort on other Budapest bus routes.

The transport centre had previously announced the arrival of the specially equipped vehicles, highlighting the dedicated space for luggage on the increasingly popular airport service.

Budapest’s bus fleet is also being renewed

The introduction of the new 100E buses forms part of a wider programme to modernise public transport vehicles in the Hungarian capital.

The renewal programme, launched in 2025 on behalf of the BKK, is expected to bring more than 380 new diesel and electric buses into service by the end of 2027.

The newer vehicles are designed to produce fewer emissions, helping improve air quality in Budapest while offering passengers a more comfortable and reliable service.

World.title: Texas executes man who murdered Hungarian-born diamond dealer – His execution took more than an hour
World.content:
Texas has executed a 70-year-old man convicted of murdering Hungarian-born diamond dealer János “Johnny” Szűcs in 1996. Reinaldo Dennes spent 29 years on death row before receiving a lethal injection on Thursday, but the procedure took more than an hour as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for the intravenous lines.

According to the Associated Press (AP), Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 pm local time at the penitentiary in Huntsville, Texas. The execution was completed 63 minutes after he had been strapped to the gurney.

Execution delayed by difficulties inserting IV lines

The execution did not proceed smoothly. Prison staff made several unsuccessful attempts to find suitable veins before eventually inserting the needles into Dennes’ left foot and the left side of his neck.

Once the lethal drug began flowing, Dennes repeatedly complained of pain, groaned and asked God to end his suffering. At one point, he said his right leg was hurting severely.

Prison spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all procedures had been followed correctly. She suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or pretended to be in pain, noting that he had started complaining before the drugs began flowing and had reported pain in areas without intravenous lines.

Hernandez also said that using alternative injection sites was not unprecedented and that there had been no irregularities on the prison staff’s part.

The execution came amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the United States following a botched execution in Tennessee in September, when death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital.

Hungarian-born businessman was killed during a diamond robbery

Dennes was convicted of capital murder for killing 44-year-old János “Johnny” Szűcs in January 1996. The Hungarian-born diamond dealer was shot multiple times in his Houston office, and Dennes stole diamonds worth USD 3.6 million. The stolen gemstones have never been recovered.

According to Telex, Szűcs was also known for his generosity towards the local Hungarian community, which he supported financially.

The robbery also involved security guard David Copeland, who was shot but survived his injuries. He died five years ago. His wife, Janice Copeland, told AP that her husband had always believed Dennes would outlive him. She said she felt justice had finally been served after three decades.

Florida carries out record 20th execution of the year

Dennes was the second person executed in the United States on Thursday. Earlier that day, Florida put Thomas Mitchell Overton to death, bringing the state’s total number of executions this year to 20 and breaking its previous annual record.

World.title: Breaking: EC partially approves Hungary’s EUR 10 billion EU recovery fund payment request
World.content:
Hungary has met 126 of the 127 milestones required to unlock funding from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility. The European Commission has therefore given its preliminary approval to almost the entire EUR 10 billion payment request, although one outstanding issue could still result in a small deduction.

The European Commission partially approved Hungary’s first and final payment request under the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) on Friday, 20 November. According to the Commission’s preliminary assessment, Hungary has fully met 126 of the 127 reforms, targets and investment milestones required to receive the funding.

The package is worth EUR 10 billion (approximately HUF 3,700 billion at current exchange rates) and was established to support economic recovery following the COVID-19 pandemic.

The funding had remained inaccessible to Hungary for years because of outstanding conditions, many of them related to anti-corruption measures, transparency and the rule of law. Following a political agreement reached in May between Prime Minister Péter Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the new Hungarian government had only a few months to revise the recovery plan, complete outstanding reforms and launch the necessary investment programmes.

The previous government had agreed on Hungary’s commitments at the end of 2022 but failed to fulfil all of them. The new administration therefore had to complete the remaining requirements or find alternative ways to meet them.

According to Investment and Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy, Hungary managed to fulfil the conditions just hours before the 31 August deadline. Member states had until that date to meet the milestones and so-called super-milestones, while payment requests had to be submitted by 30 September. Hungary submitted its requests together, having previously been unable to access the funding.

One milestone remains only partially fulfilled

The Commission has not yet provided a final decision on the full payment. Its assessment found that one milestone, linked to the submission of an interim evaluation report on the effectiveness of tax rules, had been only partially fulfilled.

The Hungarian government has been informed of the issue and will have to explain its position. If the Commission considers the response satisfactory, it may ultimately recognise the milestone as completed, allowing the associated funding to be released as well.

If the explanation is rejected, the amount linked to the outstanding requirement will be deducted proportionately from the EUR 10 billion request. The Commission has not specified how much money is at stake, although the potential loss is expected to be relatively small compared with the overall package.

The Commission has sent its preliminary assessment to the Economic and Financial Committee (EFC), which has four weeks to deliver its opinion. A positive opinion is required before the Commission can adopt a formal payment decision. The funds linked to the approved milestones are expected to be transferred by 31 December.

Funding covers several key areas

The payment request concerns reforms and investments in a range of areas, including the rule of law, energy efficiency, transport, education, healthcare and social infrastructure, as well as housing.

The Commission said Hungary had demonstrated a serious commitment to implementing major reforms and investments with tangible benefits for its economy.

The approval is an important step towards finally unlocking the funding, but it does not mean that the entire EUR 10 billion has already been transferred. The final amount will depend on the remaining assessment and the formal payment decision.

World.title: Republika Srpska Ban on 1990s Bosnian Army Symbols Ruled Unconstitutional
World.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Constitutional Court. Photo: Constitutional Court.

The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on Friday declared unconstitutional a recently-amended part of the criminal code of Serb-led entity Republika Srpska that criminalises the public display, wearing, production or marketing of flags, symbols, insignia and slogans that promote or glorify the 1990s Bosniak-led Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The National Assembly of Republika Srpska amended the entity’s criminal code in July, introducing prison terms for the new offence. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina fought against the Army of Republika Srpska during the 1990s war.

“In its reasoning, the Constitutional Court stated, among other things, that the contested provision was not in line with the laws governing the use of official symbols and insignia of members of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which regulate the use of the official symbols and insignia of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” the court said in a statement.

It said that the entity-level National Assembly of Republika Srpska is “not authorised to decide on the repeal of legal acts adopted by the institutions of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina”.

The legal provision adopted by Republika Srpska MPs declared that anyone who “publicly displays, shows, wears, produces, reproduces or otherwise puts into circulation flags, symbols, insignia, greetings, slogans or other markings that promote or glorify the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina” can be punished with up to three years in prison.

The provision envisages a penalty of between two and five years if such acts result in unrest, violence, or other serious consequences for relations among peoples and other communities living in Republika Srpska.

The provision also criminalised displaying or promoting flags and symbols of the Independent State of Croatia, a World War II-era fascist state allied with Nazi Germany.

World.title: Bosnia Federation’s PM and Interior Minister Indicted Over Police Appointments
World.content:
Nermin Niksic. Photo: BIRN.

Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Federation entity Prime Minister, Nermin Niksic, and six others have been indicted on charges colluding to commit a criminal act, abuse of office and influence peddling, the Federation prosecution said on Friday.

The indictment, filed by the Special Department of the Federation Prosecutor’s Office for the Suppression of Corruption, Organised and Inter-Entity Crime, POSKOK, also names Federation Interior Minister Ramo Isak, former Federation Police Administration chief Vahidin Munjic, Muhamed Ohranovic, Arijana Huseinovic Ajanovic, Ervin Musinovic and Mirela Bubalo.

According to the prosecution, the alleged offences took place between April 2023 and August 2024 in Sarajevo Canton and Mostar.

Niksic and Isak are accused of abusing their positions to appoint Munjic as head of the Federation Police Administration, FUP, and subsequently extend his mandate, allegedly in violation of Federation law. The prosecution says Munjic did not meet the legal requirements for the position.

Isak, as Federation interior minister, and Niksic, as entity prime minister, are accused of proposing and signing government decisions that enabled Munjic to take charge of the FUP.

The indictment alleges that Ohranovic, a FUP police officer, and Huseinovic Ajanovic, head of the Federation Prime Minister’s Office, acted as intermediaries in granting and extending Munjic’s authorisation. They are also accused of intervening in the appointment of Munjic’s relative as acting director of the state-owned BH Post.

Bubalo, a department head in the office of the Federation Interior Ministry, and Musinovic, an inspector responsible for overseeing security agencies, are accused of using their positions to facilitate employment at the FUP.

Isak is also accused of exceeding his authority in August 2024 by assigning Munjic to head the FUP Criminal Investigation Department, allegedly allowing him to continue directing the police administration until November 2025.

The indictment also covers alleged irregularities involving promotions and recruitment within the FUP, as well as the unauthorised disclosure of confidential information about prosecutorial checks and investigations.

The prosecution has requested that Niksic be barred from performing his duties as Federation PM and Isak from serving as Interior Minister. It has also proposed prohibiting both men from holding other official positions within the Federation government or senior posts in its institutions.

It has sought an extension of an existing ban preventing Huseinovic Ajanovic from performing official duties within the Federation government, as well as a ban preventing Musinovic from holding any official position within the FUP or the Federation Interior Ministry.

Security measures involving the seizure of items have also been proposed for Munjic, Huseinovic Ajanovic, Musinovic, Ohranovic and Isak.

For the trial, the prosecution has proposed hearing more than 60 witnesses and presenting over 500 pieces of material evidence.

The indictment has been submitted to the Special Department of the Federation Supreme Court for confirmation.

World.title: Week in Review: Protests, Hopes and Reality Checks
World.content:
Albania is moving towards local elections in May 2027 in an unusual atmosphere. Both traditional parties of power – the ruling Socialists and opposition Democrats – are gearing up for the fight.

This is not unusual. But the protests that have rocked Albania for more than half a year have shown that voters are keen to get rid not only of the Socialists but the Democrats as well. Serbia’s protesting students successfully squeezed out both the ruling and opposition parties. Can a similar force do the same in Albania?

World.title: Serbia Formally Drops ‘Violent Overthrow’ Case Against Student Protesters
World.content:
Court proceedings against nine students accused of calling for a violent change to Serbia’s constitutional order were formally concluded on Friday at Belgrade’s Palace of Justice, after the prosecution dropped the charges due to insufficient evidence.

After leaving the Palace of Justice, the students said the proceedings had been legally unfounded and politically motivated.

“It is not enough that the proceedings have been discontinued. We should never have had to wait a year and a half for justice. Justice must not depend on the will of those in power, but on the law. We would like this to mark the beginning of a new chapter – one in which the rule of law is restored to institutions and the state is returned to the people,” one student, Dimitrije Stefanovic, said after the court session.

Ivana Milenkovic, another defendant, called for accountability for all those who she said had participated in the arrests of her and her colleagues in an “unlawful and humiliating manner”.

“From plainclothes police officers to prosecutors, no one can or should be above the law. As the saying goes, let justice take its course. After all, they know very well what they did,” Milenkovic said outside the Palace of Justice following the hearing.

The nine students were arrested on June 29, 2025, a day after a major anti-government protest in Belgrade. They were accused of planning to radicalise the protests during meetings at the Faculty of Civil Engineering and the Faculty of Philology earlier that month.

Ahead of the protest, secretly recorded conversations from these meetings were broadcast on pro-government television channels. According to the prosecution, the students had discussed plans to blockade several state institutions, among other locations.

On September 11, 2026, the Higher Court in Belgrade ruled that evidence obtained through secret surveillance by Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA, had been collected unlawfully and should be excluded from the case. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in October.

On November 9, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it had dropped the charges.

According to the prosecution, the excluded evidence constituted a significant part of its case, and the remaining material was insufficient to support a justified suspicion that the students had committed the alleged offences.

The students’ lawyer Aleksandar Radojicic, told N1 TV on Friday that it was rare for prosecutors to drop charges and that he hoped this would mark “the final act of the drama that the outgoing regime created against the children”.

Radojicic added that the judiciary had “shown integrity”, but there was still a “bitter taste” because they had not been able to hear the truth in the courtroom.

World.title: Former Ally of Albania’s PM Rama Denounces Ruling Party’s Governance
World.content:
Then Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali at a press conference in Tirana, February 2026. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA.

Former Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali, once a close ally of Prime Minister Edi Rama, spoke out publicly against her own Socialist Party in a TV interview on Thursday evening after she was reportedly dismissed from all party structures at the Socialists’ general assembly on November 14.

“I joined the Socialist Party, as a reformist force to change Albania; but what is the value of that today?” Spiropali, who was also speaker of the Albanian parliament between 2024 and 2025, said in the interview with Top Channel TV.

The Socialist Party came to power in 2013 and Spiropali was a key figure until March this year, when she refused to follow Rama’s line on the scandal around Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Infrastructure Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering with public procurements and corruption.

The Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution called on parliament to remove Balluku’s immunity to allow for her arrest.

Reportedly, one day before the parliamentary vote on Balluku’s immunity, Rama ordered his MPs to vote against the prosecution’s request. However, Spiropali did not participate in the vote.

In the interview with Top Channel’s ‘Top Story’ programme, Spiropali described the Balluku incident as “the worst example of governance by our political force”, and said the now-ousted minister was “the latest victim of a model that must change”.

“This is what I believed when I chose not to go to parliament to vote on the immunity issue,” she said.

Interviewer Grida Duma asked Spiropali how Balluku could represent the “worst example” and also be a victim.

Spiropali responded: “At a time when power becomes so personalised that all filters and internal checks within a political force vanish, and it is now abundantly clear that political courage has disappeared, that there is no longer any willingness to raise issues for discussion within party forums, and that no one confronts significant matters concerning governance or the Socialist Party, then, inevitably, a pattern emerges defined by phone calls, text messages, arbitrary personal choices and grave errors.”

Spiropali claimed that Balluku still maintains some power within the party because all its internal democratic mechanisms have failed.

She declared: “We can no longer continue with people in political forums who are using the Socialist Party as a shield for their own personal predicaments. The Socialist Party is not a bunker where they can hide.”

Asked if she had personally come under political pressure, she said: “From morning till night.” Asked by whom, she replied: “By Belinda Balluku and the institutions of this state.”

Balluku has not responded publicly to these allegations. She has however denied wrongdoing in the corruption case. Rama has made no comment on Spiropali’s interview so far.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechs, Slovaks Mark Velvet Revolution but Both Find Unity Elusive
World.content:
Russian drones hit close to Hungarian border; Orban used taxpayer money for sport trips

The war in Ukraine is getting closer to Hungary’s borders. On Tuesday, Russian drones struck Transcarpathia, Ukraine’s westernmost region – only 30 kilometres from the Hungarian border – and home to a significant Hungarian ethnic minority. While no casualties have been reported, the attacks caused infrastructure damage, and one of the drones exploded near the railway station in Mukachevo. In response, PM Peter Magyar announced the suspension of railway traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days. The attack was immediately seized on by the opposition Fidesz party, which accused the Tisza government of adopting Brussels’ “pro-war politics” and putting the security of the Hungarian minority at risk. “Peter Magyar’s government has abandoned its pro-peace policy and chosen to support the war instead of neutrality. This policy poses a threat to Hungary,” Fidesz wrote in a statement. The Hungarian government condemned the attack. Foreign Minister Anita Orban warned that “this is not the first air attack on Transcarpathia, and unfortunately, it will certainly not be the last,” expressing solidarity with the Ukrainian people. Russia also targeted Transcarpathia in 2025, but attacks on the region have been rare. Meanwhile, Russia’s ambassador to Hungary complained, in an interview with Demokrata, a Fidesz-aligned publication, about what he described as unfriendly steps taken by Hungarian diplomacy, including the expulsion of 10 Russian diplomats. He nevertheless expressed hope for mutually beneficial relations, saying that their future would depend on the Magyar government. He also issued a not-so-subtle warning about potential serious financial and legal consequences should the Hungarian government terminate its contract with Rosatom to construct the Paks II nuclear power plant. The project has been under review for several months.

This week it emerged that the Foreign Ministry under the previous government spent more than 280 million forints (about 760,000 euros) on sport-related trips for Orban and his retinue over the past decade, 444.hu reported. The revelations show that the former prime minister, a devoted football fan, financed most of his trips using taxpayers’ money via the Foreign Ministry’s budget. The report by 444.hu, based on data obtained by the publication through a lawsuit, found that the largest chunk, 180 million forints, was spent on accommodation, followed by transport at 79 million forints, airport VIP lounge services at 8.3 million forints, and miscellaneous expenses – taxis, parking, restaurant bills etc – another 10.3 million forints. These figures do not include trips made using a military aircraft or private jets, meaning the total public cost could be considerably higher. The most expensive trip was to Qatar in December 2022, where Orban attended the World Cup semi-final and final. Those two events cost taxpayers 131 million forints, of which 126 million went on accommodation. The second most expensive jaunt was to the 2016 Rio Olympics, costing 70.7 million forints, including 32 million for accommodation, flights, restaurant bills, sightseeing and other expenses. Other trips also raised questions about the use of public funds. Orban’s October 2017 visit to Switzerland for a World Cup qualifier cost nearly 2.5 million forints, including 1.3 million for a single night at the luxury Les Trois Rois hotel in Basel. Orban also attended Hungary’s World Cup qualifier against Ireland in 2025. Government offices and the Hungarian Football Federation had issued contradicting information about who paid for that trip, but the newly obtained records make clear that taxpayers covered the 14 million forints outlay. A subsequent trip to Portugal cost a further 7.9 million forints. The investigation into the football-related trips and their costs is part of a series by 444.hu about lavish spending habits of Orban and government delegations.

World.title: Russian Despatch: Without Vucic, Moscow Faces a Very Different Balkans
World.content:
November has turned into a month of frenetic diplomatic activity for Russia.

Moscow has not only resumed trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington on the settlement of its war against Ukraine, but also managed to expand the agenda to cover how the new security architecture of the whole of Europe should look after the end of hostilities.

And on Thursday, the leaders of Russia, the United States and China held an unprecedented trilateral meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China.

There are serious doubts that any of the above undertakings will produce tangible results, but their optics have largely overshadowed a major setback Moscow suffered in the Balkans - the fall of Serbia’s Aleksandar Vucic, widely seen as a rare European ally for Russia.

World.title: Bulgaria issues warning of dangerous weather for November 23 over forecast strong winds
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for numerous districts for November 23 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Vidin, Montana, Vratsa, Pleven, Veliko Turnovo, Sliven, Yambol, Haskovo, Plovdiv, Pazardzhik, Kurdzhali, Sofia city, Sofia district, Pernik and Lovech.

All other districts are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of strong winds.

The meteorological bureau said that on the morning of November 23, a moderate and strong southerly wind will blow. It will be cloudy with rain in many places.

It will be relatively warm for the season, with minimum temperatures between 5° and 10° Celsius and maximums between 14° and 19°.

In the afternoon, cold air will flow in a temperatures will drop quickly and significantly.

In a separate announcement, the Road Infrastructure Agency said that from November 23, a serious cold snap with rain is expected, and in the morning hours, negative temperatures and icing conditions are expected.

“The Road Infrastructure Agency appeals to drivers to prepare their vehicles for winter conditions, to set off on the road only with suitable tyres, to drive at a reasonable speed and to keep a distance so as not to block traffic and the work of snow removal equipment,” the agency said.

The national road network has been in winter maintenance mode since November 16. The regional road departments and the involved companies are monitoring weather forecasts for timely treatment of the pavements, especially in the passes and high-mountainous regions, it said.

World.title: Gavriil, Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech, dies at 76
World.content:
Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech Gavriil died on November 22 after a short illness, the church’s governing body the Holy Synod said in a statement.

Gavriil, who had been Metropolitan of Lovech since January 28 2001, was 76.

“His Eminence will remain in the history of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church – Bulgarian Patriarchate as a proper hierarch, a zealous monk, a fervent prayer leader, a clergyman with deep and sincere faith, and a true follower of Christ, who not only with his words, but also with his entire life and deeds proclaimed the gospel truth,” the Holy Synod said.

The statement said that the Holy Synod would meet in special session to decide on the date and time of the funeral of Gavriil, and to appoint a temporary head of the diocese.

Gavriil was born on July 16 1950 in Sofia with the secular name Tsvetan Metodiev Dinev. He took monastic vows in 1979 at the Klisura Monastery St. Petka near Bankya.

He held various clerical posts, including as head of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church in Moscow, before being elected Metropolitan of Lovech.

In 2012, a check into the Holy Synod of the time by the Dossier Commission found that Gavriil was one of only four members of the church’s 15-member governing body for which there was no evidence that he had worked for communist-era secret service State Security.

More recently, Gavriil opposed the decision of the Ecumenical Patriarchate to grant autocephaly (church independence) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew signed the decree in January 2019.

Metropolitan Gavriil was among the three candidates for Bulgarian Patriarch both in 2013, when Neofit was elected, and in 2024, when Daniil was elected.

Gavriil’s death creates a vacancy in the church’s governing body, for which an election will be held in the coming months.

In Bulgaria’s 2021 national census, close to 63 per cent of Bulgarians said that they identified as Eastern Orthodox Christians.

(Photo via the website of the Bulgarian Patriarchate)

World.title: EC approves Bulgaria’s final payment request under NextGenerationEU
World.content:
The European Commission said on November 20 that it has partially greenlighted Bulgaria’s fifth and final payment request for 1.82 billion euro under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of the bloc’s NextGenerationEU post-pandemic economic recovery plan.

Bulgaria submitted the payment request on September 30, the deadline set by the European Commission, which aims to wind down the NextGenerationEU programme at the end of this year.

The Commission said that its assessment found that Bulgaria “has satisfactorily completed 53 out of 59 milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision.”

As such, the EC said that it would withhold part of the funds requested, but did not give an exact figure, noting only that it would be “proportional.”

Speaking to reporters in Sofia after the announcement, Deputy PM Atanas Pekanov, the Cabinet’s senior official tasked with securing RRF funds, said that Bulgaria was slated to receive more than 1.7 billion euro under the fifth payment request.

The policy areas in which Bulgaria pursued reforms and investments tied to this payment request include decarbonising the energy sector, strengthening the anti-corruption framework, enhancing the sustainability of transport and improving social inclusion and healthcare, the EC said.

The disbursement of the payment can be made after the Economic and Financial Committee, a body composed of senior officials from national administrations and central banks, the ECB and the EC, has issued an opinion on the Commission’s preliminary approval. It has four weeks to do so.

This is the second large RRF payment request received by Bulgaria this year, following 1.1 billion euro granted by the EC in June.

Due to years of political instability and short-lived governments, the country has lagged behind other EU member states in making the requests, raising the prospect that it could miss out on a significant amount of the 6.17 billion euro allocated to it under the RRF.

Pekanov said that this year’s two payment requests would take the amount received by Bulgaria under the RRF to between 98.7 per cent and 99 per cent of the allocated funding.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament elects 11 members of Supreme Judicial Council
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 20 to appoint 11 members of the country’s Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), the body tasked with the appointment of senior magistrates in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

Parliament held individual appointment votes for all 21 nominees. Vote tallies showed that the candidates that secured appointment were uniformly backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria, alongside the opposition We Continue the Change (WCC) and Democratic Bulgaria.

The three parliamentary groups have a combined 168 MPs, enough to meet the qualified two-thirds majority of 160 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, required for the appointment of SJC members.

Most successful candidates, save three, were also backed by the opposition GERB and Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) parties. Only pro-Kremlin party Vuzrazhdane, whose sole nominated candidate was not elected, voted against all successful appointments.

Of the 11 members of the SJC appointed by MPs on November 20, seven were nominated by Progressive Bulgaria and two apiece by WCC and Democratic Bulgaria.

The council has 25 members and is presided over by the Justice Minister, who is not, however, a member of the SJC. Of the 25 members, 11 are elected by Parliament, 11 by magistrates and three are members ex officio – the country’s prosecutor-general and the heads of the two high courts, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court.

The 11 members elected by magistrates are voted by their respective branches – six by judges, four by prosecutors and one by investigators. This last one is part of the prosecutors college of the SJC, as the National Investigative Service is subordinated to the prosecutor’s office in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

MPs similarly elect six members of the SJC to the judges college and five to the prosecutors college.

The current SJC line-up, often criticised as being unduly under the influence of MRF leader Delyan Peevski – who is subject to US sanctions under the Magnitsky Act – has been in office nearly five years past the expiration of its five-year term.

That is because Bulgaria’s pollical instability since 2021, which saw eight parliamentary elections in five years, resulted in fragmented parliaments, some of them very short-lived, that had little appetite for tackling the issue of electing SJC members.
