Three men have been arrested for stabbing two youths following an altercation near Chauhan Patti bus stand in northeast Delhi’s Sonia Vihar, police said on Sunday (November 22, 2026). The screwdriver used in the attack, along with the clothes worn by the accused at the time, has been recovered.

Editorial | Force of law: On the Delhi police

The incident took place around 9 p.m. on November 20, when the two victims, identified as Suraj Sen (18) and his friend Arpit Mishra, were returning from work by bus. After getting off at Chauhan Patti bus stand, they noticed a group of boys quarrelling.

When Mr. Mishra attempted to intervene and pacify them, two to three members of the group tried to stab him. During the ensuing altercation, the assailants also stabbed Mr. Sen on his left shoulder before fleeing the spot after threatening the two, police said.

A case under Sections 109(1) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) was registered at Sonia Vihar police station on November 21.

The accused, identified as Shourya Singh (18), Aman (23) and Bobby (18), all residents of Ambedkar Nagar in Loni, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, were arrested. The screwdriver and clothes allegedly worn by them during the attack were recovered at their instance, police said.

Police said Aman and Bobby were previously involved in another stabbing case registered at Sonia Vihar police station in 2025 under similar sections of the BNS.

Further investigation is under way.

World.title: Mumbai Police to issue cards with QR code for identity checks
World.content:
Mumbai Police will issue cards with QR code and NFC to personnel, and citizens can scan the code through the Mumbai Police Citizen App to check a person’s photograph, name, date of joining and posting, a measure that follows cases in which fraudsters posed as police and sought money from citizens.

Also read | Zebra Tech develops crime investigation platforms for Indian Police

Devendra Fadnavis inaugurated the measure on Saturday (November 21, 2026), and cards were distributed to personnel, including traffic police, as part of steps to digitise the force. Mumbai Police states that printing has been completed, that personnel will receive cards within a month, that the project covers 51,308 posts and that the government sanctioned about ₹4 crore in February.

Personnel must carry the card while on duty, in uniform or not; officers who visit premises where people live, question citizens or approach people during investigations will have to carry it, so that those whom they approach can verify credentials; and a scan through the app directs users to a platform that displays photograph, name, date of joining and posting, which citizens can compare with the person who presents the card.

The card will have NFC technology, which personnel with authorisation can use for access to police establishments and for purposes, and the measure comes against a pattern in which criminals use cards that carry police identity and claim to be from crime branch to intimidate people into handing over cash or valuables, with fraudsters stopping citizens during walks and businessmen while claiming to conduct checks.

The system could offer a means of verification in scams in which fraudsters pose as police, CBI or officials from law enforcement during video calls and circulate cards with identity to establish credibility, and citizens can check credentials of anyone who claims to be a Mumbai Police officer rather than rely on a card.

Mr. Fadnavis said criminals use technology and police must stay ahead, and that technology works without bias and can improve efficiency.

World.title: Takshashila University confers honorary doctorates on author S. Ramakrishnan and playback singer K.S. Chithra
World.content:
Takshashila University conferred honorary doctorates upon Tamil author and screenwriter S. Ramakrishnan and playback singer K.S. Chithra at its second convocation held at Ongur in Tindivanam recently.

According to a press note, the University awarded gold medals to 19 students and recognised 186 students who secured first class with distinction.

In his address, M. Dhanasekaran, University Chancellor underscored the role of quality education, perseverance, discipline and moral values in shaping responsible citizens.

In her address, Former United Nations-Habitat Executive Director Maimunah Mohd Sharif, spoke about inclusive governance, sustainability and women’s empowerment.

Dr. Vivek Inder Kochhar, Vice-Chancellor and Pro-Chancellors D. Rajarajan and Dr. Nila Priyadarshini participated.

World.title: Man injured in crocodile attack near Chidambaram
World.content:
A 42-year-old man sustained minor injuries on his left thigh after being bitten by a crocodile that strayed into a house in Koppadi village near Chidambaram on Sunday.

According to police sources, P. Ilavarasan of Koppadi village was staying in his house when a dog began to bark continuously. When he went outside he was shocked to see a crocodile. The reptile lunged at him and attacked Ilavarasan on his left thigh. Hearing his cries, neighbours rushed to the spot and alerted the Forest Department.

Forest Department personnel arrived and, with the help of residents, safely captured the crocodile and released it into the Vakkaramari lake in Chidambaram.

World.title: Stray cattle knocks down senior citizen near Tambaram
World.content:
An 83-year-old person is battling for life after a stray cow knocked him down while he was riding a two-wheeler in Sembakkam near Tambaram on Saturday night.

The Tambaram police said Loganathan was a resident of Pavananthiyar Street in Sembakkam near Tambaram. On Saturday night, he was riding his two-wheeler near his home to purchase grocery in the nearby street.

As he was proceeding on his two-wheeler, a stray bull which was chasing a cow collided with his vehicle. In the impact, Loganathan fell from the vehicle and suffered a severe head injury. The locals rescued him and admitted him to a private hospital for treatment.

The incident has gone viral on the social media.

World.title: Any talks with India on terrorism must be 'evidence-based', says Musadik Malik
World.content:
Federal minister Musadik Malik said on Sunday that any dialogue between Pakistan and India on terrorism must be “based on evidence”.

Malik is in New Delhi on a three-day trip to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, making him the first Pakistani minister to visit the neighbour since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended an SCO meeting in May 2023.

Pakistan has repeatedly offered to hold talks with India to resolve outstanding disputes, including the water issue.

In video clips shared by India’s ANI news agency on Sunday, Malik responded to queries from Indian media and stressed that he had repeatedly presented Pakistan’s stance before the reporters.

“I am giving you a stable response that whenever discussions take place, they will be based on evidence, and they will certainly happen,” he affirmed, saying if New Delhi wanted a “lasting solution”.

“You must also have some issues, [though] our issues are much greater than yours, and we also need a lot of evidence […] Whenever dialogue takes place, it will be based on evidence,” the climate change minister reiterated.

Malik said Pakistan had repeatedly stated that evidence relating to terrorism could be presented through both bilateral and multilateral forums. “You may bring evidence; we also have evidence that we want to present,” he added.

India’s foreign minister had said in June 2024 that his country wanted to “find a solution to the issue of years-old cross-border terrorism” with Pakistan. However, a military conflict between the neighbours last year has intensified tensions and escalatory rhetoric from India.

In May 2025, a four-day confrontation between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan.

Islamabad had strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation .

In another clip, Malik noted that India had invited a representative from Pakistan to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a multilateral event.

“I am your guest. You invited me to a specific forum; I am present before you. I answered all those questions you asked about this forum,” the minister said, remarking that he had conveyed the “voice of my heart” to the people across the region through the forum.

Malik stated, “You are today asking me questions for which you did not invite me. When you invite me for that question, I will appear. However, you first ought to invite me and say ‘we want to speak bilaterally with you’.”

‘Will speak on IWT when invited to do so’

The minister was also asked about his remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), but said he would comment on the matter when invited to do so.

“You have currently invited me to speak on topics about which I have already spoken, that when temperatures rise, climate is destroyed, Glofs happen. Glofs and glaciers are blind, they do not know whether to fall on the right or the left,” he said, highlighting the shared threat climate change poses to both neighbours.

He further said, “You have called me for culture and civilisation [discussions]. I am your guest, you are my host […] You have asked me the same question a 100 times and I have responded to it a 100 times.”

In his remarks at the SCO forum on Saturday, Malik had termed climate change an “enemy” of civilisations and pointed out its impact on South Asian countries that bore the brunt of climate destruction.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between Pakistan and India, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after the Pahalgam attack, which was followed by the four-day military conflict between the two sides.

Following India’s move, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that New Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

Backing Islamabad’s stance, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) on Aug 31 ordered New Delhi to uphold the IWT, declaring that the treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

The IWT, brokered by the World Bank in 1960, allocates the three western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — largely to Pakistan, and the three eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India.

The treaty has survived wars, crises, and political tensions for more than six decades and is considered a rare example of durable water-sharing cooperation between the two neighbours.

World.title: Varma century in vain as Pakistan Shaheens down India A in Asia Cup Rising Stars clash
World.content:
Pakistan Shaheens overcame a late challenge from Tilak Varma to beat India A by 48 runs in their Asia Cup Rising Stars match in Doha on Sunday, defending a total of 313 after bowling out their opponents with five balls to spare.

Skipper Varma struck a century before becoming the last man dismissed for 100 off 149 balls, while Shahbaz Ahmed made 56 in a seventh-wicket stand that briefly revived India’s hopes.

But Pakistan’s bowlers held their nerve in the closing overs, with Hasan Nawaz claiming three wickets and Ali Raza taking three for 56.

India’s chase had begun to unravel after an explosive start from Abhishek Sharma. The left-hander made 70 off just 42 balls, hitting six fours and six sixes, but his dismissal at 93-3 in the 16th over left the visitors with considerable ground to make up.

Pakistan’s spinners then tightened their grip. Sufyan Moqim bowled Kumar Kushagra for two before Hasan removed Rinku Singh and Suryansh Shedge, leaving India struggling at 129-6 in the 26th over.

Varma, who had struggled to find the boundary during the middle overs, found support in Shahbaz.

The pair added 112 runs for the seventh wicket, taking the score to 241 before Raza broke the stand by having Shahbaz caught by Hasan for 56 off 49 balls.

Raza then bowled Vipraj Nigam for a duck, while Imran Randhawa dismissed Harshit Rana to leave India nine down.

Varma reached his second century of the tournament, but the milestone offered little consolation as Ahmed Daniyal had him caught by wicket-keeper Rohail Nazir in the 50th over to seal Pakistan’s victory.

Controversial toss

Earlier, Pakistan had posted 313 after winning a dramatic toss and electing to bat on a slightly dry surface.

The toss decision was initially called incorrectly by the match referee, who announced tails after Varma flipped the coin on Pakistan skipper Abdul Samad’s call of heads.

Samad pointed out the error and the officials corrected the decision in Pakistan’s favour. The captains did not shake hands, continuing the protocol observed in recent encounters between the sides.

Pakistan’s openers Shamyl Hussain and Maaz Sadaqat gave their side a flying start, putting on 66 for the first wicket. Shamyl made 33 off 23 balls before Ayush Badoni had him caught by Harshit Rana at short third. Rana then trapped Rohail leg-before for a duck, with Pakistan on 67-2.

The exchanges between Rana and the Pakistan batters had added an edge to the powerplay, with the Indian fast bowler involved in heated verbal exchanges and giving Shamyl an animated send-off.

Maaz and Hasan rebuilt the innings, with the former scoring 59 off 63 balls for his second successive half-century.

Hasan went on to make 79 off 82 deliveries, while Farhan Yousaf’s 56 off 48 balls and Imran’s quickfire 23 helped Pakistan push past 300, which was proven enough for the side at the end.

World.title: Naqvi hits back at minister for repeated criticism: report
World.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has hit back at a federal minister for what he said was repeated criticism against him, Geo News reported on Sunday.

The news website reported that Naqvi, without naming the minister, claimed the latter had been commenting on him on television almost every day to “gain attention”.

The report described the remarks as part of an informal conversation with Geo News and further quoted Naqvi as saying that he had been patiently listening to the minister’s statements for the past two-and-a-half years — the tenure of the incumbent government since the 2024 elections.

“The day I comment on this minister, he will not be able to show his face,” Naqvi warned, according to the outlet.

Naqvi also defended the businesspeople present at an economic forum who he said were criticised by the minister. He said the attendees were respectable citizens who had served as presidents and office-bearers of chambers of commerce at the federal and city levels, according to the report.

While the report did not quote him as mentioning any specific details in this connection, Naqvi’s remarks at the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad in July had been making headlines in recent months. Naqvi had whipped up a political storm by calling for creating new administrative units in the country to “reset” the current “system” of governance while speaking at the forum, which was attended by businessmen.

In his remarks to Geo News, Naqvi stated that the businessmen were also among the country’s highest taxpayers.

“If these businessmen are so bad, why do you take billions of rupees from them in the name of party funds at every election?” the interior minister was quoted as saying.

Naqvi’s remarks have been reported a day after Inter-Provincial Coordination Minister Rana Sanaullah questioned the objectives of some of the businesspeople at that July forum.

In an interview on Geo News programme ‘Jirga’ aired on Saturday, Sanaullah said the “matter got worse in such a way that the debate on provinces began from an economic forum” and Naqvi started the discussion.

Sanaullah, also Naqvi’s predecessor, contended that there were “some objectionable businessmen sitting among the audience of that economic forum”.

“It has been their background that in each tenure, they keep on telling the incoming ruler, especially the army chief, that ‘sir, the whole world is looking at you and only you are the saviour,’” Sanaullah said.

The PML-N leader clarified that he was not referring to the entire business community, but rather “a few people who keep committing crime in business, and here as well”.

On differing stances among federal cabinet members on the issue of new provinces, Sanaullah contended that politicians could express their opinions, as “regimental discipline” could not be brought into the cabinet.

Sanaullah stressed that the debate on provinces was “not wrong”, but he contended that the “debate was being entangled with other matters; saying that the system has collapsed; after that some remarks were made about the prime minister, and similarly about politicians contesting elections in so and so manner”.

The PML-N leader also criticised PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari for further complicating the situation by referring to various matters in his Nov 17 speech, rather than merely voicing his objection to carving out new administrative units out of Sindh.

Sanaullah further termed both Bilawal and Naqvi as “sons” of President Asif Ali Zardari, adding that they were “under his discipline”.

Asked about the independent senator being “under President Zardari’s discipline”, Sanaullah reiterated, “Yes, definitely. He has not disowned him yet. He himself calls him (Naqvi) his son; it is not that we are saying so.”

Referring to a recent meeting between President Zardari and PM Shehbaz Sharif, during which Naqvi was also present, Sanaullah said a “ceasefire was decided” there.

He claimed that, according to information he had, a meeting was held at President House recently, which was attended by President Zardari, Bilawal and Naqvi, and it was decided to reduce tensions.

Replying to a query about the independent senator, Sanaullah remarked that Naqvi was a senator of both PPP and PML-N, as leaders from both parties contributed to the votes for his election.

In September as well, Sanaullah had said that the “debate should have been started in Parliament”, adding that issues of such magnitude should not be reduced to speeches, social media, seminars or business forums.

The PML-N leader has also taken jibes at the interior minister on a few other occasions since the ruling coalition came to power.

On the other hand, Sindh Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah also took exception to Sanaullah’s remarks, asserting that Bilawal was the only son of President Zardari.

“Mohsin Naqvi sahib is worthy of respect in his place, but nothing about him compares to the chairman (Bilawal),” he told reporters.

Shah maintained there was “no such thing” as suggested by the PML-N minister, declaring, “There is only one Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, and only his words will prevail here.”

World.title: More than 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Pakistan to mark Guru Nanak's birthday
World.content:
LAHORE: Over 2,300 Indian Sikh pilgrims arrived in Pakistan through the Wagah Border on Sunday to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of Sikhism.

The visiting pilgrims were received by Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) Chairman Qamar Zaman, Secretary Nasir Mushtaq, Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee (PSGPC) President and Punjab Minorities Minister Sardar Ramesh Singh Arora, the committee’s secretary general Satwant Kaur and other officials at the Wagah border, where the jatha leaders were presented with bouquets.

Indian Sikh pilgrims wave to the camera after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

According to ETPB spokesperson Amir Hashmi, 2,339 Sikh pilgrims arrived from India here on Sunday to take part in the festivities in Nankana Sahib.

The Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi had reportedly issued around 3,100 visas to Indian Sikhs.

Special counters were set up at the Wagah Border to facilitate immigration and baggage screening, while Rangers were deployed to ensure security.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

The ETPB had also established currency exchange facilities at the border, while its teams promptly issued identity cards and bus tickets to the pilgrims to ensure a smooth onward journey, he added.

“The pilgrims subsequently left for Nankana Sahib in three separate convoys under tight security to attend the main ceremony on Nov 24 marking Baba Guru Nanak’s birth anniversary at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, his birthplace,” Hashmi said.

He added that over 20,000 Sikhs — from Pakistan and across the globe — are expected to take part in the formal festivities, which begin today and continue until Nov 24.

Indian Sikh pilgrims gather after arriving in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Federal Minister for Religious Affairs Sardar Muhammad Yousuf, along with other federal and provincial ministers, will attend the event as special guests.

The event participants will perform religious rituals, including Bhog and Akhand Path Sahib, followed by a traditional palanquin procession, known as Nagar Kirtan.

Speaking on the occasion, ETPB Chairman Zaman said the board was making every effort to ensure that the visiting pilgrims faced no inconvenience during their stay in Pakistan.

He said the Indian Sikh pilgrims would return home with fond memories of love, peace and brotherhood.

Indian Sikh pilgrims including a wheelchair-bound woman arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

Minister Arora urged the Indian government to immediately reopen the Kartarpur Corridor, which provides Sikh pilgrims with access to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, one of the holiest sites in Sikhism.

India suspended movement through the Kartarpur Corridor in May 2025 amid the four-day conflict between the countries.

Kaldeep Singh Gurgaj, a leader of the Akal Takht authority from India, said the Sikh community shared a deep bond of reverence with Pakistan, where its members were always treated with respect and honour.

“Our gurdwaras in Pakistan are safe and preserved in their original state,” he said.

Parmjeet Singh, a leader of a Delhi Gurdwara Management Committee delegation, said Pakistan held special significance for Sikhs as the land associated with their guru.

“Pakistan is the land of our guru, and we love it very much,” he said.

Indian Sikh pilgrims arrive in Lahore through the Wagah Border to attend celebrations marking the 557th birth anniversary of Baba Guru Nanak Dev Ji, on Nov 22. — White Star

After attending the main ceremony, the Sikh pilgrims will visit Gurdwara Sacha Sauda in Farooqabad on Nov 25 before proceeding to Hassan Abdal, where they will stay overnight at Gurdwara Panja Sahib.

They will travel to Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur, Narowal, on Nov 27.

The visiting devotees will then spend Nov 29 and 30 visiting various historic gurdwaras in Lahore before returning to India through the Wagah border by road on Dec 1.

Sikh pilgrims frequently visit Pakistan to observe events of religious significance. In June, around 600 Sikhs arrived from India to observe the death anniversary of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, known as Jore Mela; before that, about 2,800 visas were issued to pilgrims to celebrate the Baisakhi festival in April.

World.title: Washington governor calls ICE 'out of control' after Seattle airport arrests
World.content:
The governor of Washington state called US federal immigration agents “out of control” after they arrested two people at Seattle’s main airport on Saturday.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have conducted raids across the United States, part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, which has forged ahead despite a rebuke by voters at this month’s midterms.

Video footage widely shared on social media on Saturday showed two people being apprehended by masked men at an airport jet bridge.

ICE later confirmed it had detained two people it said had overstayed their visas.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said the agency was “completely and totally out of control”.

“Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” Ferguson wrote on X.

“Today’s actions at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport are just the latest example of ICE’s deeply un-American tactics.”

Ferguson said at a news conference that the ICE agents may have broken a state law limiting facial coverings for law enforcement, and that he was looking into how they accessed the jet bridge.

The federal immigration agency said its officers “conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa” on Saturday morning.

The agency confirmed it had detained a second person whom it said would be charged with assaulting a federal officer, alleging she had thrown hot coffee on an ICE agent.

“The individual… was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well,” ICE posted on X.

Alaska Airlines, which operated the flight that Mendoza and Mejia tried to board, said on Saturday it was “concerned by this morning’s law enforcement action”.

“Alaska Airlines is required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials” but does not “direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity”, the company added.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, said: “We are outraged about this morning’s incident involving ICE and two passengers.”

This month, Trump appointed Stephen Miller, architect of his hardline immigration policy, as his new chief of staff.

Miller faced widespread criticism after the deadly shootings of two protesters by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January — incidents that sparked mass demonstrations.

World.title: Multiple Karachi routes briefly closed as political parties hold demonstration, rally
World.content:
Multiple roads were closed briefly in Karachi on Sunday as the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) staged a demonstration in the city and the Jeay Sindh Rehbar Committee (JSRC) — a conglomerate of four Sindhi nationalist groups — held a rally.

The JUI-F staged its main demonstration at Guru Mandir, while the JSRC organised a rally from Sachal Goth to the press club via Sharea Faisal, some stretches of which had been shut for vehicles, the traffic police said.

Traffic was allowed again on the stretch of Sharea Faisal leading to Drigh Road and Karsaz at 4:16pm after about an hour-long closure. Commuters coming from the airport had been diverted via Rashid Minhas Bridge towards Millennium Mall.

The route from Askari 4 to Drigh Road on Main Rashid Minhas Road was reopened for traffic at around 4:30pm following its reported closure at 3:30pm.

The route from Guru Mandir towards Jamshed Road was reopened for vehicles at around 5pm after being closed to traffic shortly after 2pm.

The stretch of Sharea Faisal from Avari Towers towards FTC was reopened at 8:45pm. Vehicles had been diverted from Avari Towers towards Fatima Jinnah Road and Sindh Club.

Both sides of Deen Mohammad Wafai Road had also been closed to traffic, with vehicles diverted from MR Kiani Chowrangi towards Thana Gali and from Fawara Chowk towards Zainab Market.

Main Korangi Road from CSD towards Sharea Faisal was closed at around 11am due to “security” reasons and was reopened to traffic at 9:30pm.

The alerts for road closures had cited “security” as the reason, except for the blockade of the route between Guru Mandir and Jamshed Road. The alert for this closure said the road had been blocked due to a planned demonstration by the JUI-F.

The JUI-F had said in a statement that while its main demonstration would be held at Guru Mandir, protests would also be held at its headquarters, press clubs and other locations across Sindh against the “violation of the sanctity of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s residence, the ongoing smear campaign against him, and the conspiracy to divide Sindh”.

Meanwhile, the JSRC had announced a rally to protest the proposal to create new provinces and divide Sindh.

A four-member PPP committee began efforts on Friday to persuade nationalist parties to postpone their planned rallies in Karachi, but failed to do so.

Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up a political storm since he called for the formation of new administrative units in the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

The PPP, which is in power in Sindh, has been clear in its stance against carving out any new federating units in the province but has been calling for the creation of a South Punjab province.

The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan, which is an ally of the ruling PML-N along with the PPP in the Centre and in opposition in Sindh, has been insisting on the creation of new provinces and has thrown its weight behind the proposal to hold a referendum on the matter.

World.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as EU and others reject deal
World.content:
UN climate talks collapsed on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkiye and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

The failed talks reflect world governments’ struggle this year to muster ambitious action to address the worsening consequences of climate change, as wars, economic pressures and other crises compete for their attention.

After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime — making it the longest COP on record — Turkiye’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.

“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.”

He later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed” that the climate talks ended without consensus.

“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” Guterres said in a statement.

“Those who profit from the destruction of our planet must never dictate the terms of the fight to save it. Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. ”

Australia’s COP31 President of Negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers.

Earlier, multiple countries and negotiating blocs said they could not accept the version of the text put before them.

“It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” Kurum said.

The last time UN climate talks failed to end with a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

The collapse this time is against the backdrop of competing crises, including wars and public outcry over the cost of living, that have overshadowed the problems caused by a warming climate.

Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving global warming.

“It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels,” he said.

Panama also said it could not support the current text because it fails to meet the scale of the climate crisis.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body in October that confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius, a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

Belgium’s Climate Minister Jean-Luc Crucke said the failure of the deal was a difficult outcome, but appropriate.

“It’s not the end of multilateralism, but there has to be courage to say no,” he said.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous UN conferences or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.

Pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil producers

The proposed deal had acknowledged the overshoot, but called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

Observers at the venue said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping explicit mention of fossil fuels out of the text, and carbon removal technologies in.

While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere when paired with steep emissions cuts is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the deal said they worried the carbon removal language would be used as a licence to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit he was surprised at the resistance to technology.

“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important, it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions… will be taken off the table,” he said.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new climate finance to help them adapt to a warming planet. The deal had called for a tripling of such finance, but did not specify from what baseline.

The failed deal had also included a goal put forward by Turkiye to expand electricity’s share of total final world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from around 23pc now.

Proponents of that pledge said it could cut greenhouse gas emissions by speeding the transition away from fuel-powered cars, furnaces, and other equipment. But critics said it could force more costs onto poor nations without providing a clear path away from fossil fuels.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual summit provides an opportunity for nations to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

World.title: Oman to supply petroleum products, $200m credit facility to PSO under new agreement
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Oman on Sunday signed an agreement under which the Gulf country’s state-owned OQ Trading would supply petroleum products, as well as a $200 million credit line, to the Pakistan State Oil (PSO).

This could provide Pakistan with a means to strategically diversify its sourcing of petroleum products as the Strait of Hormuz continues to be choked by the US-Iran conflict into its ninth month.

According to an announcement from the Petroleum Division, the agreement between the two state-owned entities was signed during Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik’s visit to Muscat, where he met with Oman’s Minister of Energy and Minerals Eng. Salim Al Aufi.

The two sides discussed opportunities for strengthening bilateral cooperation in the oil, gas and minerals sectors.

During the meeting, both ministers discussed avenues for mutually beneficial cooperation and welcomed the establishment of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Working Group on Oil and Gas. They agreed to make optimal use of this institutional mechanism to further strengthen bilateral engagement and advance cooperation in the energy and mining sector.

Following the meeting, the two ministers witnessed the signing of a Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA) for petroleum products between PSO and OQ Trading (OQT), Oman’s global commodity trading company. OQT has also agreed to extend a $200m credit line to PSO to facilitate petroleum purchases.

Welcoming the agreement, both ministers expressed confidence that its implementation would further strengthen Pakistan-Oman energy ties and support Pakistan’s efforts to enhance energy security through diversification of energy imports.

“The agreement marks an important milestone in the commercial relationship between the two companies and provides a structured arrangement for petroleum product supplies from OQT to PSO, supporting supply reliability amid continued volatility in regional energy markets,” the Petroleum Division’s statement said.

It noted that OQT has already established itself as a major supplier of gasoline to PSO, supplying more than 1m tonnes during 2026. The newly signed agreement builds on this established trading relationship and provides a framework for expanding commercial cooperation, the statement added.

Beyond gasoline, OQT has also strengthened its presence in Pakistan’s liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) market, supplying both state-owned and private sector buyers.

According to the Petroleum Division, OQT’s LPG supplies to Pakistan are expected to exceed 120,000 metric tonnes by the end of 2026, reflecting the company’s continued commitment to meeting market demand and maintaining energy flows amid regional supply disruptions.

The meeting and the signing of the agreement underscore the shared commitment of Pakistan and Oman to expanding bilateral energy cooperation, strengthening commercial partnerships and exploring new investment opportunities across the oil, gas and minerals sectors, the statement added.

Last month, Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi made a two-day visit to Pakistan, meeting its top leadership.

He attended the eighth session of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC), during which both sides emphasised the importance of promoting exchanges of business delegations from both countries to unlock new opportunities for trade, investment and institutional collaboration.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
