“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

The ICJ president said Myanmar had failed to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible for acts punishable under Article III of the Genocide Convention.

The Myanmar military also disseminated and promoted hate speech in a systematic and coordinated way during the 2017 operation, the court said.

The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations of its obligations under the Genocide Convention and to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of those who fled the violence to their homes. It also ruled that Myanmar must investigate suspected perpetrators and prosecute and punish those found responsible, and provide compensation. The amount would be determined in future proceedings, it said.

The ruling cannot be appealed. Rather than prosecuting individuals, the verdict determined that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide.

As a result of the military operation in Rakhine, over one million Rohingya now live in what is effectively the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh. For some of them, the case offered a glimmer of hope for accountability.

“I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor told AFP before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.

“There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity.

“This is a historic ruling. For the first time, the World Court has found a state responsible for committing genocide—and the man who commanded those operations is now Myanmar’s president,” said Richard Horsey, senior adviser for Asia at the International Crisis Group.

Horsey pointed out that the court lacks the power to enforce the orders contained in its ruling.

“What matters now is whether the governments engaging Naypyitaw are prepared to attach any cost to ignoring it,” he said.

Myanmar should comply with the court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya, said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

“Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar,” she said.

Agnès Callamard, secretary general of Amnesty International, said international governments should not welcome putschist president and former Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw a campaign of crimes against humanity and other crimes under international law against the Rohingya.

“Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar,” she said.

All other states, including members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, must also uphold these obligations under the Genocide Convention and general international law, taking every measure within their power to prevent and punish genocide, Callamard said.

She urged the UN Security Council to impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court.

The Myanmar military’s 2017 “clearance operations” in northern Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee amid widespread killings, sexual violence and arson attacks, according to UN investigations.

World.title: Seat at Global Table: How Astana Is Embracing World Gastronomy
World.content:
ASTANA – A dinner table can be many things: a place to share a meal, exchange stories or, sometimes, bring cultures closer together. In diplomacy, it can even become a meeting point where conversations flow more naturally than they might across a conference table. That idea was at the heart of an Italian gastronomic evening at Selfie Astana restaurant on Nov. 20, when Anthony Genovese, chef and owner of Rome’s two-Michelin-starred restaurant Il Pagliaccio, brought his interpretation of Italian cuisine to Kazakhstan’s capital.

Organized in cooperation with the Italian Embassy in Kazakhstan, the dinner was part of the 11th edition of the Week of Italian Cuisine in the World. But it also reflected a broader development: Astana’s growing role as a destination for international culinary experiences, where renowned chefs, local ingredients and different food traditions meet.

For Genovese, whose cooking combines Italian roots with French techniques and Asian influences, the invitation offered an opportunity to explore another culinary culture. Asked whether he had discovered anything from Kazakhstan that caught his attention, he mentioned camel and horse milk, as well as local cheese.

“I am very interested in using camel milk and horse milk,” he said, adding that he would like to explore the possibilities of working with Kazakh cheese.

It was a small exchange, but one that captured the spirit of the evening. International gastronomy is not simply about bringing familiar dishes to a new audience. It is also about discovering what another place has to offer.

A growing international table

Astana has been building this kind of culinary dialogue through Astana Global Gastro, an annual project launched in 2023 by Good Project. The initiative brings internationally recognized chefs to Kazakhstan’s capital for special gastronomic dinners.

By the end of 2024, the project had hosted 11 gala dinners, featuring chefs associated with Michelin stars and international restaurant rankings. Among its guests have been Spanish chef Paco Pérez, who has received four Michelin stars across his restaurants, and Italian chef Chiara Pavan, a two-Michelin-starred chef whose work also focuses on sustainable gastronomy. In 2024, the program welcomed French chef Vladimir Mukhin, among other international names.

The project has since continued to expand its international reach. In April 2026, it opened a new season with a dinner by Seoul-based chef Jun Lee, whose restaurant SOIGNÉ has two Michelin stars. The sequence of events suggests that Astana is becoming more than a place where international chefs make occasional guest appearances. It is developing a platform for culinary exchange, bringing different gastronomic traditions to an increasingly curious local audience.

Italy has become a particularly consistent partner in this effort. The Italian Embassy has collaborated with Astana Global Gastro on dinners during the annual Week of Italian Cuisine, including events with Chiara Pavan in 2023, Giuseppe Postorino, the Michelin-starred chef of L’Alchimia, a renowned Milanese restaurant ranked among the Top 50 Italy 2023, and Andrea Antonini in 2025. This year’s dinner with Genovese continued that tradition. For Italy’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan Antonello De Riu food offers a language that needs little translation.

“I think Italian cuisine has an international language, like Esperanto,” he said. Italy, he added, is already well loved by people in Kazakhstan for its culture, historic sites, shopping and, of course, food.

Bringing a Michelin-starred chef to Astana gives local audiences an opportunity to discover another side of Italian cuisine: one that respects tradition while exploring new techniques and interpretations.

In 2025, UNESCO recognized Italian cuisine as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The recognition, De Riu noted, was not about a single dish, but about a collective tradition shaped by biodiversity, craftsmanship, family practices and knowledge passed down through generations.

“Cuisine is founded on traditions, but it is also innovation,” he said.

The ambassador also sees the dinner table as a natural setting for cultural diplomacy. Whether the conversation concerns business, politics or culture, people often find it easier to connect when they sit down together.

“The table is a perfect tool also for diplomats,” he said.

Beyond imported flavors

Yet the appeal of such events lies not only in the opportunity to experience international cuisine. It also raises a question about what Kazakhstan itself can bring to the global table.

Genovese, who had previously visited Almaty, was impressed by the city’s emerging restaurant scene and young chefs working with local ingredients. He recalled seeing restaurants where chefs took pride in cooking with regional produce, including lamb and horse meat.

His advice to young Kazakh chefs was not to imitate established culinary traditions, but to embrace their own.

“You have to be proud of who you are,” he said, encouraging young chefs from Kazakhstan to bring their ingredients and culinary traditions to Europe and introduce them to international audiences, rather than simply coming to Europe to learn how to cook European food.

He sees considerable potential in Kazakhstan’s food culture, particularly its distinctive ingredients and traditions. Camel and horse milk, local cheeses and other regional products, he said, offer possibilities worth exploring.

This is where Astana’s growing international gastronomy scene could become especially interesting. A city that invites the world to its table can also use that opportunity to introduce the world to its own.

The capital’s geographical position between Europe and Asia offers a natural backdrop for such encounters. But geography alone does not create a culinary destination. It takes restaurants willing to experiment, organizers prepared to build international partnerships, chefs interested in local traditions and an audience open to discovering something unfamiliar.

Astana Global Gastro and the Italian Embassy’s recurring culinary events are contributing to that process, one dinner at a time.

Perhaps the most meaningful measure of their success is not how many famous chefs have visited, or how many Michelin stars have appeared on a menu. It is whether these encounters leave something behind: a new collaboration, a curiosity about unfamiliar ingredients, or a greater appreciation of the culinary traditions that make each place distinct.

After all, a good meal may end in a few hours, but the conversations it inspires can last much longer. And perhaps that is what makes such encounters more important than the meal itself.

World.title: First Time in Almaty’s Mountains: Visitor’s Guide to Shymbulak
World.content:
ALMATY – As Ayaz Kara, a travel blogger from Azerbaijan, snowboarded down a floodlit run at Shymbulak Mountain Resort, the lights of Almaty spread out below him.

“I can’t remember ever enjoying snowboarding that much,” he said, recalling how long the run was and how good the ride felt that evening.

Ayaz Kara visited Kazakhstan for the first time this year on an impromptu trip to Almaty with friends. He knew little about the city before arriving and got his first look at its mountains from a gondola cabin, a ride he now recommends to anyone who wants to see the area.

For many international visitors, the first question is what to do once they reach the top.

Temirlan Zhussupov, who has worked at Shymbulak for five years and leads its guest services team, said he hears it often at the resort’s information center.

Getting there

Shymbulak is located around 20 kilometers from the center of Almaty. Zhussupov recommends starting the trip in the morning at Medeu, which can be reached from the city by bus routes 12 and 21. On online maps, the gondola boarding point is listed as Medeu base station. Parking is available nearby, though drivers are advised to check vehicle access rules in advance.

Before heading up, visitors can walk around the Medeu ice rink or visit the 842-step Health Stairway, a popular outdoor fitness landmark near Almaty that leads to a panoramic viewpoint overlooking the mountain valley.

The gondola takes them to Shymbulak station, which has a restaurant overlooking the slopes, a souvenir shop and a kids club with a playground and creative activities.

From Shymbulak station, one can continue to the top station or take a separate ride on the open-air Quad 4 chairlift. The Combi-1 lift leads to the mid station, where another restaurant overlooks the gorge. Both routes are marked on the resort’s English-language map.

“I’d especially like visitors to see the mountains in the morning, when they can take their time, enjoy the scenery and take photos,” Zhussupov said.

The round trip from Medeu takes four to five hours, including lift changes and stops. Visitors who begin with a morning walk near the rink can expect to return to Medeu around 3 p.m.

Temperatures in the mountains are lower than in the city, so a warm jacket is recommended, along with a raincoat if rain is forecast. Clothing and accessories are also sold at the resort’s Shymbulak Wear shops.

Tickets and prices

The route to the summit includes three lifts: the gondola from Medeu to Shymbulak station, Combi-1 to the mid station and Combi-2 to the highest point, around 3,200 meters above sea level.

The Shymbulak Ticket covers all three lifts in both directions.

It costs 12,000 tenge (US$27) for visitors aged 15 and older and 4,000 tenge (US$9) for children aged 6 to 14. Children aged 5 and under ride free.

A 360° ticket offers a ride in a gondola with a glass floor, while the separate Quad 4 chairlift serves the Konus slope. Tickets are sold online, and the full list of fares is available on the website.

First lessons and night skiing

The resort’s instructors advise first-time skiers and snowboarders to book a lesson in advance and start on a beginner slope.

In the online booking form, visitors can select the “First Time” level, choose a private or group lesson and request English as the language of instruction. Details are available on the page of the ski and snowboard school and in the booking terms. Equipment rentals are offered at both Medeu and Shymbulak stations.

To experience Shymbulak by day and after dark, Kara recommends setting aside at least three days. This allows time for skiing or snowboarding during the day, an evening on the floodlit slopes and a few hours of sightseeing. The resort announces its night skiing and snowboarding season separately.

Before visiting, travelers are advised to check the resort’s current prices for sightseeing tickets and day and night ski passes.

On the day of the trip, they should confirm which lifts and runs are open, as mountain weather can affect operations, and note the last boarding time for each lift on the way back.

Night skiers should also check that evening’s schedule and the time of the last gondola to Medeu. Updates are posted in the resort news and on its official Telegram channel.

World.title: Is It Harder to Make Friends After 30?
World.content:
It has been a difficult few months for me personally. Perhaps that is why I have found myself returning to comfort shows I grew up watching. There is something reassuring about familiar characters, predictable storylines and the simple pleasure of hearing conversations you almost know by heart. It is also a good way to keep my English from getting rusty.

Recently, I found myself watching Friends again. Beyond the fame and fortune it brought its six main cast members, the show has offered comfort to millions of people around the world. And watching it made me think about something that rarely gets discussed: how do we navigate loneliness in a century when so many of us no longer have that close-knit circle of friends who feel almost like family?

Especially after 30. By this age, life tends to get complicated. We have jobs, mortgages, responsibilities and expectations. Some of us get married, some get divorced, some remain single. We move cities, change careers, build families or start over. Our lives take different directions, and sometimes the people who once knew us best are no longer part of our everyday world.

I caught myself feeling a little envious of the relationships in Friends. Of course, I know it is television, not real life. Six people sharing an apartment, spending most of their time together, and always being available for one another is hardly realistic. But perhaps what I envy is not their lifestyle. It is the sense of belonging. The feeling that no matter what happens, there is a place where you are expected, understood and accepted.

So, is it harder to make friends after 30? I think the answer is both yes and no. Yes, because friendship used to happen almost automatically. At school or college, we were surrounded by people our age, sharing the same routines, worries and ambitions. We did not have to schedule a coffee three weeks in advance or find an evening when everyone was free. Proximity did much of the work for us.

As adults, friendship requires intention. You have to make time, reach out, show interest and, sometimes, make the first move. And not everyone has the energy for that.

But I also think there is something special about the friendships we develop later in life. For me, one of the greatest revelations of getting older has been becoming more comfortable with who I am. Of course, like many women, I sometimes worry about aging and would love to remain young and attractive for as long as possible. But there is another side to growing older: you gradually stop negotiating with yourself over every little thing. You become more aware of what matters to you, what you can accept in others and where your boundaries lie. And that changes the way you build relationships.

When we are younger, we often try too hard to be liked. We hide parts of ourselves, avoid difficult conversations and compromise our own peace just to keep people around. We mistake being agreeable for being close. With time, you realize that a good friendship does not require you to perform. You can show up with your flaws, your strengths, your complicated history and your less attractive moments. And so can the other person.

Of course, there is a special gift in having friends since childhood. Growing together, witnessing each other’s transformations, surviving heartbreaks, career struggles, and all the unexpected turns life takes. Knowing someone long enough to remember who they were before they became who they are today. Learning how to handle disagreements, forgive misunderstandings and stay present through difficult periods. That kind of friendship is priceless.

I still keep in touch with some of my school friends. But if I am honest, those relationships are no longer what they once were. They are held together, to some extent, by shared memories, by nostalgia for who we were and the dreams we had. And there is something beautiful about that, too. Not every friendship has to remain the same to have mattered.

Most of us went through our own version of growing up, sometimes without those people by our side. We had to figure things out, make mistakes, experience disappointments and find our way back to ourselves. Perhaps that is why meeting someone who genuinely understands you in your thirties can feel like an even greater joy. Two people, each with their own history, strengths and imperfections, choosing to make room for one another. Not because they have to, but because they want to.

I suspect that vulnerability is what makes this both a gift and a challenge. Real friendship means allowing someone to see you without the usual filters. It means accepting that the other person will not always meet your expectations, say the right thing or fit neatly into the image of a perfect friend you might have carried for years.

Growing up, I think, is partly about making peace with life’s imperfections. You stop demanding that reality follow the perfect list of expectations you once wrote in your head. This is not always easy. But it is liberating. And perhaps making friends after 30 is part of that liberation. You are no longer looking for someone to complete the picture you imagined for yourself. You are looking for someone with whom you can be exactly as you are, without having to explain or apologize for every part of it.

Maybe that is what friendship in adulthood really offers: not the comfort of having everything figured out, but the freedom to be imperfect together. And in a world that often makes us feel increasingly alone, that is a pretty extraordinary thing.

World.title: American Archaeologist Uncovers Christian Past of Medieval Silk Road City in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – For three decades, Steven Gilbert had lived in Kazakhstan as a humanitarian worker and English teacher. Today, the American archaeologist is helping rewrite the history of the Zhetisu Region. He leads the excavations at Ilibalyk, a medieval Silk Road city where his team found the first clearly Christian cemetery in Kazakhstan dating to before the arrival of the Russian Empire.

Gilbert drew wide public attention this summer after a video of him speaking fluent Kazakh spread on social media, where viewers praised his pronunciation.

Born in Amarillo, Texas, in 1964, Gilbert came to Kazakhstan in 1993, shortly after independence, together with his wife, Elizabeth, through a humanitarian organization. In an interview with The Times of Central Asia, he said their work included food aid in the Aral Sea region and exchange programs. The couple began learning Kazakh as soon as they arrived and lived in the country continuously until 2024. Earlier Russian-language media reports said Gilbert headed the humanitarian organization Senim and taught English.

His path to archaeology began in 2014, when a schoolteacher in the village of Usharal in the Panfilov District found a one-meter Christian gravestone. The stone, now kept at the Center for the Rapprochement of Cultures in Almaty, connected Gilbert with archaeologists from Kazakhstan and the United States, and he returned to the U.S. to study archaeology. Today, he is an assistant professor of intercultural studies and associate director of the Tandy Institute for Archaeology at Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary in Texas, and he divides his time between the two countries.

Ilibalyk lies in the Ili River valley near the Chinese border, just beyond the Dzungarian Gate. Armenian, Persian, and Chinese sources from the 12th to 14th centuries mention the city, which was a stop on the road to Almaliq, the capital of the Chagatai rulers. Excavations began in 2016 as a joint project of the Lanier Center for Archaeology in the U.S. and Kazakh specialists. The site covers about five square kilometers and had never been excavated before, although part of it was damaged after 1933, when the area became a Soviet collective farm.

According to Gilbert, a Turkic-speaking Christian community lived in Ilibalyk for almost two centuries, from the 12th to the 14th century. Its members lived alongside Muslims, Buddhists, Manichaeans, and followers of the traditional beliefs known today as Tengrism. Christian cemeteries of that era had already been found in neighboring Kyrgyzstan, but Ilibalyk provides the first reliable evidence of such a community on the territory of modern Kazakhstan.

The team has found more than 50 gravestones, known as kairaks, bearing cross images. Six carry epitaphs: four in Old Turkic, a predecessor of modern Turkic languages including Kazakh, and two in Syriac, the liturgical language of the Church of the East. The names include biblical ones such as Petros and Isho, as well as Central Asian names such as Shirin and Tegiz.

In one section of the cemetery, archaeologists found at least five women buried with boqtaq headdresses, worn by high-status married women, often called khatuns. Their graves contained scissors, daggers, and rings. Gilbert believes the women may have come from the kereit or naiman tribes, whose daughters often married Mongol rulers, including Genghis Khan’s sons. Next to the cemetery, the team uncovered the foundations of a funerary chapel measuring 23 by eight meters, where local Christians prepared the dead for burial. Gilbert said it is the first such structure archaeologists have ever found.

The city’s place on the trade routes is also visible in the finds. The news media El.kz reported that excavators uncovered pearls and corals, goods that could have reached the steppe only by long-distance caravan trade and that point to wealthy residents.

Yet the burials also reveal hard lives. Signs of malnutrition appear in almost everyone buried at the site, child burials are about as numerous as adult ones, and few people lived to old age. Gilbert links the famines to harsh winters and civil wars between the Chagatai and Yuan uluses, as well as within the Chagatai ulus itself.

The team combines traditional digging with LiDAR-equipped drones, ground-penetrating radar, radiocarbon dating, and preliminary ancient DNA analysis. The work is carried out under Kazakh law together with Rutrum, an Almaty-based cultural resource management company, and international partners including the Swiss Society for the Exploration of Eurasia. Specialists and volunteers from South Korea, Australia, the United Kingdom, Singapore, Uzbekistan, Russia, and different regions of Kazakhstan have joined the project. This year’s team numbered almost 40 people, including residents of Usharal.

All artifacts belong to Kazakhstan and leave the country only when the government lends them to international exhibitions. The state protects the site, and Gilbert said residents have begun to take pride in it and report illegal metal detectorists. He hopes museums in the Panfilov District and other regions will one day display the Christian gravestones and tell the story of Ilibalyk’s people.

Gilbert says the Kazakh language has been central to his work. “Knowing Kazakh brings you closer to the heart of the people,” he told Kazakhstanskaya Pravda.

He noted that most Kazakhs he talked to did not know that Christians lived on their land almost a thousand years ago. For him, these discoveries show how religiously diverse the ancestors of the Kazakh people were, long before the modern state emerged.

World.title: Trump, Xi and Putin at One Table: What Does It Mean for Central Asia?
World.content:
ASTANA — The unprecedented gathering of the leaders of the United States (U.S.), China and Russia projected an image of great-power diplomacy. The image was striking: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sitting at the same table in China, the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers convening in an unprecedented trilateral meeting. The summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meetings, carried unmistakable symbolism and inevitably revived comparisons to the Yalta Conference of 1945, when Allied leaders discussed the postwar order.

Trump declared they were “really making history,” while Xi spoke of peace when major powers live in harmony. Yet the summit produced little concrete progress on the conflicts and disagreements that brought the leaders together. The three issued a symbolic declaration reaffirming that nuclear war must never be fought and agreed to pursue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but announced no arms-control negotiations or breakthroughs on Ukraine, Iran, trade or other major disputes. The spectacle was historic. Its substance was considerably more modest.

The distinction matters for Central Asia, a region positioned between Russia and China, increasingly connected to global trade routes, and working to maintain relationships with the U.S., Europe and other partners. If the meeting offered a glimpse of a world managed by its biggest powers, did it signal a shift in the international system or simply demonstrate how difficult it remains for them to agree? For Kazakhstan and its neighbors, the answer may lie less in what the three leaders agreed on than in what their meeting reveals about the limits and opportunities of great-power politics.

No new geopolitical bargain

Temur Umarov, a fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center whose research focuses on Central Asian foreign and domestic policies and China’s relations with Russia and the region, sees little evidence that the summit represents a fundamental geopolitical shift.

“I don’t think that we’re living in times of major geopolitical shift. I don’t think that this trilateral summit has started a new chapter in the history of global politics,” Umarov said in a comment to The Astana Times.

Rather than a breakthrough, he sees the gathering as largely symbolic, with its limited outcomes reflecting the current state of international relations. He said that the fact that the leaders could agree only on broad, formal principles speaks to how difficult it is to reconcile their competing interests.

The summit was always unlikely to produce a major agreement, Umarov said, given the state of international politics and the differences among the three powers.

But he cautioned against interpreting this uncertainty as necessarily negative for countries caught between competing powers.

“For countries like Kazakhstan or other Central Asian countries, or other regions that are in between these countries that are in rivalry or in confrontation, it doesn’t necessarily mean that it’s a bad period or dark times. It actually provides a lot of ground for maneuver,” Umarov said.

That space, he noted, can open opportunities for deeper cooperation with different partners: provided regional governments can translate the attention they receive into tangible benefits.

Central Asian governments, accustomed to navigating competing interests, have become adept at multilateral diplomacy. The region’s growing international visibility is no accident, Umarov said, as countries seek to turn current geopolitical momentum into something more concrete. The challenge, however, is to convert diplomatic access into economic partnerships, investment, connectivity and political leverage, rather than simply enjoy a moment in the global spotlight.

The danger of being placed on someone else’s map

Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute focusing on Greater Asia, takes a more cautionary view of what a great-power arrangement could mean for countries across Eurasia. Moriyasu notes that Washington should be careful about institutionalizing a trilateral format with Beijing and Moscow, warning that the U.S. could find itself negotiating from a structurally disadvantaged position.

“I do not believe President Donald Trump went to China to divide the world into spheres of influence with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin,” Moriyasu said in a comment to The Astana Times.

He believes Trump was pursuing specific objectives, including nuclear arms reductions, and hoping for a diplomatic breakthrough. But the underlying problem, Moriyasu said, is that China and Russia share a strategic interest in challenging U.S. global leadership, potentially putting Washington in a two-against-one position.

Instead, he advocates elevating the Board of Peace as a diplomatic platform where the U.S. could work with countries that seek greater engagement with Washington while maintaining independence amid great-power competition. He identifies Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Türkiye, Pakistan, Mongolia and Hungary among strategically positioned countries whose interests include preserving their autonomy.

His argument carries a warning for Kazakhstan and the wider region: a world organized around spheres of influence could narrow the space for independent foreign policy. In such a scenario, Kazakhstan could risk being viewed through the prism of Russia’s traditional influence or China’s expanding continental reach, rather than as a sovereign actor pursuing its own priorities.

That is precisely the outcome Astana’s balanced and constructive diplomacy is designed to avoid.

World.title: Almaty Named Among BBC Travel’s 20 Best Places to Visit in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Almaty has been named the only Central Asian city among BBC Travel’s 20 best places to visit in 2027, with the British publication highlighting its contemporary art scene, traditional crafts, national cuisine and mountain landscapes.

The annual list also features Burgundy in France, Sardinia in Italy, Alberta in Canada and Christchurch in New Zealand. This year’s selection focuses on destinations where tourism supports cultural heritage preservation, environmental protection and local communities.

BBC Travel recommends exploring Almaty, located at the foothills of the mountains, through its growing cultural scene and connections to Kazakhstan’s traditions.

Among the featured attractions is the Almaty Museum of Arts, which the publication describes as the first major contemporary art museum in Central Asia. Opened in September 2025, its collection includes works by artists from Kazakhstan and other countries in the region.

The publication also highlights Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture, housed in a former cinema renovated by British architect Asif Khan. The restoration included the preservation of graffiti artwork by prominent artist Yevgeny Sidorkin.

The city’s culinary scene also features in the selection. BBC Travel recommends the Auyl restaurant, located in the Medeu area, for its contemporary interpretation of Kazakh cuisine. Its architecture draws inspiration from the traditional Kazakh yurt, while the interior features carpets and handmade decorations.

Among the dishes highlighted by the publication are horse meat tartare and bone marrow served with flatbread. The restaurant also offers mountain views and can be included in a trip to Medeu and Shymbulak.

World.title: Love, Loneliness and Algorithms: How AI Is Entering Our Personal Lives
World.content:
ASTANA – Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a confidant for people navigating loneliness, emotional struggles and complicated relationships. Chatbots offer instant advice, a sympathetic response and a seemingly nonjudgmental space to discuss personal problems. In some cases, they are taking on roles traditionally filled by friends, therapists or relationship counselors.

From analyzing text messages and preparing users for difficult conversations to offering emotional reassurance, AI tools are becoming part of people’s private lives. It can act as a dating coach, help interpret a partner’s messages, offer guidance during a personal crisis or simply serve as a companion available around the clock. However, as the line between digital assistance and emotional intimacy grows less distinct, questions about psychological dependence, accountability and the limits of artificial companionship are becoming harder to ignore.

Humans are inherently social, according to the 2025 report of the World Health Organization’s Commission on Social Connection. Social interaction shapes brain development and mental health throughout life, while strong social connections are essential to overall well-being.

Yet loneliness and social isolation remain widespread. Between 2014 and 2023, one in six people worldwide experienced loneliness, the report found. Social disconnection is associated with increased risks of heart disease, stroke, depression and anxiety, as well as difficulties at school, university and work.

Against this backdrop, AI is increasingly entering a space traditionally occupied by human relationships.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has also discussed AI’s potential role in addressing people’s need for connection. Speaking on a podcast, he said people want to feel understood, express themselves and avoid loneliness. He suggested that AI could become an additional source of support, particularly for those who do not have access to a therapist.

Zuckerberg also described how users turn to Meta AI to talk through personal problems, prepare for difficult conversations or discuss relationship issues. He said voice-based AI could make these interactions more useful by allowing people to rehearse conversations.

At the same time, Zuckerberg said AI should complement, not replace, human relationships, helping people become more thoughtful and attentive in their interactions with others.

An always-available listener

“Tell me if you want to talk about it. I’m here.”

ChatGPT responds with variations of this reassuring message to users who bring personal problems to the chatbot. It creates an environment that can feel comfortable and safe, where users feel heard and accepted.

Muragul Muratbekova, a software engineer and research associate at the Kazakhstan-British Technical University, said AI has become part of everyday life across almost every field, and she is no exception.

“I often use AI for work, and it definitely helps me automate routine tasks. I also use it in everyday life. For example, when I’m cooking, it’s much easier to ask AI for a recipe. There are millions of recipes online, and you have to spend time choosing one. AI narrows down the options, so you do not have to waste your energy on that,” Muratbekova told The Astana Times.

She also uses AI as a digital wardrobe assistant.

“You can take pictures of all your clothes, tell AI which city you live in, what the weather is like and what your lifestyle looks like. It can then help you put together a capsule wardrobe, suggest what to get rid of and what to buy. Normally, people spend hours browsing the internet and scrolling through pictures to get inspiration. Now you can simply delegate these small decisions to AI,” she said.

Muratbekova noted that she does not necessarily consider AI a friend, but she does see people using it as a kind of psychologist.

“I think it’s partly because life moves so fast. I cannot always wait for my friends to be free, or wait for an appointment with a psychologist. Everything feels urgent, and you want to find a solution right away, whatever the problem is. Maybe we have just become used to getting everything here and now,” she said.

In this sense, AI can act as a first-response tool. It may help ease emotional distress or make a problem feel more manageable in the moment.

However, it does not necessarily offer a lasting solution. There is also a question of whether temporary relief leads to lasting benefits. If interacting with AI encourages people to build real-world connections, it may be helpful. But if it replaces contact with friends, family and other people, the long-term effects could be quite different.

Muratbekova finds AI useful for discussing health concerns, particularly topics that may feel uncomfortable to raise with other people.

“AI is also useful for health-related questions. Of course, it doesn’t replace a doctor, and everyone should understand that. But sometimes you are simply not sure what’s normal and what isn’t. AI chatbots can be particularly helpful with topics you might not feel comfortable discussing with other people,” she said.

Muratbekova does not believe AI will replace professional psychologists. However, she thinks it is more likely to replace jobs that do not require emotional engagement or personal responsibility.

“First, AI does not have empathy. Second, it tells you things you already know, essentially reflecting your own thoughts. Working with a psychologist helps you develop new behavioral strategies and ways of thinking. Psychologists conduct extensive research and preparation to guide their clients. AI, by contrast, tends to follow the direction in which the user leads it,” she said.

AI enters the dating scene

Online dating has quickly become another testing ground for AI.

Some people are skilled at creating attractive profiles and writing witty self-descriptions. For many others, however, putting together a dating profile can be a challenge. AI can make the process easier.

Some users ask ChatGPT to edit their photographs or generate images that look like they came from a professional photo shoot. Some practice conversations with virtual partners, while others let AI handle exchanges with real people in an effort to arrange dates more quickly.

Muratbekova noted that AI can save time in the dating process.

“One of my friends uses ChatGPT to review dating profiles and identify people who might be a good match. The chatbot can even help initiate conversations with potential partners, making the search for a compatible match easier,” she said.

AI can also help people prepare for a date by suggesting venues, activities and conversation topics, or even rehearsing jokes and possible responses.

“Dating has its ups and downs, and you always want someone to share your experiences and concerns with. AI is always available. I think I would turn to it more as an adviser, especially when I’m struggling to understand someone else’s behavior,” Muratbekova said.

ChatGPT can analyze messages users upload, assess each person’s contributions to a conversation, and validate the user’s feelings. It can then offer an interpretation of what happened – one that may closely reflect the user’s own version of events, shaped by the information and perspective they provide in their prompts.

The user is, after all, at the center of the interaction. The AI sees only the information it receives, which means that the other person’s perspective, intentions and feelings may be missing from the analysis.

The risks of artificial intimacy

Ekaterina Talimanchuk, a therapist, noted that AI systems learn about users’ preferences and interests and then mirror them in their responses.

“AI can create the feeling that it understands you completely. That’s why people can become attached to it quite quickly and start turning to it more and more. But we need to remember that AI cannot replace human communication, with all its empathy, disagreements and different points of view,” Talimanchuk told The Astana Times.

She warned that becoming accustomed to constant agreement from AI could make people less tolerant of differences in real-life relationships.

Chatbots can adapt to users’ preferences and respond to almost any request, while partners and friends have their own opinions, ambitions and needs, which do not always align with ours.

Talimanchuk described excessive interaction with AI as a potential “dopamine trap,” warning that avoiding uncomfortable conversations and criticism could make people less prepared to deal with difficulties in real life.

“AI does not frustrate or criticize you, and avoiding uncomfortable situations can make people less mature and resilient. But dealing with difficulties is necessary. It’s an important part of personal development and growth,” she said.

She also emphasized that AI systems can make mistakes and should not be used as a substitute for professional intervention in serious situations.

“Mental health crises, suicidal thoughts, and complex trauma require immediate professional help. An algorithm may offer some support, but it should never become someone’s only source of help. Human contact remains essential to effective therapy,” Talimanchuk said.

Ultimately, she said, no algorithm can replace genuine human interaction.

“No algorithm can replace real human connection – a simple touch, the warmth of a loving gaze, that awkward pause before someone first admits their feelings. Relationships are not always perfect, and they can be difficult. However, we need to build them face to face, not through smartphone screens,” Talimanchuk said.

World.title: Caspian Seals Under Threats as Shrinking Sea Reshapes Their Habitat
World.content:
ASTANA – Falling water levels and shrinking ice cover in the Caspian Sea as well as human activity are putting pressure on the habitats seals depend on to rest and raise their pups. In an interview with The Astana Times, Assel Baimukanova, a researcher at the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, said that protecting the species requires stronger regional cooperation and continued research.

She said changes in the sea are disrupting the animals’ natural habitat, particularly in the northern Caspian, where they rely on islands for resting and winter ice for breeding.

“The health of the Caspian Sea is the health of the Caspian seal. By observing the condition of the seals, we can understand the condition of the sea. And right now, the sea is not doing very well,” said Baimukanova, who has studied Caspian seals for 13 years.

Baimukanova has taken part in more than 30 field expeditions. With her family, she also makes documentary films about the species. Their team has produced nine films about the Caspian seal.

During regular expeditions, she has observed how the sea and the animals’ living conditions have changed over time.

“I first saw the seals in 2013, and I realized that I wanted to stay close to them, study them and work for their protection,” she said.

Shrinking habitat

The Caspian Sea, shared by Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Iran, is divided into northern, middle and southern sections. The Northern Caspian plays an important role in the seals’ seasonal cycle, as the animals use its islands and shallow waters as resting areas.

In spring, the seals gather to molt before moving to feeding grounds to build up energy for winter. In fall, they return to the islands to rest until ice forms. The ice is particularly important because Caspian seals give birth and raise their pups on it.

But falling water levels and shrinking water ice are disrupting this seasonal cycle.

“The current period of sea-level decline began in 1995. Since then, the level of the Northern Caspian has fallen by 2.28 meters. This affects coastal areas and gradually changes the islands and shallow waters that provide important habitats for the animals,” Baimukanova said.

Researchers counted approximately 25,000 seals at the Durnev Islands in Komsomolets Bay in the northeastern Caspian during a helicopter survey in April 2009. The count fell to 20,000 in April 2011. Photographs from those years show large groups resting along the shores.

When Kazakh researchers surveyed the same islands in 2016, they found only around 300 seals. By 2019, the number had dropped to 69. By 2021, the Durnev Islands had merged with the mainland and ceased to exist, and seals no longer haul out there.

“The islands where the seals used to gather are disappearing. They need these places to rest, molt and prepare for winter, but there are fewer suitable areas now,” Baimukanova said.

According to a satellite-imagery analysis published by the team in Frontiers in Marine Science in 2026, the northeastern coast of the Caspian Sea in Kazakhstan has been retreating westward. The study covered the area from the mouth of the Ural (Zhaiyk) River to the Buzachi Peninsula, including Kaydak and Komsomolets bays.

“The coastline retreated by an average of around 2.7 kilometers per year until 2020. Between spring 2022 and spring 2023, however, it shifted by 23 kilometers in a single year,” Baimukanova explained.

Over 1995–2023, the coastline moved by an average of 44 kilometers along most of this stretch and by up to 175 kilometers near Kaydak Bay, while the total area of islands shrank more than 15-fold. These changes make it increasingly difficult for researchers to monitor habitats and for seals to find suitable resting places.

Climate change and human activity

Falling sea levels are not the only concern. Climate change is also affecting the availability of ice, which is essential to the reproduction of Caspian seals.

“Where will Caspian seals reproduce if the ice disappears? This is one of the main questions we need to understand,” Baimukanova said.

Human activity is adding to the pressure. The Volga and Ural rivers are major sources of freshwater flowing into the Caspian Sea, but water regulation and withdrawals for economic activities affect how much reaches the sea.

Fishing nets, marine pollution, shipping, tourism and offshore oil and gas activities pose additional risks. Some seals become trapped in abandoned fishing gear, while human activity can disturb their resting areas.

Between 2019 and 2023, scientists examined 395 seal remains and found that 9.4% bore marks of entanglement in fishing nets.

Over five years of fieldwork, researchers also collected more than 36 tons of marine waste, including approximately 17 tons of abandoned fishing nets.

“During one of our visits to a coastal area on the Tyub-Karagan Peninsula in 2013, we recorded around eight tons of rubbish. When we returned five years later, the amount had increased to nine tons. This shows that waste remains a persistent problem along the Caspian coast,” she said.

What research reveals about the seals

Monitoring Caspian seals requires regular fieldwork and multiple research methods. Since 2016, Kazakh scientists have conducted state-commissioned studies, building on earlier research by international teams.

Scientists use drones, aircraft and satellite imagery to count seals, track their distribution and identify changes in their habitats. They also use satellite imagery to identify new islands and resting sites. Researchers also conduct boat-based surveys to monitor conditions in the Caspian Sea.

“Recent aerial counts on island haul-outs in the north-eastern Caspian have raised further concerns about the animals’ numbers and distribution. Researchers counted 59,642 seals on the surveyed islands in spring 2020 and 62,105 in spring 2022. By autumn 2023, the number had fallen to 44,573. These figures refer to seals counted on the surveyed islands, not to the total population of the species,” Baimukanova said.

Researchers also study the seals’ diet and health. Their findings show that Caspian seals feed primarily on small fish, particularly gobies, rather than commercially valuable species.

“Researchers also examine the age of the animals by studying the teeth of dead seals found along the coast. This helps estimate how old they were when they died. In earlier observations, the oldest recorded seals were 50 years old. In more recent research, the oldest recorded animals were 32, while few individuals were found to have reached 20,” she said.

Determining the causes of death remains difficult because researchers need fresh carcasses to conduct detailed laboratory and toxicological examinations. However, available findings point to serious health problems among the animals.

Baimukanova said pollution can weaken the seals’ immune systems, making them more vulnerable to disease. When animals gather in large numbers, infections can also spread more easily.

Efforts to protect the species

Kazakhstan has taken several steps to strengthen the protection of the Caspian seal. The species was included in Kazakhstan’s list of rare and endangered animals in 2020. In 2024, a specially protected natural area dedicated to its conservation was established. Kazakhstan and Russia have also developed a joint action plan, while a seal rehabilitation center is planned within the protected area.

“Further efforts should focus on reducing pollution, preventing illegal fishing and protecting the places where the animals gather. However, the conservation of the Caspian seal cannot be the responsibility of one country alone. Since the Caspian Sea is shared by five states, cooperation among all of them is essential to protecting the species and its habitat,” Baimukanova said.

For researchers, the work also means drawing attention to animals that cannot communicate their problems themselves.

“I think every zoologist considers themselves the voice of the animal they study. The Caspian seal cannot knock on our door and tell us that it is struggling or ask us to improve its living conditions. It cannot speak for itself, so we have to speak for it,” Baimukanova said.

Her words underline a broader point: the fate of the Caspian seal is closely tied to the health of the sea it inhabits. Protecting the species means protecting the ecosystem on which both wildlife and people depend.

World.title: Neighbors mourn the dead and collect belongings from the ruins of their homes. Explosion in Tbilisi
World.content:
Explosion in Fonichala

Six people were killed in a gas explosion in a residential building in Ponichala, a district in Tbilisi. Two of the victims were young children who died alongside their mothers.

One of the five people injured in the explosion remains in critical condition. Two minors are also still receiving hospital treatment.

The destruction left 28 families homeless. They are currently staying in hotels.

Photographs of the six victims at a small park next to the building. Neighbours have set up an impromptu memorial here.

What is happening near the site of the explosion

In Lower Ponichala, where a gas explosion on the morning of November 19 caused two stairwells of a residential building to collapse, the area remains cordoned off with yellow tape. Rescue workers are still at the scene.

Trucks loaded with construction debris stand in the courtyard. Rescue teams are clearing the collapsed building of concrete rubble.

A makeshift memorial has been set up in a small park near the building. It is covered with photographs of the victims, flowers, candles and colourful stuffed toys. Little girls are tying black ribbons around the memorial.

The small park next to the building where the explosion occurred. Photo: Interpressnews

It has been raining in Tbilisi for several days. To protect the photographs, flowers and candles from the rain, the memorial has been covered with a tarpaulin.

Relatives of the victims, neighbours and acquaintances keep coming to the park. No one seems able to talk about what happened. People are still struggling to hold back their tears.

The victims’ classmates and friends also come to pay their respects, bringing dozens of large stuffed toys.

With the help of rescue workers, survivors are returning to their damaged apartments to retrieve whatever personal belongings remain intact. They carry them out in plastic bags.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook – we thought it was an earthquake.” What happened in Ponichala

At around 9 a.m. on November 19, a powerful explosion rocked Lower Ponichala, at 16 Rustavi Highway. People were getting ready to leave for school and work. Some were already out on the street.

The explosion was caused by a build-up of natural gas on the fifth floor of a five-storey residential building. The blast wave destroyed part of the building, brought down the floor slabs and turned two stairwells into a pile of concrete within seconds.

People jumped from windows in an attempt to escape.

The blast wave threw a young man out of the fifth-floor apartment where the explosion occurred. He was the owner of the apartment. He is now in hospital with severe burns.

“There was a terrible noise and everything shook. At first, we thought it was an earthquake,” survivors who narrowly escaped the building recall.

Seven people were trapped under the rubble.

Neighbours say that in the first minutes after the explosion, they could hear several people screaming for help from beneath the debris. They were trapped under enormous concrete slabs, and it was impossible to reach them.

Of the seven people trapped, only one — three-year-old Taiya — was rescued alive. The other six were found dead. The rescue operation ended around midnight.

November 22 was declared a national day of mourning in Georgia.

Survivors: children remain in hospital, 31-year-old man in critical condition

Five people were taken to hospital following the explosion. Four were admitted in the morning, immediately after the incident. The fifth, a three-year-old girl, was brought to hospital later.

Three of the five injured people remain in hospital. They include two minors — 11-year-old Andria and three-year-old Taiya.

As of November 20, both children’s conditions were stable and satisfactory. According to doctors, a psychologist is also working with them. The three-year-old girl is expected to be discharged before the 11-year-old boy.

The third patient, a 31-year-old man, remains in critical condition.

The other two injured people sustained minor injuries and have already been discharged from hospital.

Three-year-old Taiya – eight hours under the rubble

Footage of the rescue of three-year-old Taiya.

Three-year-old Taiya was the only person rescued alive from the devastating collapse. She spent eight hours trapped beneath the rubble.

Firefighter and rescue worker Gaga Gigashvili describes the operation to save her:

“There were what amounted to three floors of debris on top of her – concrete slabs, blocks and wooden materials. When we reached her, only one leg was visible. When we touched it, she moved her leg slightly. Then we managed to reach her hand. She was holding a toy, as well as a hair clip, which she had kept clenched in her fist for all eight hours. When we opened her hand and took the clip, we held her hand and asked her to squeeze ours if she could hear us. When she squeezed our hand, we realised she was conscious and responding to us.”

The footage of the girl’s rescue is deeply moving. She is wearing a blue sweater covered in dirt and white tights. Her face is also smeared with soil and concrete dust. Rescuers carry her out of the rubble in their arms.

“Bless you, my dear,” one of the rescuers can be heard saying. It is Gaga Gigashvili. His face is contorted with emotion and exhaustion.

Gaga hands the little girl to another rescuer, who holds her close and runs towards the ambulance.

A huge crowd has gathered outside the building. People greet Taiya’s emergence with applause and tears. Her rescue gives those gathered hope that the other six people might also be found alive.

By this point, it is already known that Taiya’s mother and her seven-year-old sister are among those trapped beneath the rubble.

11-year-old Andria sustained serious injuries

Eleven-year-old Andria remains in hospital. He was admitted together with his mother, a 38-year-old woman.

According to Gia Bibilashvili, a doctor at Ingorokva Clinic, the boy was brought to hospital with more serious injuries than his mother.

Andria sustained focal brain injuries, several areas of bruising, a lung contusion, skull bone injuries, damage to his outer ear, and multiple injuries to his skin and soft tissues. He also required plastic surgery to repair the damage to his ear.

His condition is now relatively stable. Doctors plan to transfer him from intensive care to a regular hospital ward soon.

Andria’s mother suffered a concussion. She was discharged from hospital shortly afterwards.

31-year-old Ilia Isaev – the man whose apartment was the site of the explosion

The most seriously injured of all the survivors is 31-year-old Ilia Isaev. He was admitted to hospital with burns covering 87% of his body. According to doctors at the burns centre, his respiratory tract was also damaged.

Ilia was initially conscious. Before being taken to hospital, he managed to describe how the explosion happened.

He did not live in the apartment permanently. He had returned to Tbilisi from Batumi just one day before the incident. According to his account, he had tried to switch on the gas heater during the night but was unable to do so.

In the morning, he tried again. A powerful explosion followed. The blast wave threw Ilia out of the apartment.

He is now in hospital in extremely serious condition and is on a ventilator. Doctors continue to describe his condition as critical.

Who were the victims of the Ponichala explosion?

Six people died in the explosion: two young mothers and their young daughters, a 54-year-old woman and a 28-year-old man.

Nino Chelidze and her seven-year-old daughter Nutsa

Nino and seven-year-old Nutsa

Nino Chelidze was the mother of three-year-old Taiya. She was raising five children and worked at a clothing store.

At the time of the explosion, Nino was at home with two of her children — three-year-old Taiya and seven-year-old Nutsa. Her husband had taken their other three children to school shortly before the blast.

Nino’s body was found shortly after rescuers managed to pull Taiya out of the rubble. Nutsa was found much later, after hours of searching.

“Nino and her husband were raising five wonderful children. They were very happy – cheerful, good people. And suddenly, everything came crashing down on them. I have no words. When Taiya was found, I truly hoped the others would also be found alive, but unfortunately, that did not happen,” a family friend, still shaken by the tragedy, says.

Veriko Vanishvili and first-grader Ariana

Veriko Vanishvili and Ariana

Veriko Vanishvili lived on the second floor of the apartment building in Fonichala with her six-year-old daughter, Ariana Ristich. Both mother and daughter were at home that morning.

Veriko worked as the head of marketing at Grand Bellagio casino.

“Her smile, sincerity and dedication to her work will remain with our team forever,” the casino wrote in a Facebook post.

Ariana is remembered by staff at Tbilisi Kindergarten No. 58 and by her classmates.

“You will forever remain a tremendous pain, an irreplaceable loss, an emptiness and an unhealed wound for us, our bright, lively, warm and sweet girl,” kindergarten staff wrote.

“Ariana, you were and will always remain a little part of our school. It is difficult to come to terms with the fact that your childhood smile will no longer light up the classroom,” the administration of Helios private school wrote.

Lali Shishmanashvili — “the mother of the twins”

Lali Shishmanashvili

Lali Shishmanashvili, 54, lived on the first floor. Her twin daughters were also at home when the explosion occurred.

According to neighbours, when the building began to collapse, Lali managed to shout to her daughters to jump out of the window. This helped save their lives.

“The mother managed to shout: ‘Jump!’” one neighbour recalls. The neighbours called Lali “the mother of the twins”.

According to the neighbour, Lali was calling for help and pleading to be rescued. She said she was afraid of the dark.

“Her bedroom door was blocked by concrete slabs, and a slab had also collapsed inside the room. There was nothing anyone could do to help her. I kept telling her: ‘The rescuers are already here. They will get you out soon,’” the neighbour recalls.

Lali was a philologist and also tutored students at home.

“She was a mother who lived for her children. She did everything she could to give them a good life,” recalls a friend of Lali. She spent the entire night outside the building, hoping her friend would be rescued.

Jaba Sakevarashvili — a 28-year-old courier

Jaba Sakevarashvili

Another victim of the Fonichala explosion was 28-year-old Jaba Sakevarashvili. He worked as a courier for Georgian Post.

His colleagues remember him as a responsible, hardworking employee who was dedicated to his job.

According to someone close to Jaba, the young man had only recently moved into the apartment.

28 families left homeless, while 62 remain in the same building

The building where the explosion occurred is a multi-apartment residential block with six entrances. According to Tbilisi City Hall, 90 families lived in the building. All residents were evacuated immediately after the explosion.

Initially, Tbilisi City Hall said it was ready to accommodate all evacuated residents in hotels. On the same day, a municipal service inspected the building. Following the inspection, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said that only two entrances were affected – the one where the explosion occurred and the adjacent one. The remaining four entrances were considered safe for residents to return to.

The 28 families who lived in the two collapsed entrances – a total of 143 people – are currently staying in hotels.

According to the mayor, the municipality will offer these families a housing replacement programme. Until new apartments are built for them, they will be accommodated in rented housing, with the rent covered by the city.

Remains of family photo albums near the collapsed building. Photo: Georgian Public Broadcaster.



Late in the evening on November 20, the ruling Georgian Dream party released a condolence letter from Bidzina and Eka Ivanishvili. The letter stated that the Ivanishvilis would purchase apartments for the 28 families left homeless.

The announcement followed an earlier statement by the Tbilisi mayor. It is not yet known where the Ivanishvilis will purchase the apartments, when the families will receive their new homes, or how the assistance will be distributed. It has also not been clarified how this initiative will be coordinated with the housing replacement programme proposed by the municipality.

According to Tbilisi City Hall, residents of the building’s four surviving entrances will also be offered the opportunity to participate in the housing replacement programme. These are the 62 families who are still living in the building.

Could the tragedy have been prevented? The investigation must establish the facts

Giorgi Lefsveridze, deputy technical director of the gas distribution company Tbilisi Energy, said that the apartment where the explosion occurred was listed in the company’s database as disconnected from the gas supply.

According to him, no gas consumption had been recorded at the address from December 2025 until the day of the explosion, and the subscriber had received zero-balance bills every month. The company also said it had received no reports of a smell of gas from this address over the previous two years.

Lefsveridze said that scheduled inspections of the building had been carried out in January 2025 and January 2026. However, in January 2026, company employees were unable to enter the apartment where the explosion later occurred. With the help of neighbours, they contacted the owner, who said he was outside Tbilisi and would allow the inspection once he returned.

The investigation must establish what exactly caused the explosion and who bears responsibility for what happened.

A criminal investigation has been launched under Article 240 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which concerns violations of safety regulations during construction work.

In parallel, the Energy Ombudsman’s Office has also launched its own examination of the incident. On the day of the tragedy, the office requested relevant information from Tbilisi Energy.

One-off incident or systemic problem? Tbilisi has seen similar tragedies before

The explosion in Ponichala is not the first incident of its kind. Gas explosions have occurred periodically in Tbilisi for years. Some have claimed lives, while others have caused such extensive damage that dozens of families have been temporarily left homeless.

In 2019, the organisation FactCheck published statistics based on data from the gas distribution company KazTransGaz.

“According to KazTransGaz data, between 2016 and the first quarter of 2019, 101 people died and another 285 were poisoned in Tbilisi as a result of explosions caused by natural gas leaks and gas-related intoxication.”

Every such tragedy reignites the debate over responsibility: who is accountable for these incidents? Who should inspect the structural integrity of residential buildings and ensure that gas distribution networks are functioning properly and safely?

Now, new questions have emerged: what happens when gas company employees cannot gain access to an apartment? Does zero gas consumption mean that an apartment is safe? What mechanisms are in place when a property owner is away for an extended period and a technical inspection cannot be carried out?

Engineer and professor Temur Mikiashvili, speaking to Netgazeti, says that the absence of gas consumption does not guarantee safety. According to him, a meter may fail to register a small leak, while gas can gradually accumulate inside an unoccupied apartment.

He also points to the deterioration of plastic pipes and rubber hoses connected to gas appliances, which can cause leaks that go unnoticed.

According to the expert, gas detectors are an important preventive measure. These devices sound an alarm or send a notification when they detect a leak. Some models can also automatically shut off the gas supply.

Another problem in Tbilisi: ageing residential buildings

Faulty gas systems are not the only problem facing Tbilisi. The residential building in Fonichala collapsed so rapidly that the tragedy has once again raised questions about the lifespan and structural safety of residential buildings.

Tbilisi has numerous old and deteriorating apartment blocks. Many buildings constructed decades ago no longer meet modern safety standards.

Tbilisi City Hall has a dedicated programme and budget for addressing the problem of unsafe residential buildings.

According to data published by corruption researcher Irakli Abesadze, two main municipal budget programmes are being implemented in this area:

Reinforcement of unsafe buildings – between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced.



– between 2018 and 2025, during Kakha Kaladze’s tenure as mayor, a total of GEL 87,742,800 was spent on the programme. A total of 269 buildings were fully or partially reinforced. Replacement of unsafe buildings – launched in 2022, the programme received a total of GEL 19,081,700 in funding between 2022 and 2025.

Abesadze compares the funding allocated to these programmes with sums allegedly misappropriated through suspected corruption schemes.

According to him, the GEL 41,105,298 allegedly embezzled from the Tbilisi metro carriage modernisation project alone would have been enough to increase funding for the building reinforcement programme by 50%.

Abesadze estimates that this additional funding could have enabled the reinforcement of around 100 more buildings. The same amount, he says, would also have made it possible to triple the budget of the unsafe building replacement programme.

Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association: The state’s responsibility does not end with launching an investigation

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) also points to the scale and systemic nature of the problems. According to the organisation, the state’s obligations do not end with launching an investigation. It is necessary to establish whether inspection requirements under the gas distribution network regulations are being properly enforced and what measures are taken when access to a consumer’s apartment cannot be secured.

GYLA refers to the regulations approved by Resolution No. 80 of the Georgian National Energy and Water Supply Regulatory Commission (GNERC), dated December 31, 2021. Under these rules, the system operator is required to regularly inspect the gas supply system within a consumer’s property. If violations are identified, the consumer must be notified in writing and appropriate measures must be taken.

This issue is particularly important in older residential buildings, where infrastructure installed decades ago, modified pipes, outdated heating appliances and inadequate ventilation systems remain in use.
