World.title: NT Police seek public help in search for missing 7yo boy in Alice Springs
World.content:
Northern Territory Police are seeking help from the Alice Springs community to find a seven-year-old boy who has not been since yesterday morning.

In a statement this morning, an NT Police spokesperson said Kane Rubuntja went missing almost 24 hours ago after he went to play with other children on Nicker Crescent in Gillen.

"Kane’s mother had searched for him last night and reported him missing after she was unable to locate him," they said.

"Kane is described as having an olive complexion, with short brown hair and he was last seen wearing a green Larapinta Primary School shirt."

Anyone who has seen Kane or knows where he is is being urged to contact police immediately.

World.title: Remote public housing tenants moved after two-year maintenance wait
World.content:
Public housing tenants in Western Australia's far north are saddened it took questions from the ABC for the state government to move them into a safer home.

CONTENT WARNING: This story contains details of a death some readers may find distressing.

Grandparents Tanya Spider and Robin Dann say WA's Department of Housing and Works (DHW) ignored repeated maintenance requests for more than two years for their home in Derby, 2,000 kilometres north of Perth.

Tanya Spider says she made multiple calls to the DHW maintenance line but never received a response. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

The couple's longstanding concerns about the home's safety came to a head in January, when a family member died inside, and paramedics struggled to carry their body through a narrow doorway.

Mr Dann said once the body was brought out, in a compromised position, paramedics still faced hazards outside.

"The stretcher couldn't come out safely because of this drop here," he said, pointing to the fractured concrete slab beneath the house.

Mr Dann has rheumatic heart disease and required surgery last year to replace a damaged heart valve.

Robin Dann says the narrow doorway of the home could stop paramedics from reaching him in an emergency. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

With the severity of his disease, the couple was anxious his access to emergency treatment could be impeded due to the state of the house.

Maintenance requests go unanswered

The couple said the 10 gaping holes at the property were already present when they moved in, and worsened over time.

DHW did emergency repairs when the roof collapsed from water ingress during the last wet season, but further maintenance did not take place.

More than 10 gaping holes in the walls of the property caused rat infestations, according to the tenants. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Ms Spider said the remaining holes had resulted in rats eating their food and chewing wiring, routinely interrupting the electricity.

Despite multiple calls to the Department of Housing and Works maintenance line over two years, she never received a response.

Significant maintenance issues in the Derby house are only now being addressed. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

That changed when DHW organised a sudden inspection a day after the ABC sent questions to the department regarding the couple's struggles to get the home repaired.

"It just came out of the blue," Ms Spider said.

"After all those years of me and my partner asking for them."

After the inspection, the family was moved to temporary accommodation while renovations began.

Rats entered the home through gaping holes in the interior walls and chewed through the wiring, causing frequent power outages. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

The DHW also told the couple they had found a new permanent property for them, four days after the ABC query.

A department spokesperson confirmed the temporary relocation of the family as the property was renovated and issued an apology for the delay in maintenance repairs.

"DHW apologises to Ms Spider and Mr Dann for the inconvenience caused by the delays in responding to their maintenance requests," they said.

"Planned maintenance to refurbish the kitchen has commenced, and DHW is addressing the other maintenance issues that have been identified."

Tanya Spider and Robin Dann say having their maintenance requests go unheeded was demoralising. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Mr Dann said he was frustrated by the process.

"It's sad it had to come to this," he said.

"We pay top dollar in rent and not getting the support with the amount of money we pay is quite upsetting."

Grandchildren living at the fenceless property had open exposure to the remote town's busiest road. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Class action underway

A class action is being pursued against DHW on behalf of Aboriginal public housing tenants across Western Australia.

Slater and Gordon principal lawyer Gemma Leigh-Dodds, who is leading the case, said she understood the couple's frustrations.

"For years, Aboriginal tenants in remote WA have been living in public housing nobody would find acceptable," she said.

"We say the WA housing authority and state of Western Australia have failed for years to provide safe and habitable public housing while continuing to collect rent."

Gemma Leigh-Dodds says despite not seeing the couple's home, she understands their frustration. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

Ms Leigh-Dodds said the degree of maintenance issues in homes was a statewide reality.

"The class action I'm working on is looking at extensive repair issues across the whole state. These aren't cosmetic issues. We are talking about significant structural problems," she said.

"The state has not upheld its end of the bargain as the landlord. It can't just collect rent and do nothing."

The DHW spokesperson said it managed more than 45,000 public housing, Aboriginal housing and Government Regional Officer Housing tenancies and responded to more than 280,000 maintenance requests per year.

World.title: Sam Neill's final Australian role is as a mouthy magpie
World.content:
There is a strange cosmic gift in the fact Sam Neill's final role in an Australian film is as a mouthy magpie.

Writer and director Dario Russo's feature debut, The Fox, is a pitch-black comedy about the follies of romantic couples and a very wily animal (voiced by Academy Award-winner Olivia Colman).

Neill's magpie acts as a Shakespearean messenger: spreading secrets and stirring up emotions in exchange for some fresh barbecue chook.

"The first thing he tells me is, 'I don't know how to do a magpie, I reckon this is more of a crow,'" Russo tells ABC Arts.

"He said he knew some local crow that was very characteristic and that he based the performance on that crow. I actually secretly think it's a Bryan Brown impersonation.

"We did a Zoom call with Sam, and he scratched all the performances in one session while he was in a hotel room in Perth."

Warning: Videos in this article contain coarse language.

Loading Instagram content

When talking bush animals aren't on screen, The Fox revolves around four humans: Nick (Jai Courtney), his reluctant fiancee Kori (Emily Browning), her best friend Diana (Claudia Doumit) and her husband/Kori's boss Derrick (Damon Herriman).

Pampered housewife Diana is stoked to hear Kori and Nick are tying the knot; Derrick less so, mostly because he's been having a secret affair with Kori.

A talking fox (Colman) trades Nick information on Kori's adultery in exchange for release from a trap. Disturbed by his new-found knowledge, Nick returns to the fox, who proposes a foolproof plan: drop Kori in a deep, dark hole in the bush and the perfect partner will emerge. It's the ever-watching magpie who warns Nick that the fox is trying to get one over him. But who would take the advice of a bird …?

Nick (Jai Courtney) is visited by a troublemaking animal in The Fox. (Supplied: Madman)

"Everybody in the world of The Fox is in a state of self-denial of one kind. They're all dealing with a major life problem that they're not solving through productive or healthy means," Russo says.

"I find a lot of humour in constructing characters that are believable in that respect, then seeing them doing the wrong thing over and over again.

"That inherently becomes kind of a comedy of errors."

Make 'em laugh

Despite the dark subject matter, The Fox is bursting with Australian humour that wouldn't be out of place in classic, albeit adults-only, Round The Twist episodes.

"I think it was probably about 10 pages in, when I'd already laughed out loud to myself multiple times, that I knew I had to be involved," Browning says.

"I was a little scared, mostly because I needed to assess if Dario is as good a director as he is a writer, because if we didn't pull it off it could be a massive failure, but after we talked I knew it was going to be great. The film is very much the script."

Diana (Claudia Doumit) gets tangled up in Nick's plan to turn Kori into the perfect partner. (Supplied: Madman)

Russo, already a cult favourite from his comedy series Danger 5 and short film Italian Spiderman, had been percolating on The Fox for years, but only went after his ultra-ocker fairytale after spending years in the US pitching pilot episodes to networks.

Italian Spiderman shorts net more funding A full-length Italian Spiderman feature may become a reality after a $10k funding boost.

"I got stuck in the kind of classic development-hell situation where I was writing pilot scripts that just went nowhere," he says.

"I knew I wanted to make a kind of contemporary folk tale about talking animals. So, I wrote a whole bunch of short stories. One was about a frog, one about a goose, one about badgers, and one about foxes.

"I drafted the final version millions of times and then called it my first draft and took it out to producers."

Russo's outlandishly debaucherous script caught the eye of Causeway Films, the Australian production house which helped take local movies like The Babadook, Talk To Me and Leviticus international. While Causeway might be famous for horror, The Fox brings a whole new genre to the company's glittering slate.

"Nick is obviously deeply in love with Corey, probably for the wrong reasons. Corey has fallen out of love with Nick and is too terrified by the prospect of what it means to break up," Dario Russo says of his central couple. (Supplied: Madman)

"We did a Q&A where somebody asked me whether or not art-house films were booming in the Australian production scene. And I was kind of like, 'Do you think [The Fox] is an art-house movie?" Dario says.

"I see it foremost as a dark comedy with hopefully some nuances and something to say about life in one way or another."

Take my wife, please

The greatest trick Russo pulls with his characters in The Fox is their precarious morality.

No-one deserves to be cheated on, but Nick's true rural nepo baby character is revealed further after he throws his soon-to-be-betrothed down a dank pit. For Russo, it was a commentary on the hereditary nature of bad behaviour.

"He's never really had to do anything besides just help his dad out around their massive estate," he says.

"I feel like that speaks to some kind of a specific sort of privileged obliviousness."

Nick and his Dad (Frankie J. Holden) are more alike than they realise. (Supplied: Madman)

As much as Nick's innate blindness to his own relationship was vital to the progression of the story, so too was creating the perfect foxy foil, not with CGI but practical effects.

Sam Neill's advice when the world seems dark The world has been remembering Sam Neill's incredible film and television career in the wake of the actor's death, but his off-screen antics left a robust impact.

"In the past, I've done very intentional, corny sort of fishing wire, visible styles of puppetry and all the rest," Russo says.

"It was a dream come true to be able to use sophisticated animatronics that were made by Odd Studio in Sydney."

Russo points to Jim Henson's 1988 series The Storyteller as a basis for his vision.

"It's a masterpiece. That was actually one of the root inspirations for why I wanted to make the movie because I want to do a contemporary, grown-up version of it basically," Russo says.

"The fox took one person operating behind the head with a rod and then two people on radio control units doing all of the electronically operated ears, eyes, nose and mouth."

Dario Russo's aim for the look of his creatures was "nature taxidermy brought to life". (Supplied: Madman)

Pulling a triple threat also as the film's editor, Russo gave his creatures their own personalities.

"I didn't want to do like a Disney-style lip sync; it's sort of more rudimentary than that," he says.

"In the edit, I had room to mix and match. Sometimes it's one line that wasn't actually that line that I'm using because the emotion from the creature was better for that moment.

"I hope it's a believable fantasy universe that people find immersive and can actually fall into."

The Fox is in Australian cinemas from November 26.

World.title: Molly Meldrum, the 'most important person in pop', dies aged 83
World.content:
Molly Meldrum, the former host of Countdown, has died aged 83.

For decades, if Meldrum urged viewers to "do yourself a favour" and buy your record, you knew you had made it in the music business.

Meldrum was a highly influential figure in Australia's music industry as a critic, producer, interviewer and television presenter.

Molly Meldrum updates: Read our blog for the latest reaction to the death of Australia's pop music and TV legend.

As the host of the ABC's music show Countdown, he brought the world's biggest pop stars into people's homes, and recorded some of the most iconic — if sometimes chaotic — interviews ever broadcast on Australian television.

Instantly recognisable in his trademark cowboy hat, Meldrum was described by some as "the most important person in pop", whose influence on the chart success of performers — particularly Australians — could not be overstated.

The ABC spoke to a close friend of Molly Meldrum's who said he had been in a Melbourne hospital for a number of days before dying.

From country beginnings to the centre of the pop world

Molly Meldrum appeared in the Mann Collection film reels shot at his school in Quambatook in 1954. (ABC Archive: Mann Collection)

Ian "Molly" Meldrum was born in Orbost, in regional Victoria, on January 29, 1943.

He spent the first 10 years of his life in the small country town before moving to the even smaller country town of Quambatook to live with his grandmother.

"My grandmother was one of my biggest influences on my life and I lived a fair bit with her and I absolutely adored my grandmother," he said.

" She taught me one of the great things that I've tried to live my life by and she told me that no-one's above you and no-one's below you and you should treat all people as equal. "

Meldrum's interest in music surged when The Beatles toured Australia in 1964, taking the country by storm.

Meldrum and his friend Ronnie Burns — who would later have a successful recording career of his own — were kicked out of The Beatles' concert in Melbourne for being "too enthusiastic".

Just a few years later, Meldrum, who had been writing for Go-Set magazine and working on local TV shows, relocated to London to document Australian band The Groop's attempts to crack the UK music scene.

It was there that he got the scoop that took his career to a new level, securing an interview with John Lennon during which the Beatle dropped the bombshell that the band was splitting up.

"The story later went worldwide on radio, in Rolling Stone, everywhere," Meldrum said in 1981.

Molly Meldrum worked as a reporter for Go-Set magazine in the 1960s and 1970s. (Supplied)

Meldrum had also been learning the ropes as a music producer, assisting with the recording of music by artists such as The Masters Apprentices.

In 1969 he produced Russell Morris's recording of The Real Thing, transforming the song, which was written by Johnny Young as an acoustic ballad, into a six-minute, effects-laden epic.

The song was a number one hit domestically and is widely regarded as a milestone in music production in Australia.

Countdown took Molly into every home in Australia

Meldrum had experience as a television music reporter, but taking a job with brand new ABC music show Countdown was to be the single most important move in his career.

The show's executive producer, Michael Shrimpton, told the ABC in 2003 that he and a fellow producer were meeting in a Melbourne pub to discuss who to hire as the show's talent scout when Meldrum drove up onto the footpath outside.

He was initially hired as the show's talent coordinator, but progressed to an on-air role presenting a music news and review segment.

Countdown was an instant hit, capitalising on the lack of other prime-time music TV shows while being one of the first Australian programs recorded in colour.

Molly Meldrum interviewed Rod Stewart for Countdown in 1978. (ABC Archives)

The arrival of Countdown coincided with the emergence of music videos, making the show the ideal place for local and international acts to promote their new music — usually on Meldrum's "Humdrum" segment.

Meldrum's influence was summed up by his promotion of Abba's Mamma Mia, which was not even considered as a single by the group until Meldrum plugged it repeatedly on Countdown.

The song was number one in the Australian charts for 10 weeks and went on to become a worldwide hit.

Rather than telling viewers to go out and buy an album — which was against the ABC's policy around direct endorsements — Meldrum would tell viewers to "do yourself a favour". It became his iconic catchphrase.

Even Molly's 'stuff-ups' were magic television

Molly Meldrum (right) speaks with Elton John on the set of Countdown. (ABC Archives)

It was said that electricity consumption would spike when Countdown was on air becasue practically every teenager in Australia switched on their TV sets.

Holding the attention of the nation's youth made Countdown, and Meldrum, extremely influential on what music made an impression on the charts.

That also gave Meldrum access to some of the biggest stars in pop music and he would have been the first to admit that some of the resulting interviews were not exactly from the live TV textbook.

But what Meldrum lacked in polish, he more than made up for in knowledge and pop music credibility.

Molly Meldrum's interview with then Prince Charles in 1977 was fondly remembered by the royal nearly 40 years later. (Supplied: National Archives)

One of his most iconic interviews was not with a pop star at all, but with a future king.

Meldrum interviewed then Prince Charles on Countdown in 1977 and — in his own words — "stuffed up" badly, fumbling his way through an introduction while the bemused royal watched on.

Meldrum dropped a few "f-bombs" and even committed a royal faux pas by touching the prince, but in the process created a priceless moment in Australian television history — one that Charles himself remembers well.

"There is an old show business saying which warns never to work with animals or children, but nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum," now King Charles recounted in 2014.

Life after Countdown

Even after Countdown ended in 1987, Meldrum was still in demand as a TV music authority, hosting a regular segment on Hey Hey It's Saturday.

He also started his own record label, Melodian Records, producing albums for Indecent Obsession, Jo Beth Taylor and Peter Andre.

Molly Meldrum suffered a serious fall in 2011 that left him in a coma. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Meldrum received an ARIA for special achievement in 1993 and was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014.

He was inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame in 2012, with tributes from pop stars such as Elton John and Delta Goodrem.

"I know I speak for many artists and music lovers around world when I say,'Thank you. There's no-one like you," Elton John said.

Meldrum was described as "the single most important person in the Australian pop industry for 40 years" in the book 1001 Australians You Should Know.

"He's a very giving and sharing person and he's done so much for the music business," Australian music promoter Michael Chugg said.

"He's loved by everybody. He's just a wonderful person and a true Aussie icon."

More than just a hat and a catchphrase

A serious fall at his Melbourne home in 2011 left Meldrum critically injured with a fractured skull and in a coma.

The passionate St Kilda Football Club fan recovered, but later said the fall made him realise he was not bulletproof.

His colourful life was made into a successful Channel Seven TV mini-series in 2016.

Actor Samuel Johnson won the Silver Logie in 2017 for his portrayal of Molly Meldrum.

In an interview with Andrew Denton on Enough Rope, Meldrum explained that his passion for music was just one aspect of his life.

"Molly Meldrum, I guess, is the image or the person or whatever that has been on Countdown, has been on Hey Hey [It's Saturday]," he said.

"Whereas there is the other side of Molly Meldrum which is the Ian Meldrum, [and] I take things very, very seriously.

" I have an intense interest in politics. I'm sort of apolitical in one sense, but I follow it religiously. I'm addicted all the time to say, BBC World News or CNN. And there is those two sides. "

Several public outings in 2023, including one in which he bared his naked backside to the crowd at an Elton John concert, may have threatened to tarnish his image in later life, but Meldrum took it in his stride.

"Elton might have been singing The B*tch is Back but it was more a case of The Idiot is Back," he told The Herald Sun.

He may have been accident prone and unpolished at times, but nobody with Meldrum's gift for picking a hit song could ever be called an idiot.

World.title: Democrats clinch their largest House majority since 1992
World.content:
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached on Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated his opponent in a House race in North Carolina. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and a Republican president in the White House.

Battle for Democrat Party's soul The Democratic Party is no longer just a broad church, but a huge multi-faith centre.

The Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Mr Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

Their majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257).

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Jason Crow, a Democratic member of the House of Representatives from Colorado.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their health care, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorised from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

" If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome. "

Mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with the president.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate in January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver.

The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in more than a decade.

The Democrats are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

They have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power.

That includes plans to probe how Mr Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Mr Trump for a third time.

House Democrats voted to nominate Hakeem Jeffries as their leader. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive Democratic leader Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change".

Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York, said the House Democrats should focus 75 per cent of their time on affordability issues and 25 per cent on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Mr Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality".

A new generation of leaders

After the current House Speaker, Republican Mike Johnson, struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority, the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides them with much more room to manoeuvre.

Mr Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job in January, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage.

The 'king' has been humbled but his empire survives US voters have rejected Donald Trump's excesses, divisiveness and alleged corruption. Yet the political realignment many Democrats crave may be a long way off.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Democrat Troy Carter, who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades.

They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election.

Republican Jim Jordan, who was elected by his colleagues to be the minority leader in the House of Representatives, vowed the Republicans would fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Mr Jordan said.

AP

World.title: Woman's brush with death sparks new career farming mushrooms
World.content:
A near-death experience convinced Emma Court to ditch her four-hour commute to a corporate job in Brisbane and start farming fancy, nutrient-packed fungi.

"My neurosurgeon said to me, if I had left it another couple of months, I would not be standing here," Ms Court said.

Nine years ago, the Sunshine Coast resident suffered through weeks of chronic fatigue, excruciating headaches, blurred vision, weak limbs and night sweats.

Refusing to accept repeatedly being told that she was "a tired, anxious, overworked woman" who needed antidepressants, Ms Court booked an eye test that triggered life-saving emergency brain surgery.

Emma Court is lucky to be alive. (Supplied: Emma Court)

An inflammatory mass had engulfed the pituitary gland at the base of her brain, crushed the optic nerves to her right eye, and played havoc with her hormones.

Undergoing neurosurgery, immunotherapy and years of maintenance treatment, Ms Court said modern medicine saved her life.

Emma Court started with the Lion's mane variety. (Supplied: Rocky Creek Mushrooms)

Looking to improve her health with nutrient-packed fresh food, the mother of two began growing gourmet mushrooms.

Turning her hobby into a farm that could reliably supply restaurants while keeping a low environmental footprint was a challenge.

Ms Court's husband, Wayne, who once worked as an avionics engineer and a race team engineer for McLaren F1 motorsport, helped bring her designs to life for her Rocky Creek Mushrooms business.

Together they built grow rooms, automated lighting and humidity controls, and a sterile laboratory to produce mushroom cultures without chemical pesticides or synthetic sprays.

Wayne Court's engineering skills have been invaluable to the farm. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Last year alone, the mother of two attended more than 90 weekend markets, made 624 restaurant deliveries, took on a wholesaler, and upskilled to obtain a food license and wholesale and commercial food supervisor qualifications.

The 47-year-old took part in CSIRO's Innovate to Grow program and spent hundreds of hours mastering how to meet the specific needs of more than 30 mushroom varieties.

She drew on her research and organisational skills as a product, systems and service designer; farm management studies at school; and years spent baling hay and mucking out stables as a teenager to help pay for her own horses' upkeep in the English countryside.

Chefs enjoy experimenting with the mushroom varieties. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The farm now produces around 100 kilograms of gourmet mushrooms a week to supply wholesale, retail, restaurants and farmers' markets.

To minimise waste and maximise income, Ms Court makes seasonings, teas, extracts, preserves and mushroom grow bags.

Her marinated forest mushrooms with smoked garlic and charred pimiento won a silver medal at the 2026 Melbourne Royal Australian Food Awards.

Emma Court secured food safety licenses to value add to their farm's mushrooms. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Jacki Hinchey from the regional Food and Agribusiness Network said that by focusing on value-adding, Ms Court has defied the national downward trend for the wider mushroom industry.

The most recent figures from the Australian Horticulture Statistics Handbook for 2024/25 show mushroom production decreased by 12 per cent to 52,784 tonnes, valued at $338.3 million.

Ms Hinchey said it was "notoriously difficult" for mushroom farmers to maintain a profit.

"You have to manage mushrooms really carefully, and it's very hard to sell everything because they're so perishable."

Emma Court is proud of her farm. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

Award-winner

Rocky Creek Mushrooms is a finalist in the 2026 Sunshine Coast Business Awards in both the Food and Agribusiness and Sustainability categories, to be held on November 28.

The family has invested in solar and battery storage, harvests rainwater, and grows mushrooms on Australian hardwood sawdust, an agricultural by-product.

Compost gets donated back to the community, and the mushroom grow bags are recycled to create new plastics.

Emma Court has brainstormed ways to use spent mushroom substrate. (ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols)

The fungi farmer has also used mycelium, the root-like filaments of fungi, to grow containers, a body board and plant pots from spent substrate, which is then air-dried as an environmentally friendly alternative to plastics and foams.

"I guess my biggest problem is that I have so many ideas and things I want to work on that the whirlwind can at times turn into a full-blown tornado," Ms Court said.

"It's quite a busy life; I'm feeling busy but fulfilled. I love doing this."

NSW Premier Chris Minns has abandoned his Monday morning press conference after a Greens candidate crashed the event to yell at the premier about the war in Gaza and his captains picks candidate announcements.

Shane Bazzi, who is number four on the Greens upper house ticket, stood outside the East Hills Medical Centre where the premier and several senior ministers were scheduled to speak about ADHD reforms.

Bazzi was not let into the press conference however his yelling drowned out Minns as he attempted to speak.

“Shame on you Chris Minns, shame,” Bazzi shouted.

Minns said he would reconvene the press conference at parliament instead. He got into a waiting car as Bazzi continued to shout “shame on you”.

World.title: Chris Bowen takes ‘share of responsibility’ for UN climate talks failure
World.content:
Updated EnvironmentClimate changeParis Agreement Chris Bowen takes ‘share of responsibility’ for UN climate talks failure Nick O'Malley Updated November 23, 2026 — 9:13am ,first published 12:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Global climate talks led by Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen have failed to secure an agreement in Turkey after a stand-off between oil producing nations led by Saudi Arabia and nations seeking more ambitious action on climate change, including Europe. Bowen described the outcome as “very disappointing” and said disagreements over fuels and climate finance were the dealbreakers. Telling reporters he had not slept since Friday as he worked with negotiators to try and salvage the talks, Bowen said he took his “share of responsibility. Ultimately, you know, people can judge what could have been done or couldn’t have been done. Ultimately, it’s a party-driven process”. Chris Bowen president over COP31 negotiations. AP After more than two weeks of negotiations that dragged two days into overtime – making it the longest COP on record – Turkey’s conference president Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.



“There is nothing to do, we did all that we could,” he said. “There will be no new text from now on.” On Sunday (Turkey time), the Saudi-led bloc backed by Russia rejected a final agreement – known as a cover decision – that repeated calls for a transition away from fossil fuels. The European Union said it could not support an agreement that would take backwards steps by refusing to address the need to do so. Further objections were raised by other nations over the inclusion of a call to increase the use of controversial climate capture and storage (CCS) technology, also championed by the Saudi-led bloc, and by the failure of developed nations to pledge more financial support for poorer nations hardest hit by climate impacts. Cover decisions at UN climate talks can only be adopted by consensus of all parties. Bowen attributed the collapse of the talks to the “red lines” on fossil fuels where nations would not compromise.



“Despite many, many attempts, and on-reflection, those red lines, on behalf of different parties, were just not able to be met,” Bowen told reporters at the conference. “An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that it must be mentioned, other parties insisted that if it was mentioned they would not be involved.“ The failure of negotiators to arrive at an agreement comes as a huge blow to the COP process, at which almost 200 parties to the Paris Agreement sought to advance climate action, and to Bowen, who secured the role of president of negotiations when the bid he led for Australia to host the talks failed last year at talks in Brazil. While Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the COP31 outcome as evidence of difficult geopolitical times and Environment Minister Murray Watt said Australia had no veto powers, the Coalition is already calling for Bowen to resign over the failure. “It’s pretty extraordinary, isn’t it? We’ve spent $150 million to get Chris Bowen to COP, to host COP. Then we found out it was actually a co-host deal. Now we’re walking away without a deal at all,” Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume told News24. Bowen had sought to sidestep the stand-off over references to fossil fuel in the cover decision by including language recognising the agreement made at previous talks in Dubai, where the world pledged to “transition away from fossil fuels”.



He commended delegations for pulling all-nighters to try to reach a deal, but said “the situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory. “An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels, where some parties insisted that must be mentioned, other parties insisted that if it was mentioned they would veto.” While many representatives paid tribute to Bowen’s work, others were more critical. Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and a member of The Elders, an independent group of global leaders founded by Nelson Mandela in 2007 to work on peace, human rights, and global challenges like climate change was scathing.



“Recognition of the dangers of overshoot should have shaken leaders into action, instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia,” she said in a statement. “This was compounded by disturbing politicised attacks on the science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action.” Climate talks collapsed on Sunday. Getty Images Speaking on behalf of the EU, Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, energy and the Environment, rejected the draft agreement on the floor of the final plenary session. “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change, and we will not accept negotiating backward in time, and we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel. “I do want to, however, Mr President, commend both you and the president of negotiations [Chris Bowen] for your unstinting efforts. However, the draft put before us does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face.



“It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuel either. And it is for that reason and those reasons that the European Union strongly objects to this text.” Speaking after the EU, a member of the Panamanian delegation also rejected the deal, saying: “We need to be clear: our message is not a criticism of the presidencies. “Our disagreement is with a much deeper problem... One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it wages too much upon technologies such as CCS capture storage of carbon instead of calling for deep changes and three because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback.” Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen (right) with Turkey’s Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum in Fiji at pre-COP. Getty A representative of the Marshall Islands said her nation had been failed by all sides at the COP. “We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot, a response to enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.



“Over the past two weeks, we have been offered next to nothing. Even as we have said again and again, our needs are so great, the costs are so high, the finance gap keeps growing. We cannot do this on our own. We cannot survive on empty promises. People are dying, seas are rising, ecosystems are collapsing.” As it became clear that the negotiations had failed Bowen remained silent while Turkish officials oversaw the meeting, with many speakers noting that the talks were being held just weeks after the UN Environment Program had acknowledged that the world was set to miss the Paris target of 1.5 degrees warming and head into what is now being described as climate “overshoot”. A Russian delegate told the session that Russia stood by the goals of the Paris Agreement, but that the conference made rapid phaseout of fossil fuels that he said should not have been included central to the talks. He said that the UN’s own scenarios charting a course to limiting warming to 1.5 degrees acknowledged the world would continue to use approximately 40 per cent of the oil and 50 per cent of the gas of the levels of 2019. A Saudi representative said the 22 member states of the Arab League represented less than 2 per cent of historical greenhouse gas emissions, “whereas other groups are responsible for 55 per cent of those emissions.”



In line with this he said the Arab League had called for a tripling of climate finance from wealthy to poorer nations. “This was removed from the text due to lack of flexibility from some parties on mentioning any quantitative aspects related to climate finance.” Related Article Electricity The biggest energy crisis in history brings on the age of electricity Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, took aim at the EU, which he said had failed to offer new financial support to developing nations. “Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel road maps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition. Without money and credible action at home, those demands are hollow. The EU cannot help sabotage the negotiations, then pose as the climate conscience of the world.” China noted its reservation about some of the content of the agreement, but said to demonstrate unity of collective efforts it had decided to accept the cover decision and called on “all parties to show necessary compromise spirit to push forward our process.”



As president of negotiations Bowen had declared at the pre-COP meeting in Fiji that the presidency would pursue the cover decision that the COP has just rejected, in order to drive more momentum for action than might have been achieved with a series of agreements over individual agenda items. Australia had hoped that in doing so it would champion the cause of Pacific island nations which view climate change as an existential threat, thereby deepening ties across the region as China’s influence grew. Fiji’s Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya said that although the cover decision text was not perfect she regretted it was not adopted. “Honorable Chris Bowen, you have tried your utmost best, and we have seen it,” she said. “Your commitment, patience, and determination throughout these negotiations have not gone unnoticed. “This work is hard. Sleepless nights, hours and days of constant negotiations, managing over 190 parties. This is not easy, but we do it. We do it for our people. The failure to reach consensus on the cover decision is not yours to carry. It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Music was everything to Molly Meldrum
World.content:
CultureMusicObituaries Music was everything to Molly Meldrum Glenn A. Baker November 23, 2026 — 9:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Music was not something Ian Meldrum, who has died aged 83, ever just listened to. Left on his own as a child, raised primarily by his grandmother, he would crank up the soundtracks of West Side Story, Oklahoma! or even a piece of opera on the family gramophone and madly flail away with a makeshift baton. Molly Meldrum at the announcement of The Australian Music Vault , a new exhibition space dedicated to sharing the story of Australian contemporary music at The Arts Centre. Eddie Jim At the first Melbourne concert by the Beatles in June 1964, he and friend Ronnie Burns, a rising pop star, were tossed out of Festival Hall by over-zealous security men just before the final song, for screaming too loudly, and spent the duration of Long Tall Sally pounding on the back door in a tearful state of near-collapse. Shortly after, Kiwi chart sensation Dinah Lee, taken home for dinner one night by Burns and introduced to housemate Meldrum, was astonished to encounter the 17-year-old hiding, quivering and barely coherent under a bed. Over all the years of public life, Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum remained in the thrall of music and its practitioners. Wearing a great many hats – cub reporter, television mimer, artist manager and publicist, record producer, television presenter and talent co-ordinator, disc jockey, magazine columnist, product endorser, government adviser, record label operator, television producer and confidant to the stars – the former Protestant altar boy became a highly visible part of Australian life, celebrated for his gushing effervescence and his ceaseless championing of Australian music.



Ian Alexander Meldrum was born on January 29, 1943, in Orbost in eastern Victoria, the son of Robert Meldrum and his wife Isobel (nee Geer). It was while juggling law studies at the University of Melbourne with a job as an ace pop reporter on plucky Go-Set magazine that Meldrum covered the walk-out of the miming stars of the Kommotion pop television show and found himself recruited as a replacement. The name Molly was bestowed by veteran DJ and fellow Go-Set contributor Stan Rofe. It stuck, as a household name that rolled easily off the tongue. In time, it would come tumbling from the lips of Madonna, David Bowie, Elton John, Jon Bon Jovi, Kylie Minogue, Rod Stewart and Michael Jackson, among many others of note. After travelling to London with popular chart entity The Groop and landing a short stint working within the Beatles’ Apple organisation at the end of the 1960s (when he gained the scoop of John Lennon declaring he’d left the Beatles), Meldrum was ready to stop promoting other people’s music and start creating his own. Loading



He produced a hit for the Melbourne group Somebody’s Image and persuaded vocalist Russell Morris to pursue solo fame with a song by Johnny Young. Before EMI Records had realised what was happening, Meldrum had spent $10,000 of their money (sufficient budget for two to three albums at that time) recording a wizard’s brew of swirling electronic noise and mesmerising chants – a spectacular six-minute epic that the distraught record company presumed to be a B-side. Meldrum was sacked from the project but refused to let go and when a corporate decision was made to release the single in Victoria to cut costs, he hit the road to Sydney with Morris to persuade influential Harbourside disc jockeys to air the song. In April 1969, The Real Thing was No.1 around Australia, and by the end of the year, the pair had been awarded a rare gold disc. Molly Meldrum with Tina Turner in 1984. Over his career, Meldrum produced recordings when the mood took him, his most successful endeavours being Smiley by Ronnie Burns, Day By Day by Colleen Hewitt, Don’t Fall In Love by the Ferretts (which he produccd under the alias Willie Everfinish) and I Like It Both Ways by Supernaut. Key to his studio approach, indeed to his career in general, was instinct. “It’s the only talent I may have in my life,” he once said. “As a record producer, I always knew what people wanted to listen to, even though I was often faking it technically.”



Related Article 'Supposedly I'm an icon … I don't like that': Molly Meldrum Meanwhile, the law dimmed as a pursuit as the young Meldrum became immersed in pop and the energy of the times. The front cover of the September 16, 1972, issue of Go-Set carried the headline “Bob Hawke Talks to Ian Meldrum – A Time To Change”. The meeting with the ACTU leader in a pub and at the Trades Hall, was initiated by Meldrum against the wishes of the editor, who thought politics incompatible with pop. In London, Meldrum had been arrested at the “Battle of Grosvenor Square” in March 1968, when police and protesters fought outside the American embassy in London. “I hated the Vietnam War,” he would later say. The making of Meldrum as a national figure was the arrival in 1975 of the ABC television program Countdown, on which he’d landed the job of talent co-ordinator. He was not the compere, a role which fell to guest hosts, but he did seem to be always there, verbally stumbling over himself, ever exhorting “do yourself a favour” as he thrust this and that record or group forward for attention. Elton John and Molly swap hats in Sydney in 1990. “I know nobody believes this but I’ve never been comfortable about being on television,” he would insist. “In the early days of Countdown , I was told I had to do a rock report and I said no. In the end, it came down to paying the rent. The ABC employed me and they wanted a rock report. That’s how Humdrum happened.”



Countdown held court until July 19, 1987, followed by the 1986 Countdown Awards, at the end of which Meldrum appeared wearing a Stetson hat, which he doffed to reveal a shaved head, in imitation of Peter Garrett of Midnight Oil, who had steadfastly refused to appear on the show. Like the nickname, the hat stuck. Molly Meldrum and Kylie Minogue. Publicity Many things about Molly Meldrum stuck, including his fanatical devotion to the St Kilda AFL team and, later, the Melbourne Storm in the NRL. A star all over again on television’s weekly Hey Hey It’s Saturday program, he had the ear of politicians and the pulse of the country. He would be crowned King of Moomba on one hand and renowned for his fascination with the oft-visited Egypt and his vast collection of artefacts of the ancient realm. Molly proudly displaying his passion for the St Kilda AFL club and the Melbourne Storm NRL team when both sides made the finals in 2008. Joe Armao. Far brighter and more aware of global affairs that was realised, Meldrum managed the not-inconsiderable feat of winning half a million dollars for charity on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire? In 1986, the year after he hosted the Australian leg of the global telecast Live Aid, he was made a member of the Order of Australia for “service to the fostering of international relief and to youth”.



In 1993, the Australian Recording Industry Association bestowed a Special Achievement ARIA award upon him. Loading Though there was often much that merited it, Australia was pleased to never take Meldrum too seriously, accounting for why the country felt so comfortable with him for so very long. He knew he was charmed. Booked onto the Air India flight that crashed into the Irish Sea in 1985, he was one of the few no-shows. “Rod Stewart and his old manager Billy Gaff after a lot of argument got me to stay over for a dinner party,” he would say afterwards. “By the grace of God, I’m still here. That’s the way you’ve got to look at life. As long as I’m enjoying this, we’ll all have a giggle.” Ian Molly Meldrum. Meldrum had a more immediate near-death experience in 2011 when he was critically injured in a fall from a ladder at home in Richmond, in inner Melbourne. He was taken to hospital in a coma with a fractured skull, broken ribs, cracked vertebrae and a punctured lung, undergoing surgery for a brain injury.



Spurred by well-wishes from the likes of Madonna, Boy George, Russell Crowe, Ricky Martin and Kylie Minogue, Meldrum recovered after a lengthy rehabilitation. Five years later, he was seriously injured when he fell outside his hotel while on holidays in Bangkok. The two incidents took a toll on his wellbeing. Samuel Johnson as Meldrum in the TV mini-series Molly. Meldrum’s dramatic, colourful life became the subject of an acclaimed TV mini-series, Molly, in which he was played by Samuel Johnson, who won a Logie for his portrayal. Meldrum famously interrupted Johnson’s acceptance speech at the 2017 awards, later apologising for his rambling performance by saying he “got a bit caught up in the moment”. It was no surprise. Being caught up in the moment had been the essence of his enduring appeal.

A young mother fatally stabbed in front of her children at a home south of Brisbane over the weekend has been identified as 28-year-old Thai national Christine Moe. Her husband, 34-year-old So Reh, is accused of murdering her and will face Beenleigh Magistrates Court on Monday. Thai national Christine Moe died at her home in Slacks Creek on Saturday night after suffering a single stab wound to the chest. Facebook Police were called to the couple’s home at Slacks Creek in Logan about 11.30pm on Saturday. Moe was found in a critical condition after suffering a single stab wound to the chest.



First responders performed CPR and tactical first aid, but the young mother could not be saved and died at the scene. Nine News reported Moe’s husband, Reh, allegedly called a relative and told them he’d stabbed his wife. That family member then contacted emergency services. Reh was waiting at the home for police when they arrived. Acting chief superintendent Chris O’Hearn said young children, believed to be the couple’s kids, were present when Moe was stabbed. Loading



“[It was a] very confronting scene for anyone to witness, let alone children,” he said. “We can’t begin to imagine what those children must be feeling.” He did not confirm whether Reh was previously known to police for domestic violence offences, or whether a murder weapon had been located. “The focus of our ongoing investigations in the coming days [will be] to get a picture of if there has been previous domestic violence between these individuals,” O’Hearn said. “That’ll be a critical element of our investigation as we move forward.”

World.title: Molly Meldrum dies aged 83
World.content:
Breaking CultureMusicVale Molly Meldrum dies aged 83 Chris Hook, Nell Geraets and Cameron Houston November 23, 2026 — 8:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian music legend Ian “Molly” Meldrum has died aged 83. The former Countdown host and Hey, Hey It’s Saturday stalwart has long been in ill health and died at 5.30am Monday at the Epworth Hospital in Richmond, in inner Melbourne, this masthead has confirmed. Molly Meldrum has died aged 83. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of Australian music legend, journalist, producer and cultural icon Ian Alexander “Molly” Meldrum AM … He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him,” his family said via a statement shared with this masthead. “Affectionately dubbed ‘The Guru’, Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music. He shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them … He lived and breathed music, believing in its power to unite, to inspire and to lift up young musicians.”



Meldrum, born in Orbost in eastern Victoria in 1943, became one of Australia’s most notable champions of music. Throughout his career, he worked as a music journalist, critic, record producer, television presenter, and musical entrepreneur. Loading Meldrum’s love of music began at an early age, when he would listen to musical soundtracks and opera pieces on his family’s gramophone. This passion continued to blossom when he picked up a job as a pop reporter at Go-Set magazine while studying law at the University of Melbourne. It was there that he adopted his nickname “Molly”, given to him by fellow Go-Set contributor Stan Rofe. Known as the “Peter Pan of Pop”, Meldrum went on to champion both local and global artists alike, helping to boost major acts like AC/DC and Russell Morris, and also bringing international icons like Elton John and Madonna to Australian television.



In 1974, he helped develop Countdown, working as a talent coordinator, interviewer and presenter on the show. His famous catchphrase “do yourself a favour” went on to become a touchpoint in Australian pop-cultural history. Related Article 'Supposedly I'm an icon … I don't like that': Molly Meldrum Shortly after Countdown ended, Meldrum joined Hey, Hey It’s Saturday, hosting the popular music and entertainment segment Molly’s Melodrama. He also hosted the Australian leg of Live Aid (Oz for Africa ) in 1985. The St Kilda Saints, the AFL team Meldrum famously supported, paid tribute to the music legend on Instagram, saying the team’s thoughts are with his family and others close to him. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of Australian music legend and lifelong Sainter, Molly Meldrum,” the team said. “An iconic and passionate supporter of our football club, Molly changed and brightened the lives of so many across a storied career.”



Australian pop group Human Nature also honoured Meldrum, who championed them during their rise in the ’90s. Meldrum was inducted to the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014. Getty “Very sad to hear of the passing of the legendary Molly Meldrum,” the group wrote on Facebook. “He was such a huge presence in the Australian music industry and was a great friend and supporter of so many up-and-coming bands and artists – ourselves included. Thanks for everything Molly. Rest easy.” Meldrum had lived with an acquired brain injury, the result of a fall from the roof of a pool house at his home in 2011 that left him in an induced coma for weeks. Often seen wearing a Stetson hat, Meldrum was practically impossible to miss.



He was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1986, and was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame in 2014. More to come The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Two teens charged over CBD stabbing death as mayor fast-tracks mental health crisis talks James Costa November 23, 2026 — 7:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Two teenagers have been charged over the fatal stabbing of a 21-year-old man in Melbourne’s CBD on Saturday night, just hours after another stabbing a few blocks away. Police said a 21-year-old Narre Warren man was killed on La Trobe Street near Elizabeth Street about 8.40pm on Saturday in a knife attack. Emergency services were called to the scene and took the man to hospital, where he died a short time later. Police set up a large cordon around the La Trobe Street stabbing crime scene at the weekend. Luis Enrique Ascui On Monday morning, a 17-year-old boy from the Maroondah area and an 18-year-old Mooroolbark man were charged with affray. They will face court later on Monday. Police said three other teenagers, aged between 17 and 19, who were arrested on Saturday and Sunday, were released pending further enquiries. Police said the investigation was ongoing.



Related Article Crime ‘Terrible to witness’: Man killed in second CBD stabbing attack “It would have been terrible for members of the public to witness, and we have a significant number of witnesses for this event,” Victoria Police Superintendent Laura McCarthy said at a press conference on Sunday. McCarthy said that police would investigate whether the attack was gang-related. In an earlier knife attack on Saturday, a 24-year-old man suffered non-life-threatening injuries after he was stabbed once in the chest about 2.30pm outside the H&M store, near the corner of Bourke and Elizabeth streets. McCarthy said it was believed the incident occurred after the man had failed to comply with the demands of the alleged attacker to hand over his phone.



A 31-year-old man of no fixed address was charged on Sunday evening with attempted armed robbery, intentionally causing serious injury and intentionally causing injury in relation to the incident. He will appear before Melbourne Magistrates’ Court later on Monday. Blood could be seen on the steps of the GPO building on Elizabeth Street. Chris Hopkins Police have also arrested a 51-year-old Gowanbrae man over a third stabbing on Saturday night in Melbourne’s north, outside a fast-food restaurant. A 33-year-old man suffered stab wounds about 8.40pm following an altercation with another man and two women on Pascoe Vale Road in Broadmeadows.



It is believed the parties were known to each other. Lord Mayor Nick Reece told 774 on Monday morning that a planned roundtable on mental health would be brought forward to next week. The forum would “ask some serious questions about what’s happening in our mental health system and why we are seeing incidents around our city where people with acute mental health issues who are on the streets appear to be a common denominator in some recent crimes,” Reece said. “I’ve been having conversations with people in the mental health sector [and am] trying to move reasonably quickly on this because we’ve just been shocked, and we think what’s happening at the moment is completely unacceptable.” Reece said people would notice an uptick in “visible safety presence around the city”, including community safety officers and police patrols.



Related Article Crime Man critical after random stabbing attack in Bourke Street Mall Premier Ben Carroll condemned the attacks on Sunday, and pointed to government funding for the Salvation Army services and Flinders Street Health aimed at preventing crime. “I want to make sure that every Victorian knows that I’m sickened by these crimes, and I’ll do everything I can in my power to prevent them,” he said. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the death of the young man was “a stain on this great state”. “We can have a team committed to ending the crime crisis in this state, to investing in Victoria Police, in strengthening our bail laws and our sentencing laws this side of Christmas,” she said.



Related Article Crime Man accused of delivery driver murder exposes himself to court Reece told 3AW on Sunday that the number of random stabbing attacks within the CBD over the past 12 months was “a big, big concern”. Earlier this month, food delivery rider Feng Jianming, 47, was killed in the CBD after he and another rider were allegedly stabbed by a man they caught tampering with their bikes. Roberto Urbano, 51, was arrested in Footscray over that stabbing and has been charged with murder. In August, a 27-year-old man was charged after he allegedly assaulted a child and stabbed the boy’s mother with a pair of scissors in the CBD outside Victoria Police headquarters.



McCarthy said she believed the city was safe, but understood community concern. With Alexander Darling, Eleanor Campbell and Shelby Brooks Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Second fire ants nest discovered in Sydney may have been there for a year
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWBiosecurity Second fire ants nest discovered in Sydney may have been there for a year Jack Gramenz Updated November 23, 2026 — 7:13am ,first published 6:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A nest of red imported fire ants, discovered more than six kilometres from a site where the invasive insects were first detected in Sydney, may have been there for around 12 months before being destroyed over the weekend. The nest at Auburn in Sydney’s west is outside the current biosecurity control zone declared at Enfield after ants were found at that suburb’s Intermodal Logistics Centre in September. Fire ants are one of the worst invasive species to reach Australia. Invasive Species Council The ants have been destroyed and samples collected as an investigation begins into their source. Experts are suggesting the nest could be around 12 months old, the NSW government said. NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty thanked a member of the public who reported the nest.



“Human movement of materials is the primary way fire ants spread, which is why we’re asking everyone to stay alert and report anything suspicious,” she said on Monday. How the ants reached the Auburn site is one part of the investigation. Whether they are from a different infestation or another source than those found at Enfield is also being examined. Related Article Updated

Environmental threats Invasive deadly red fire ants found in Sydney’s inner west Biosecurity staff have started surveillance at Auburn with detection dogs planned to be on site as soon as possible. A biosecurity control order is being developed. An order covering the Enfield zone involves surveillance within 500 metres of the discovered infestation and targeted surveillance in a two-kilometre radius. Within that zone, there have been 729 reported cases and 120 sites have been inspected by detection dogs.



The find at Auburn was a serious discovery and demonstrated the importance of public surveillance and reporting, Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough said. “If this nest’s been there [around] 12 months, it suggests there’s a good chance it’s spread into the surrounding area,” he said. The discovery in an industrial cul-de-sac home to a number of importing businesses suggested it was most likely a separate import of fire ants from overseas, Gough said. He called for a $1.15 billion commitment to combat fire ants ahead of the current national eradication program’s funding expiring in June. “This highlights just how serious this is and how important it is that all governments commit to that funding,” Gough said.



Fire ants, first detected in Queensland in 2001, are one of the worst invasive species to reach Australia according to the federal government. A fire ants mound in a paddock south of Brisbane in 2024. Dan Peled Previous detections in NSW include at South Murwillumbah near the Queensland border in November 2023, at Wardell in the Northern Rivers in January 2024, and at Tweed Heads South in July 2025. The ants, native to South America, can inflict painful bites triggering a burning sensation for up to an hour. They can potentially kill pets, native wildlife, and people sensitive to insect bites. Red imported fire ant nests appear as small mounds of dirt with no obvious exit holes.



Suspected sightings should be reported on 1800 680 244 or via an online form. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Russian warship goes up in flames at Libyan port in suspected Ukraine sea drone attack
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war Russian warship goes up in flames at Libyan port in suspected Ukraine sea drone attack David Crowe November 23, 2026 — 6:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: A Russian warship has been engulfed in flames in a suspected drone strike by Ukrainian forces off the coast of Libya, setting off a series of explosions from its ammunition stores. The attack appeared to mark another widening in the Ukraine war after a Russian tanker was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, forcing its crew to abandon the vessel. Loading The display of Ukraine’s apparent ability to strike far beyond their own territory comes as another wave of Russian strikes hit civilian targets in Kyiv – killing at least three people at an apartment building in the capital – and other cities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned again of a shortage of Patriot interceptors that could shoot down Russian missiles and declared it was “difficult to understand” why the US had delayed the air defence supplies.



His comment came hours after US President Donald Trump posted a photograph on social media showing himself shaking hands with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin beneath a message saying: “My Friend”. In the Baltic, the Finnish government named Ukraine as the likely source of a Saturday drone strike against the Sparta II, a cargo vessel owned by Russian entities that was carrying containers to the Russian port city of Kaliningrad. US President Donal Trump shared this image of himself with Russian President Vladimir Putin on TruthSocial.. TruthSocial In the Mediterranean, officials in the military regime that governs eastern Libya told the Associated Press that Ukraine was responsible for the drone strike against the Merkury, a Russian corvette that was refuelling in Benghazi. The officials said they believed Ukrainian forces launched several sea drones from a base in western Libya and that two hit the warship in Benghazi while others were intercepted.



The strike severely damaged the Merkury and set off a fire at the port, which is controlled by the Libyan National Army, the breakaway regime that has a co-operation agreement with Russia. In this photo provided by Vantor, the capsized Russian navy corvette Merkury is seen following a suspected drone strike, at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, on Sunday. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP While western Libya is ruled by a government in Tripoli that is recognised by the United Nations, the east and south of the country is controlled by the Libyan National Army. Social media posts from Ukrainian accounts on X appeared to show the Merkury being hit before dawn on Sunday (Sunday afternoon, AEDT). The initial attack was followed by a series of blasts, suspected to be the explosion of ammunition stores. Images posted by Ukrainian and other accounts later showed the Merkury submerged in the Benghazi harbour, a significant military victory given the warship was a relatively new member of the Russian fleet, launched in 2023.



At least one Ukrainian sea drone also appeared to hit a Russian cargo ship at sea off the coast of Benghazi during daylight hours on Sunday, with videos showing flames erupting from the ship. Ukrainian posts named the cargo ship as the Ascalon, which is the subject of sanctions for carrying military supplies to Russian ports. Russian convoys have been observed sailing from Kaliningrad to Libya in recent months to support the regime in eastern Libya and possibly provide military supplies to Russian military units that operate in northern Africa in the wake of the collapse of the Wagner Group mercenary corps. The Russian cargo ships, escorted by a warship, have been seen unloading at Tobruk, the port near Benghazi. There was no immediate statement from the Ukrainian government or its defence officials about the attacks.



In this photo released by the Finnish Border Guard, rescuers’ ships try to extinguish a fire in the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Sunday. Lehtikuva/Finnish Border Guard via AP Zelensky said on Sunday that Russian forces had launched 2700 attack drones, about 1460 glide bombs and 165 missiles against Ukraine over the previous week. A Russian drone strike on Kyiv on Sunday killed at least three people and injured four others at a five-storey apartment building in the capital. In the southern city of Odesa on Sunday, a Russian strike on the electricity grid put more strain on essential services and heating as winter approaches.



Related Article China relations ‘End your war, end it now’: Albanese gives Putin a serve at APEC Zelensky said in a Telegram post that the US should approve the transfer of Patriot interceptors that were being funded by a NATO initiative known as PURL, which stands for Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List. Many countries, including Australia, have contributed to PURL over recent years. The missile interceptors are paid for by European allies, not American taxpayers. “Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of anti-ballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelensky said in his Telegram post. “We need to strengthen our defences.” Trump has spoken in the past about allowing more Patriot missiles to be sent to Ukraine, and has also talked of approving an agreement for Ukraine to manufacture the interceptors, but the supplies have slowed. Zelensky has warned of delays to Patriot supplies since October, but the slowdown is yet to be resolved.



Trump received pointed criticism for describing Putin as his friend during their meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen last week, ahead of his social media post on Sunday saying the same thing. Firefighters work after a Russian attack in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, on Sunday. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky Residents stand near a car damaged in the Russian attack in Dymer. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky Zelensky told CNN it was up to the American president to decide how to describe Putin, but he added: “For us, he is an enemy. For us, he’s a killer.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted on X last Thursday: “God, protect us from such friends.” The following day, he posted a photograph of himself with Zelensky and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, adding: “True friendship.”



The leader of the Democrats in the US Senate, Chuck Schumer, responded by saying Putin had abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine and detained Americans wrongfully. “Donald Trump considers him a friend. Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer posted. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.” The Democrats will have a majority in the Senate from early January, when the chamber is expected to sit with its new members after the midterm elections this month. NSW Premier Chris Minns has abandoned his Monday morning press conference after a Greens candidate crashed the event to yell at the premier about the war in Gaza and his captain’s picks candidate announcements.

Shane Bazzi, who is No.4 on the Greens upper house ticket, stood outside the East Hills Medical Centre where the premier and several senior ministers were scheduled to speak about ADHD reforms.

Bazzi was not let into the press conference however his yelling drowned out Minns as he attempted to speak.

“Shame on you Chris Minns, shame,” Bazzi shouted.
